title: Drama study: The Proposal
body:
Objectives: identify the setting, characters, conflict and stage directions; connect comic action to a theme.
Selected substitute: Anton Chekhov, The Proposal, in Plays, Second Series, translated by Julius West. The complete play is supplied below and linked in the references; the lesson selects this work explicitly and does not pretend it is the unidentified school-prescribed play.
Teaching synopsis: Lomov visits Chubukov intending to propose marriage to Natalya. Instead of completing the proposal calmly, he and Natalya quarrel about land and later about their dogs. Chubukov becomes involved. Even the agreement to marry does not remove their readiness to argue. The conflict between the purpose of the visit and the repeated quarrels creates comedy and invites discussion of pride and social expectations.
Teaching: Drama presents action through dialogue and performance. Stage directions describe actions or delivery; they are not words every actor should speak aloud. Setting includes place and circumstances. Characterisation can be inferred from repeated behaviour, but a claim about a character needs evidence from the play.
Study sequence: session 1 read the cast, opening and land dispute; session 2 read the return, dog dispute and ending; session 3 rehearse a short exchange, explain a direction and compare the outcome with the original purpose of the visit. Read insults as features of the characters, not acceptable classroom behaviour.
Questions: Where does the play take place? Why does Lomov visit? How does the land dispute delay his purpose? Give one action showing pride. Does the ending resolve every disagreement?
Answers: Chubukov's country-house drawing-room; to propose marriage; the characters turn to competing ownership claims; accept a supported example of insisting on superiority or refusing to yield; no, agreement to marry coexists with further argument. Mark accurate detail 4, evidence 4, interpretation 4.
Revision task: compare one theme with The Gift of the Magi. Explain one difference between narrative prose and a dramatic script. Answers should discuss how each work presents action and use an example, not claim all prose or all drama has identical themes.

COMPLETE READING TEXT — Anton Chekhov, The Proposal; translated by Julius West
THE PROPOSAL


CHARACTERS

     STEPAN STEPANOVITCH CHUBUKOV, a landowner
     NATALYA STEPANOVNA, his daughter, twenty-five years old
     IVAN VASSILEVITCH LOMOV, a neighbour of Chubukov, a large and
     hearty, but very suspicious landowner

The scene is laid at CHUBUKOV’s country-house


A drawing-room in CHUBUKOV’S house.

[LOMOV enters, wearing a dress-jacket and white gloves. CHUBUKOV rises
to meet him.]

CHUBUKOV. My dear fellow, whom do I see! Ivan Vassilevitch! I am
extremely glad! [Squeezes his hand] Now this is a surprise, my
darling... How are you?

LOMOV. Thank you. And how may you be getting on?

CHUBUKOV. We just get along somehow, my angel, to your prayers, and
so on. Sit down, please do.... Now, you know, you shouldn’t forget all
about your neighbours, my darling. My dear fellow, why are you so formal
in your get-up? Evening dress, gloves, and so on. Can you be going
anywhere, my treasure?

LOMOV. No, I’ve come only to see you, honoured Stepan Stepanovitch.

CHUBUKOV. Then why are you in evening dress, my precious? As if you’re
paying a New Year’s Eve visit!

LOMOV. Well, you see, it’s like this. [Takes his arm] I’ve come to you,
honoured Stepan Stepanovitch, to trouble you with a request. Not once or
twice have I already had the privilege of applying to you for help, and
you have always, so to speak... I must ask your pardon, I am getting
excited. I shall drink some water, honoured Stepan Stepanovitch.
[Drinks.]

CHUBUKOV. [Aside] He’s come to borrow money! Shan’t give him any!
[Aloud] What is it, my beauty?

LOMOV. You see, Honour Stepanitch... I beg pardon, Stepan Honouritch...
I mean, I’m awfully excited, as you will please notice.... In short, you
alone can help me, though I don’t deserve it, of course... and haven’t
any right to count on your assistance....

CHUBUKOV. Oh, don’t go round and round it, darling! Spit it out! Well?

LOMOV. One moment... this very minute. The fact is, I’ve come to ask the
hand of your daughter, Natalya Stepanovna, in marriage.

CHUBUKOV. [Joyfully] By Jove! Ivan Vassilevitch! Say it again--I didn’t
hear it all!

LOMOV. I have the honour to ask...

CHUBUKOV. [Interrupting] My dear fellow... I’m so glad, and so on....
Yes, indeed, and all that sort of thing. [Embraces and kisses LOMOV]
I’ve been hoping for it for a long time. It’s been my continual desire.
[Sheds a tear] And I’ve always loved you, my angel, as if you were my
own son. May God give you both His help and His love and so on, and I
did so much hope... What am I behaving in this idiotic way for? I’m off
my balance with joy, absolutely off my balance! Oh, with all my soul...
I’ll go and call Natasha, and all that.

LOMOV. [Greatly moved] Honoured Stepan Stepanovitch, do you think I may
count on her consent?

CHUBUKOV. Why, of course, my darling, and... as if she won’t consent!
She’s in love; egad, she’s like a love-sick cat, and so on.... Shan’t be
long! [Exit.]

LOMOV. It’s cold... I’m trembling all over, just as if I’d got an
examination before me. The great thing is, I must have my mind made up.
If I give myself time to think, to hesitate, to talk a lot, to look for
an ideal, or for real love, then I’ll never get married.... Brr!... It’s
cold! Natalya Stepanovna is an excellent housekeeper, not bad-looking,
well-educated.... What more do I want? But I’m getting a noise in
my ears from excitement. [Drinks] And it’s impossible for me not to
marry.... In the first place, I’m already 35--a critical age, so to
speak. In the second place, I ought to lead a quiet and regular life....
I suffer from palpitations, I’m excitable and always getting awfully
upset.... At this very moment my lips are trembling, and there’s a
twitch in my right eyebrow.... But the very worst of all is the way
I sleep. I no sooner get into bed and begin to go off when suddenly
something in my left side--gives a pull, and I can feel it in my
shoulder and head.... I jump up like a lunatic, walk about a bit, and
lie down again, but as soon as I begin to get off to sleep there’s
another pull! And this may happen twenty times....

[NATALYA STEPANOVNA comes in.]

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Well, there! It’s you, and papa said, “Go; there’s a
merchant come for his goods.” How do you do, Ivan Vassilevitch!

LOMOV. How do you do, honoured Natalya Stepanovna?

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. You must excuse my apron and négligé... we’re
shelling peas for drying. Why haven’t you been here for such a long
time? Sit down. [They seat themselves] Won’t you have some lunch?

LOMOV. No, thank you, I’ve had some already.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Then smoke.... Here are the matches.... The weather
is splendid now, but yesterday it was so wet that the workmen didn’t
do anything all day. How much hay have you stacked? Just think, I felt
greedy and had a whole field cut, and now I’m not at all pleased about
it because I’m afraid my hay may rot. I ought to have waited a bit. But
what’s this? Why, you’re in evening dress! Well, I never! Are you going
to a ball, or what?--though I must say you look better. Tell me, why are
you got up like that?

LOMOV. [Excited] You see, honoured Natalya Stepanovna... the fact is,
I’ve made up my mind to ask you to hear me out.... Of course you’ll be
surprised and perhaps even angry, but a... [Aside] It’s awfully cold!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. What’s the matter? [Pause] Well?

LOMOV. I shall try to be brief. You must know, honoured Natalya
Stepanovna, that I have long, since my childhood, in fact, had the
privilege of knowing your family. My late aunt and her husband, from
whom, as you know, I inherited my land, always had the greatest respect
for your father and your late mother. The Lomovs and the Chubukovs
have always had the most friendly, and I might almost say the most
affectionate, regard for each other. And, as you know, my land is a near
neighbour of yours. You will remember that my Oxen Meadows touch your
birchwoods.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Excuse my interrupting you. You say, “my Oxen
Meadows....” But are they yours?

LOMOV. Yes, mine.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. What are you talking about? Oxen Meadows are ours,
not yours!

LOMOV. No, mine, honoured Natalya Stepanovna.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Well, I never knew that before. How do you make that
out?

LOMOV. How? I’m speaking of those Oxen Meadows which are wedged in
between your birchwoods and the Burnt Marsh.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Yes, yes.... They’re ours.

LOMOV. No, you’re mistaken, honoured Natalya Stepanovna, they’re mine.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Just think, Ivan Vassilevitch! How long have they
been yours?

LOMOV. How long? As long as I can remember.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Really, you won’t get me to believe that!

LOMOV. But you can see from the documents, honoured Natalya Stepanovna.
Oxen Meadows, it’s true, were once the subject of dispute, but now
everybody knows that they are mine. There’s nothing to argue about.
You see, my aunt’s grandmother gave the free use of these Meadows in
perpetuity to the peasants of your father’s grandfather, in return for
which they were to make bricks for her. The peasants belonging to your
father’s grandfather had the free use of the Meadows for forty years,
and had got into the habit of regarding them as their own, when it
happened that...

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. No, it isn’t at all like that! Both my grandfather
and great-grandfather reckoned that their land extended to Burnt
Marsh--which means that Oxen Meadows were ours. I don’t see what there
is to argue about. It’s simply silly!

LOMOV. I’ll show you the documents, Natalya Stepanovna!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. No, you’re simply joking, or making fun of me....
What a surprise! We’ve had the land for nearly three hundred years, and
then we’re suddenly told that it isn’t ours! Ivan Vassilevitch, I can
hardly believe my own ears.... These Meadows aren’t worth much to me.
They only come to five dessiatins [Note: 13.5 acres], and are worth
perhaps 300 roubles [Note: £30.], but I can’t stand unfairness. Say what
you will, but I can’t stand unfairness.

LOMOV. Hear me out, I implore you! The peasants of your father’s
grandfather, as I have already had the honour of explaining to you, used
to bake bricks for my aunt’s grandmother. Now my aunt’s grandmother,
wishing to make them a pleasant...

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. I can’t make head or tail of all this about aunts
and grandfathers and grandmothers! The Meadows are ours, and that’s all.

LOMOV. Mine.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Ours! You can go on proving it for two days on end,
you can go and put on fifteen dress-jackets, but I tell you they’re
ours, ours, ours! I don’t want anything of yours and I don’t want to
give up anything of mine. So there!

LOMOV. Natalya Ivanovna, I don’t want the Meadows, but I am acting on
principle. If you like, I’ll make you a present of them.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. I can make you a present of them myself, because
they’re mine! Your behaviour, Ivan Vassilevitch, is strange, to say the
least! Up to this we have always thought of you as a good neighbour, a
friend: last year we lent you our threshing-machine, although on that
account we had to put off our own threshing till November, but you
behave to us as if we were gipsies. Giving me my own land, indeed!
No, really, that’s not at all neighbourly! In my opinion, it’s even
impudent, if you want to know....

LOMOV. Then you make out that I’m a land-grabber? Madam, never in my
life have I grabbed anybody else’s land, and I shan’t allow anybody to
accuse me of having done so.... [Quickly steps to the carafe and drinks
more water] Oxen Meadows are mine!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. It’s not true, they’re ours!

LOMOV. Mine!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. It’s not true! I’ll prove it! I’ll send my mowers
out to the Meadows this very day!

LOMOV. What?

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. My mowers will be there this very day!

LOMOV. I’ll give it to them in the neck!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. You dare!

LOMOV. [Clutches at his heart] Oxen Meadows are mine! You understand?
Mine!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Please don’t shout! You can shout yourself hoarse in
your own house, but here I must ask you to restrain yourself!

LOMOV. If it wasn’t, madam, for this awful, excruciating palpitation,
if my whole inside wasn’t upset, I’d talk to you in a different way!
[Yells] Oxen Meadows are mine!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Ours!

LOMOV. Mine!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Ours!

LOMOV. Mine!

[Enter CHUBUKOV.]

CHUBUKOV. What’s the matter? What are you shouting at?

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Papa, please tell to this gentleman who owns Oxen
Meadows, we or he?

CHUBUKOV. [To LOMOV] Darling, the Meadows are ours!

LOMOV. But, please, Stepan Stepanitch, how can they be yours? Do be a
reasonable man! My aunt’s grandmother gave the Meadows for the temporary
and free use of your grandfather’s peasants. The peasants used the land
for forty years and got as accustomed to it as if it was their own, when
it happened that...

CHUBUKOV. Excuse me, my precious.... You forget just this, that the
peasants didn’t pay your grandmother and all that, because the Meadows
were in dispute, and so on. And now everybody knows that they’re ours.
It means that you haven’t seen the plan.

LOMOV. I’ll prove to you that they’re mine!

CHUBUKOV. You won’t prove it, my darling.

LOMOV. I shall!

CHUBUKOV. Dear one, why yell like that? You won’t prove anything just
by yelling. I don’t want anything of yours, and don’t intend to give up
what I have. Why should I? And you know, my beloved, that if you propose
to go on arguing about it, I’d much sooner give up the meadows to the
peasants than to you. There!

LOMOV. I don’t understand! How have you the right to give away somebody
else’s property?

CHUBUKOV. You may take it that I know whether I have the right or not.
Because, young man, I’m not used to being spoken to in that tone of
voice, and so on: I, young man, am twice your age, and ask you to speak
to me without agitating yourself, and all that.

LOMOV. No, you just think I’m a fool and want to have me on! You call
my land yours, and then you want me to talk to you calmly and politely!
Good neighbours don’t behave like that, Stepan Stepanitch! You’re not a
neighbour, you’re a grabber!

CHUBUKOV. What’s that? What did you say?

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Papa, send the mowers out to the Meadows at once!

CHUBUKOV. What did you say, sir?

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Oxen Meadows are ours, and I shan’t give them up,
shan’t give them up, shan’t give them up!

LOMOV. We’ll see! I’ll have the matter taken to court, and then I’ll
show you!

CHUBUKOV. To court? You can take it to court, and all that! You can! I
know you; you’re just on the look-out for a chance to go to court, and
all that.... You pettifogger! All your people were like that! All of
them!

LOMOV. Never mind about my people! The Lomovs have all been honourable
people, and not one has ever been tried for embezzlement, like your
grandfather!

CHUBUKOV. You Lomovs have had lunacy in your family, all of you!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. All, all, all!

CHUBUKOV. Your grandfather was a drunkard, and your younger aunt,
Nastasya Mihailovna, ran away with an architect, and so on.

LOMOV. And your mother was hump-backed. [Clutches at his heart]
Something pulling in my side.... My head.... Help! Water!

CHUBUKOV. Your father was a guzzling gambler!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. And there haven’t been many backbiters to equal your
aunt!

LOMOV. My left foot has gone to sleep.... You’re an intriguer.... Oh,
my heart!... And it’s an open secret that before the last elections you
bri... I can see stars.... Where’s my hat?

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. It’s low! It’s dishonest! It’s mean!

CHUBUKOV. And you’re just a malicious, double-faced intriguer! Yes!

LOMOV. Here’s my hat.... My heart!... Which way? Where’s the door?
Oh!... I think I’m dying.... My foot’s quite numb.... [Goes to the
door.]

CHUBUKOV. [Following him] And don’t set foot in my house again!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Take it to court! We’ll see!

[LOMOV staggers out.]

CHUBUKOV. Devil take him! [Walks about in excitement.]

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. What a rascal! What trust can one have in one’s
neighbours after that!

CHUBUKOV. The villain! The scarecrow!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. The monster! First he takes our land and then he has
the impudence to abuse us.

CHUBUKOV. And that blind hen, yes, that turnip-ghost has the confounded
cheek to make a proposal, and so on! What? A proposal!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. What proposal?

CHUBUKOV. Why, he came here so as to propose to you.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. To propose? To me? Why didn’t you tell me so before?

CHUBUKOV. So he dresses up in evening clothes. The stuffed sausage! The
wizen-faced frump!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. To propose to me? Ah! [Falls into an easy-chair and
wails] Bring him back! Back! Ah! Bring him here.

CHUBUKOV. Bring whom here?

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Quick, quick! I’m ill! Fetch him! [Hysterics.]

CHUBUKOV. What’s that? What’s the matter with you? [Clutches at his
head] Oh, unhappy man that I am! I’ll shoot myself! I’ll hang myself!
We’ve done for her!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. I’m dying! Fetch him!

CHUBUKOV. Tfoo! At once. Don’t yell!

[Runs out. A pause. NATALYA STEPANOVNA wails.]

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. What have they done to me! Fetch him back! Fetch
him! [A pause.]

[CHUBUKOV runs in.]

CHUBUKOV. He’s coming, and so on, devil take him! Ouf! Talk to him
yourself; I don’t want to....

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. [Wails] Fetch him!

CHUBUKOV. [Yells] He’s coming, I tell you. Oh, what a burden, Lord,
to be the father of a grown-up daughter! I’ll cut my throat! I will,
indeed! We cursed him, abused him, drove him out, and it’s all you...
you!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. No, it was you!

CHUBUKOV. I tell you it’s not my fault. [LOMOV appears at the door] Now
you talk to him yourself [Exit.]

[LOMOV enters, exhausted.]

LOMOV. My heart’s palpitating awfully.... My foot’s gone to sleep....
There’s something keeps pulling in my side.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Forgive us, Ivan Vassilevitch, we were all a little
heated.... I remember now: Oxen Meadows really are yours.

LOMOV. My heart’s beating awfully.... My Meadows.... My eyebrows are
both twitching....

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. The Meadows are yours, yes, yours.... Do sit
down.... [They sit] We were wrong....

LOMOV. I did it on principle.... My land is worth little to me, but the
principle...

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Yes, the principle, just so.... Now let’s talk of
something else.

LOMOV. The more so as I have evidence. My aunt’s grandmother gave the
land to your father’s grandfather’s peasants...

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Yes, yes, let that pass.... [Aside] I wish I knew
how to get him started.... [Aloud] Are you going to start shooting soon?

LOMOV. I’m thinking of having a go at the blackcock, honoured Natalya
Stepanovna, after the harvest. Oh, have you heard? Just think, what a
misfortune I’ve had! My dog Guess, whom you know, has gone lame.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. What a pity! Why?

LOMOV. I don’t know.... Must have got twisted, or bitten by some other
dog.... [Sighs] My very best dog, to say nothing of the expense. I gave
Mironov 125 roubles for him.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. It was too much, Ivan Vassilevitch.

LOMOV. I think it was very cheap. He’s a first-rate dog.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Papa gave 85 roubles for his Squeezer, and Squeezer
is heaps better than Guess!

LOMOV. Squeezer better than. Guess? What an idea! [Laughs] Squeezer
better than Guess!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Of course he’s better! Of course, Squeezer is
young, he may develop a bit, but on points and pedigree he’s better than
anything that even Volchanetsky has got.

LOMOV. Excuse me, Natalya Stepanovna, but you forget that he is
overshot, and an overshot always means the dog is a bad hunter!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Overshot, is he? The first time I hear it!

LOMOV. I assure you that his lower jaw is shorter than the upper.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Have you measured?

LOMOV. Yes. He’s all right at following, of course, but if you want him
to get hold of anything...

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. In the first place, our Squeezer is a thoroughbred
animal, the son of Harness and Chisels, while there’s no getting at
the pedigree of your dog at all.... He’s old and as ugly as a worn-out
cab-horse.

LOMOV. He is old, but I wouldn’t take five Squeezers for him.... Why,
how can you?... Guess is a dog; as for Squeezer, well, it’s too funny to
argue.... Anybody you like has a dog as good as Squeezer... you may find
them under every bush almost. Twenty-five roubles would be a handsome
price to pay for him.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. There’s some demon of contradiction in you to-day,
Ivan Vassilevitch. First you pretend that the Meadows are yours; now,
that Guess is better than Squeezer. I don’t like people who don’t say
what they mean, because you know perfectly well that Squeezer is a
hundred times better than your silly Guess. Why do you want to say it
isn’t?

LOMOV. I see, Natalya Stepanovna, that you consider me either blind or a
fool. You must realize that Squeezer is overshot!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. It’s not true.

LOMOV. He is!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. It’s not true!

LOMOV. Why shout, madam?

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Why talk rot? It’s awful! It’s time your Guess was
shot, and you compare him with Squeezer!

LOMOV. Excuse me; I cannot continue this discussion: my heart is
palpitating.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. I’ve noticed that those hunters argue most who know
least.

LOMOV. Madam, please be silent.... My heart is going to pieces....
[Shouts] Shut up!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. I shan’t shut up until you acknowledge that Squeezer
is a hundred times better than your Guess!

LOMOV. A hundred times worse! Be hanged to your Squeezer! His head...
eyes... shoulder...

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. There’s no need to hang your silly Guess; he’s
half-dead already!

LOMOV. [Weeps] Shut up! My heart’s bursting!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. I shan’t shut up.

[Enter CHUBUKOV.]

CHUBUKOV. What’s the matter now?

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Papa, tell us truly, which is the better dog, our
Squeezer or his Guess.

LOMOV. Stepan Stepanovitch, I implore you to tell me just one thing: is
your Squeezer overshot or not? Yes or no?

CHUBUKOV. And suppose he is? What does it matter? He’s the best dog in
the district for all that, and so on.

LOMOV. But isn’t my Guess better? Really, now?

CHUBUKOV. Don’t excite yourself, my precious one.... Allow me.... Your
Guess certainly has his good points.... He’s pure-bred, firm on his
feet, has well-sprung ribs, and all that. But, my dear man, if you want
to know the truth, that dog has two defects: he’s old and he’s short in
the muzzle.

LOMOV. Excuse me, my heart.... Let’s take the facts.... You will
remember that on the Marusinsky hunt my Guess ran neck-and-neck with the
Count’s dog, while your Squeezer was left a whole verst behind.

CHUBUKOV. He got left behind because the Count’s whipper-in hit him with
his whip.

LOMOV. And with good reason. The dogs are running after a fox, when
Squeezer goes and starts worrying a sheep!

CHUBUKOV. It’s not true!... My dear fellow, I’m very liable to lose my
temper, and so, just because of that, let’s stop arguing. You started
because everybody is always jealous of everybody else’s dogs. Yes, we’re
all like that! You too, sir, aren’t blameless! You no sooner notice that
some dog is better than your Guess than you begin with this, that... and
the other... and all that.... I remember everything!

LOMOV. I remember too!

CHUBUKOV. [Teasing him] I remember, too.... What do you remember?

LOMOV. My heart... my foot’s gone to sleep.... I can’t...

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. [Teasing] My heart.... What sort of a hunter are
you? You ought to go and lie on the kitchen oven and catch blackbeetles,
not go after foxes! My heart!

CHUBUKOV. Yes really, what sort of a hunter are you, anyway? You ought
to sit at home with your palpitations, and not go tracking animals. You
could go hunting, but you only go to argue with people and interfere
with their dogs and so on. Let’s change the subject in case I lose my
temper. You’re not a hunter at all, anyway!

LOMOV. And are you a hunter? You only go hunting to get in with the
Count and to intrigue.... Oh, my heart!... You’re an intriguer!

CHUBUKOV. What? I an intriguer? [Shouts] Shut up!

LOMOV. Intriguer!

CHUBUKOV. Boy! Pup!

LOMOV. Old rat! Jesuit!

CHUBUKOV. Shut up or I’ll shoot you like a partridge! You fool!

LOMOV. Everybody knows that--oh my heart!--your late wife used to beat
you.... My feet... temples... sparks.... I fall, I fall!

CHUBUKOV. And you’re under the slipper of your housekeeper!

LOMOV. There, there, there... my heart’s burst! My shoulder’s come
off.... Where is my shoulder? I die. [Falls into an armchair] A doctor!
[Faints.]

CHUBUKOV. Boy! Milksop! Fool! I’m sick! [Drinks water] Sick!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. What sort of a hunter are you? You can’t even sit on
a horse! [To her father] Papa, what’s the matter with him? Papa! Look,
papa! [Screams] Ivan Vassilevitch! He’s dead!

CHUBUKOV. I’m sick!... I can’t breathe!... Air!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. He’s dead. [Pulls LOMOV’S sleeve] Ivan Vassilevitch!
Ivan Vassilevitch! What have you done to me? He’s dead. [Falls into an
armchair] A doctor, a doctor! [Hysterics.]

CHUBUKOV. Oh!... What is it? What’s the matter?

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. [Wails] He’s dead... dead!

CHUBUKOV. Who’s dead? [Looks at LOMOV] So he is! My word! Water! A
doctor! [Lifts a tumbler to LOMOV’S mouth] Drink this!... No, he doesn’t
drink.... It means he’s dead, and all that.... I’m the most unhappy of
men! Why don’t I put a bullet into my brain? Why haven’t I cut my throat
yet? What am I waiting for? Give me a knife! Give me a pistol! [LOMOV
moves] He seems to be coming round.... Drink some water! That’s
right....

LOMOV. I see stars... mist.... Where am I?

CHUBUKOV. Hurry up and get married and--well, to the devil with you!
She’s willing! [He puts LOMOV’S hand into his daughter’s] She’s willing
and all that. I give you my blessing and so on. Only leave me in peace!

LOMOV. [Getting up] Eh? What? To whom?

CHUBUKOV. She’s willing! Well? Kiss and be damned to you!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. [Wails] He’s alive... Yes, yes, I’m willing....

CHUBUKOV. Kiss each other!

LOMOV. Eh? Kiss whom? [They kiss] Very nice, too. Excuse me, what’s
it all about? Oh, now I understand... my heart... stars... I’m happy.
Natalya Stepanovna.... [Kisses her hand] My foot’s gone to sleep....

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. I... I’m happy too....

CHUBUKOV. What a weight off my shoulders.... Ouf!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. But... still you will admit now that Guess is worse
than Squeezer.

LOMOV. Better!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Worse!

CHUBUKOV. Well, that’s a way to start your family bliss! Have some
champagne!

LOMOV. He’s better!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Worse! worse! worse!

CHUBUKOV. [Trying to shout her down] Champagne! Champagne!

Curtain.

title: Expository reading: understanding drug addiction
body:
Objectives: identify an explanatory text's main idea, distinguish explanation from stigma, and organise an evidence-based paragraph.
Original reading based on NIDA's educational information:
Drug addiction involves difficulty controlling drug use despite harmful consequences. It affects brain function and behaviour and can require continuing treatment and support. It is not explained simply by calling a person weak or bad. Young people's brains are still developing, so avoiding harmful substance use and seeking trustworthy help matter. People can recover. A person who is worried about substance use should speak with a trusted adult and a qualified health professional rather than rely on classmates to diagnose or treat the problem. Medicines should be used only as directed by an appropriate health professional. Respectful support and accurate information are more useful than humiliation.
Questions: (1) What is the main idea? (2) Why is 'just be stronger' an inadequate explanation? (3) Who should advise on treatment? (4) Find a sentence showing that recovery is possible. (5) What makes this exposition rather than a fictional narrative?
Answers: Addiction is a health problem needing accurate understanding and support; it involves changes in brain function/behaviour and difficulty controlling use; a qualified health professional; the sentence stating that people can recover; it explains an issue rather than telling a sequence about invented characters. Award 2 marks each.
Writing: prepare a 150-word explanation entitled 'Why accurate information matters'. Use an introduction, two developed points and a conclusion. Do not invent treatment instructions, statistics or claims about a classmate. Mark focus 3, organisation 3, supported explanation 4, language 3 and respectful accuracy 2. This is an English explanation exercise, not a medical diagnosis or treatment plan.

title: Àkàyé ọlọ́rọ̀ geere: Ìwé tí ó sọnù
body:
Objectives: read a complete Yoruba prose passage, retrieve details, infer a character's reason, and support a moral interpretation with evidence.
Original classroom story — Ìwé tí ó sọnù:
Ní ọjọ́ Ajé, Bísí lọ sí ilé ìkàwé láti dá ìwé tí ó yá padà. Nígbà tí ó ṣí àpò rẹ̀, kò rí ìwé náà. Ó bẹ̀rù pé òun ti sọ ọ́ nù. Adé, ọ̀rẹ́ rẹ̀, ní kí wọ́n kọ́kọ́ wá a ní kíláàsì. Wọ́n wo orí tábìlì àti abẹ́ àga, ṣùgbọ́n wọn kò rí i. Lẹ́yìn náà, Bísí rántí pé òun fi ìwé náà sínú àpótí nílé kí òjò má bà á jẹ́. Ó sọ fún olùkọ́ ohun tí ó ṣẹlẹ̀. Ní ọjọ́ kejì, ó mú ìwé náà wá, ó sì dá a padà. Olùkọ́ dúpẹ́ lọ́wọ́ rẹ̀ fún sísọ òtítọ́. Bísí pinnu pé òun yóò máa ṣàyẹ̀wò àpò òun kí òun tó kúrò nílé.
Ìbéèrè / Questions: (1) Níbo ni Bísí fẹ́ lọ? (2) Kí ló mú kí ó bẹ̀rù? (3) Níbo ni ìwé náà wà? (4) Kí nìdí tí ó fi ìwé náà síbẹ̀? (5) Kí ni a lè kọ́ nínú ìtàn yìí? (6) Ṣe àkótán ìtàn náà ní gbólóhùn méjì.
Ìdáhùn / Answers: Ilé ìkàwé; kò rí ìwé nínú àpò; nínú àpótí nílé; kí òjò má bà á jẹ́; accept honesty/care supported by telling the teacher or checking the bag; summary should retain the missing-book problem and its resolution.
Teaching: Separate a detail stated in the passage from an inference. The teacher models reading with appropriate tones; pupils reread and explain the problem, search and outcome. This is a complete short teaching story, not a recovered prescribed novel.
Assessment: 2 marks each for questions 1–4; 2 for an evidence-based lesson; 4 for a coherent two-sentence summary. Second-Term extension: retell from Adé's viewpoint without changing where the book was found.

title: Ìkọ̀wé àgbọ́sọ: a fixed dictation and correction task
body:
Objectives: listen carefully, write a fixed Yoruba passage, and correct spelling, tone marks and punctuation against the supplied key.
Teacher reading script and answer key:
Bísí lọ sí ilé ìkàwé. Ó fẹ́ dá ìwé tí ó yá padà. Adé ràn án lọ́wọ́ láti wá ìwé náà. Ní ọjọ́ kejì, Bísí mú ìwé náà wá. Olùkọ́ dúpẹ́ lọ́wọ́ rẹ̀ fún sísọ òtítọ́.
Procedure: The teacher reads the complete script once at a natural pace while pupils listen. Read one sentence at a time, repeating each sentence once, with writing time between them. Read the whole script again for checking. Do not show the script during the dictation. Pupils then compare their work with the exact key and correct errors in a different colour.
Practice: group corrections under missing word, spelling, tone mark, underdot, capital letter and punctuation. Explain how an omitted mark can affect a Yoruba word. Read the corrected passage aloud with the teacher's model.
Assessment: score each sentence out of four: two for all words in their intended order, one for correct diacritics, and one for capitals and punctuation. A missing word loses only the appropriate word-accuracy credit; avoid counting it again as several unrelated errors. Total 20. Repeat the weakest sentence after feedback rather than rewarding speed alone.
This is an original fixed script based on the companion classroom story. It supplies the missing dictation exercise; it is not a claim that the school source contained these sentences. An app may show the key after practice, but a text-only quiz does not assess listening.

title: Àkàyé ewì: Ìwé mi
body:
Objectives: read a complete short Yoruba poem, identify imagery and repetition, and explain a theme with evidence.
Original classroom poem — Ìwé mi:
Ìwé mi, ọ̀rẹ́ mi,
Mo ṣí ọ ní òwúrọ̀.
Ọ̀rọ̀ rẹ ń tan ìmọ́lẹ̀,
Ó ń ṣí ọ̀nà fún mi.
Mo ka, mo ronú,
Mo béèrè, mo kọ́.

Teaching: The speaker addresses a book as a friend. Light and a path are images for understanding and discovery; they do not mean that paper literally shines or makes a road. Repeated 'Mo' keeps attention on the learner's actions. A poem need not have an English-style end-rhyme scheme to communicate through rhythm, imagery and repeated structures.
Ìbéèrè / Questions: (1) Kí ni akéwì pè ní ọ̀rẹ́ rẹ̀? (2) Ṣàlàyé 'ìmọ́lẹ̀' nínú ewì yìí. (3) Kọ àwọn iṣẹ́ méjì tí olùsọ̀rọ̀ ń ṣe. (4) Kí ni àtúnwí 'Mo' ń fi hàn? (5) Kí ni kókó ewì náà?
Answers: the book; understanding rather than literal light; any two of reading, thinking, asking and learning; focus on the speaker's active participation; learning through thoughtful reading and questions. Award two marks for each supported answer.
Practice: read the poem with pauses at the line endings, then explain whether every line ending requires a full stop. Write two original Yoruba lines about a useful learning activity. Mark meaningful imagery and clear expression; do not label a newly written poem as traditional oral literature. This complete practice poem replaces an unspecified reading exercise, not an identified government-prescribed work.

title: Àrọkọ alálàyé: explaining a familiar process
body:
Objectives: explain a process in a logical order, use focused paragraphs and revise a Yoruba composition for clarity.
Teaching: Àrọkọ alálàyé explains a subject or how something works. Decide what the reader needs to understand. Introduce the subject, develop the steps or main points, and end with a relevant conclusion. Give enough detail for the explanation to be useful; do not substitute a list of unexplained headings.
Original task: Kọ àrọkọ lórí bí a ṣe ń tọ́jú ìwé ní ilé ìkàwé. Explain how books are kept in good condition and returned to the correct place. Plan: introduction to the library; handling books carefully; recording borrowing and returning books; why the routine helps other readers.
Original opening model: 'Ilé ìkàwé jẹ́ ibi tí a ti ń ka ìwé, tí a sì ti ń kọ́ ẹ̀kọ́. Ó yẹ kí a máa tọ́jú àwọn ìwé kí àwọn mìíràn lè lò wọ́n.' Continue with your own explanation rather than copying the opening repeatedly.
Practice: write 150–200 words in Yoruba. Exchange work with a partner. Ask the partner to identify one clear instruction and one step needing explanation. Rewrite that step.
Assessment /20: relevant content 6; logical sequence and paragraphs 4; developed explanation 4; Yoruba spelling and diacritics 4; relevant conclusion 2. Answers vary, but each recommendation should explain what to do and why. This covers the composition strand only; inheritance and lineage-praise objectives in the same scheme weeks require their own teaching.

title: Yoruba oral forms and origin traditions: guided cultural study
body:
Objectives: distinguish selected oral forms and discuss an origin narrative as a cultural tradition rather than scientific evidence.
Teaching summary from NOUN YOR215: Ìjálá is associated with Ògún and hunters; iwì/ẹ̀ṣà egúngún belongs to Egúngún performance; Ọya pípè is among the forms of òrìṣà praise. Performers, occasion and delivery help distinguish genres. An origin narrative discussed in the course describes Ọbàtálá descending with earth and a cock; the earth is spread over water to form land. It is presented here as one recorded tradition, not a scientific account or the only version.
Original practice: create a three-column comparison headed form, associated context and a question for further investigation. Place Ìjálá, iwì egúngún and Ọya pípè in it. Explain why naming a genre does not supply a complete performance text. Then sequence the events of the brief origin narrative and identify which part addresses the beginning of land.
Answers: hunters/Ògún, Egúngún, and praise of Ọya respectively; a genre label lacks the actual words and delivery; descent, spreading earth, formation of land. Accept respectful discussion of differing beliefs. Do not require worship or participation in a ritual.
Assessment: three correct associations 6 marks; clear sequence 3; distinction between tradition and an observed scientific explanation 3. Extension: compare a documented variant with this account, naming the source and recording differences without declaring a family's belief inferior. This lesson supplies genre recognition and one named origin account. It does not pretend to reproduce missing chant texts or every prescribed literature selection.

title: Ogún pípín: inheritance as a changing cultural practice
body:
Objectives: explain ogún pípín, distinguish property from people, and describe why a historical account is not a current legal rule.
Teaching: Ogún pípín concerns sharing possessions left by a deceased person. NOUN YOR113 discusses it as part of Yoruba social history. Family relationships and customary practices influenced distribution; practices have changed. A historical description must not be treated as a rule governing every family today. People are not property. This lesson studies cultural vocabulary and evidence, and does not decide anyone's inheritance rights.
Vocabulary: ogún — inheritance; ohun ìní — possessions/property; ìdílé — family. When describing a custom, identify the community and period rather than saying all Yoruba families act alike.
Original worked classroom example: a fictional family records six books, two stools and one radio in an inventory. The inventory describes what exists. It does not prove who owns the items or who should inherit them. A reliable account separates the list of objects, statements by relatives, and documented decisions.
Practice questions: 1. Explain ogún pípín in one sentence. 2. List the three kinds of object in the example. 3. Does counting the objects determine each person's share? Explain. 4. Rewrite 'Every Yoruba family always distributes property in the same way' as a cautious historical statement. 5. In Yoruba, write three sentences using ogún, ohun ìní and ìdílé.
Answers/assessment: 1 sharing possessions left after a death; 2 books, stools, radio; 3 no, an inventory alone establishes no entitlement; 4 accept a statement identifying variation across communities and time. Award 2 marks per response for questions 1–4. For question 5 award one mark for each meaningful sentence and one for suitable spelling/tone marking. Correct sentences rather than demanding disclosure of a learner's family circumstances.
Source locator: NOUN YOR113, section 4.2 Ogún Pípín, PDF page 37. This is a cultural-history activity, not instructions for administering an estate.

title: Ìsọmọlórúkọ: naming, family identity and changing customs
body:
Objectives: describe a naming ceremony, explain symbolic good wishes, and recognise variation between families.
Teaching summary: NOUN YOR312 explains naming as an occasion for recognising a child within a family. A chosen elder or family representative may recount family history, announce names and offer good wishes; relatives may contribute further names. Objects such as water and sweet substances can symbolise wishes for the child's life. Practices and timing vary with community, religion and historical change. A name beginning Adé does not, by itself, prove royal ancestry. Do not infer someone's religion or ancestry simply from a name.
Vocabulary: orúkọ — name; ìsọmọlórúkọ — naming ceremony; ìdílé — family. Symbolic meaning is a cultural interpretation, not a scientific claim about an object's effects.
Original classroom activity: use written object names or drawings, not a live ceremony or substances fed to a baby. Make a three-column chart: action, intended social meaning, possible variation. Suggested actions are announcing a name, recounting family history and offering good wishes. Describe each without claiming it is compulsory for every family.
Questions: 1. Give two purposes of a naming ceremony. 2. Explain the difference between a symbol and a physical effect. 3. Why should we avoid specifying one compulsory day for every family? 4. Does an Adé name prove ancestry? 5. Write a respectful six-sentence Yoruba description of an imagined ceremony, clearly identifying it as fictional.
Answers/assessment: 1 identification/welcome, family connection, expression of hopes (any two); 2 a symbol represents an idea without proving a causal effect; 3 practices vary; 4 no. Give 2 marks each for questions 1–4. For the description award 4 marks for clear sequence, 4 for accurate vocabulary and 4 for intelligible sentences and tone marks. Accept different family practices without ranking beliefs.
Source locators: NOUN YOR312, naming-ceremony discussion and section 4.5 on changes, PDF pages 14–16; naming and Adé discussion, pages 19–21.

title: Ramúramù ewúrẹ́: complete Yoruba story and evidence-based literary study
body:
Ramúramù ewúrẹ́ — Olajide Akoni; illustrator Offei Tettey Eugene. © African Storybook Initiative 2018. Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Text reproduced with attribution; illustrations are not reproduced. Original wording is retained; paragraph numbers and the teaching guide are added. This is a selected replacement, not a claim to identify the missing prescribed book.

Complete story text:
[1] Ramúramù jẹ́ ewúrẹ́ tí ó maá n kígbe gan an.

Yí ó máa pe 'mẹ̀ẹ́ẹ̀', tí àwọn ẹ̀gbẹ́ rẹ̀ bá n sùn lọ́wọ́.

[2] Ní ọjọ́ kan, ó fun ilẹ̀kùn ìbùsun rẹ̀ ní ìpá, ilẹ̀kùn ṣí! Ó subú lulẹ̀, Ó wó kè, Ó ní, "Mo bọ́!"

Ó dá lójú pé aiyé ìyanu n bẹ tí ojú rẹ ẹ̀ máa rí níta!

[3] Aláriwo, ajá kékeré oko náà, rí Ramúramù, ó kígbe, "Wúfù! Wúfù! O kò gbọ́dọ̀ lọ!" Ṣùgbọ́n Ramúramù fún un nígbò.

[4] Ramúramù sáré gun orí òkè, ó wo òfurufú. 

"Èhén èn!" ó kígbe. "Mo ti bọ́ lóòótọ́."

[5] Ó fò sókè, ó búsẹ́ẹ́rín, ó yí títí ó fi dé ìsàlẹ̀ òkè náà, ó ba fara gbá nkan, ó dún, "Gbáún!" 

Ṣaléwá màálù ló kọ lù!

[6] Ó n fi imú  túlẹ̀, ó sì bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí jẹ koríko, ṣùgbọ́n  ó tú dàànù, ó ba ojú jẹ́.

[7] Lẹ́yìn náà, ó rí àwọn adìyẹ  tó n jẹ àgbàdo, ó sì lé wọn kiri bí wọ́n n se n kígbe, "Kú, kú, kú," gbogbo iyẹ̀ wọ́n sì n tú ká.

[8] Láìpẹ́, ó tún jí iṣu lọ́dọ̀ ẹlẹ́dẹ̀, ó sì sáré gan pẹ̀lú nkan tí ó jí!

[9] Ó dé ibi tí ilẹ̀ tí tẹ́jú, pẹ̀lú òmùgọ̀ àgùntàn, ó sì rìn wọlé láti máa jẹun.

[10] Ó gbọ́ àjèjì ìfé to jẹ́ kí àgùntàn parapọ̀ láti sá lọ, ṣùgbọ́n kò ya lára; ó dùbúlẹ̀, ó sùn lọ.

[11] Ó gbọ́ ẹ̀ẹ̀rín búburú, ó tají, ó gbòórùn líle tó jáa láyà.

[12] Ramúramù sá pẹ̀lú gbogbo okun, bí ẹ̀ẹ̀rín búburú náà ṣe n tẹ̀le.

Ó sá títí ó fi dé ìbùsun rẹ̀, láti ìgbà náà, kò dá laba láti sá lọ mó.

Teaching guide: this short, accessible story is used for JSS3 analysis of sequence, character, narrative voice and the difference between explicit evidence and inference. The original publisher labels its reading level First paragraphs; the analysis tasks below extend beyond simple decoding. Ramúramù's behaviour changes between the opening and ending. A conclusion must be supported by an event in the story, not by an invented episode. Direct speech and animal sounds help create a lively narrative voice.
Questions: 1. Put these events in order: returns to the pen; escapes; takes yam; hears frightening laughter. 2. Give two actions that show disregard for other animals. 3. Compare the goat at the beginning and end, citing paragraph numbers. 4. Who produces the frightening laughter? State whether the written text identifies the speaker. 5. Identify one use of direct speech and explain its effect. 6. In Yoruba write a 100-word alternative ending; label it your own invention, then state two differences from the published ending. 7. Explain why a summary should not add an unmentioned animal as the pursuer.
Answers: 1 escapes, takes yam, hears laughter, returns; 2 ignoring the dog's warning, chasing chickens or stealing yam; 3 noisy/restless initially, unwilling to escape again at the end, supported by paragraphs 1–2 and 12; 4 the text does not name the source, so a specific identity is unproved; 5 accept quoted direct speech from paragraphs 2–4 and a supported explanation; 7 adding such an identity confuses inference with textual fact. Mark questions 1–5 and 7 out of 2 each. For the alternative ending award 4 marks for coherent sequence, 4 for language and 4 for explicitly distinguishing invention from the source. Accept defensible interpretations with exact textual support.
Extension: compare this prose narrative with the supplied original poem Ìwé mi. Discuss paragraphs versus lines, sound patterns, speaker and how each text presents an idea. Do not assume prose has no imagery or that every poem rhymes.

title: Agricultural site visit: observation, records and reporting
origin: New teaching material prepared under the owner's 15 October 2026 authorisation to use internet equivalents; not recovered school-source text. The original incomplete source entry is retained.

sources.title: FAO — Setting up and running a school garden, Part 4

body:
Objectives: observe an agricultural site systematically, distinguish observation from explanation, sketch a labelled plan and report findings with evidence.
Teaching: An excursion is a planned learning visit, not simply an outing. A school garden or an approved nearby farm can connect classroom ideas to visible crops, soil, water, paths and working practices. FAO's school-garden guide recommends mapping a site, observing its living things and recording findings. A sketch map locates features; an observation record says what was actually seen. An explanation suggests why it matters and may need checking with the grower.
Preparation: the teacher arranges the visit with the site manager, confirms school permission and supervision, and explains the permitted route and learning tasks. Learners work in supervised groups. Observe from designated paths; do not operate machinery, enter animal pens, handle chemicals or taste unknown plants. Ask permission before photographs or interviews. Clean hands after the visit. An observation-only school-garden activity is suitable when an off-site trip cannot be arranged.
Record sheet — copy these headings: date/time; site description; feature observed; exact observation; possible explanation; question for the grower. Include at least one crop, a water source, a path or boundary, and one visible soil or drainage feature. Draw a labelled sketch map with a direction arrow if its direction is known; do not invent a north direction or pretend a sketch is a measured plan.
Original worked record: 'Bed A: water remains in a shallow hollow beside three seedlings after watering.' This is an observation. 'Poor drainage may be affecting the seedlings' is a hypothesis, not a proven diagnosis. A useful follow-up asks whether the water normally remains and how watering is managed.
During the visit: first look over the whole site, then make four detailed records. Ask the grower two prepared questions, such as how harvested produce is protected and where it is sold. Write the answers as reported statements, not as things you observed. Connect any packaging or marketing you actually see with earlier lessons; record 'not observed' when absent.
Afterwards: write a 150–200-word report with purpose, site description, four findings, two interview answers, one limitation and one evidence-based suggestion. Do not replace missing observations with guesses.
Questions: 1. Distinguish a record from a hypothesis using the worked example. 2. State two purposes of a sketch map. 3. What should be written if no packaging is seen? 4. Why distinguish a grower's statement from your observation? 5. What additional observation would help assess the drainage hypothesis?
Answers: 1 water in the hollow is recorded; poor drainage is a possible explanation; 2 locate features and communicate layout; 3 not observed; 4 the sources of evidence differ; 5 revisit after a stated interval or compare nearby areas under similar watering. Accept other relevant evidence.
Assessment: labelled map 4 marks; four specific records 8; distinction between observation and inference 4; clear report with limitation 4. The teacher records observed participation separately. A classroom case-study report demonstrates reporting skills but must not be recorded as attendance at an actual visit.

title: Simple and compound time: worked rhythm examples
origin: New teaching material prepared under the owner's 15 October 2026 authorisation to use internet equivalents; not recovered school-source text. The original incomplete source entry is retained.

sources.title: Open Music Theory — Simple Meter and Time Signatures
Open Music Theory — Compound Meter and Time Signatures

body:
Objectives: read simple and compound time signatures, count note values in a bar, and distinguish the main beat from its divisions.
Teaching: A time signature has two stacked numbers without a fraction line. In simple metre, the top number gives beats per bar and the bottom identifies the beat unit: 2 means minim (half note), 4 crotchet (quarter note), 8 quaver (eighth note). A simple beat divides into two equal parts. In compound metre, the beat divides into three. The usual compound signatures 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8 represent respectively two, three and four dotted-crotchet beats; the top number counts quaver divisions, not main beats. A dotted crotchet equals three quavers.
Original worked example A, 4/4: one minim followed by two crotchets fills a bar. With the crotchet as one beat, the values are 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. Hold the minim through counts 1–2, then play or clap on counts 3 and 4. Do not re-attack the minim on count 2.
Original worked example B, 6/8: six quavers are grouped 3 + 3. Count the subdivisions '1-la-li, 2-la-li', tapping two main beats. Each group lasts one dotted-crotchet beat. There are six quaver divisions and two main beats. The accompanying original diagram shows one beam over each three-quaver group.
Comparison: 3/4 and 6/8 each contain the duration of six quavers, but their normal grouping differs: three groups of two versus two groups of three. Duration alone does not establish the metre. These are rhythm-only examples, not pitched melodies; the single line in the illustration is not a five-line pitch staff.
Practice: 1. How many crotchet beats are in 3/4? 2. How many minim beats are in 2/2? 3. State both main beats and quaver divisions in 6/8. 4. Complete a 4/4 bar containing a minim and a crotchet with one note. 5. Complete a 6/8 bar containing a dotted crotchet with one note. 6. Explain the grouping difference between 3/4 and 6/8. 7. Clap example A, then B, while a partner taps the main beats.
Answers: 1 three; 2 two; 3 two dotted-crotchet beats/six quaver divisions; 4 one crotchet; 5 one dotted crotchet; 6 2+2+2 quavers versus 3+3. Award 2 marks per written response, including the correct unit. For performance award 2 marks each for a steady pulse, correct sustained minim, and grouping the six quavers into two beats. Give feedback and repeat if the student confuses a division with a main beat.
The original school document's blank 'e.g' remains recorded as a source gap. These examples supply replacement teaching and clarify its general top-number rule; they do not claim to recover a lost drawing.

title: Oríkì orílẹ̀: four attributed lineage-praise excerpts
origin: New teaching material prepared under the owner's 15 October 2026 authorisation to use internet equivalents; not recovered school-source text. Short attributed excerpts are selected examples, not complete lineage histories or reconstructed missing chants.

sources.title: NOUN YOR215 — Introduction to Yoruba Oral Literature, PDF page 88
NOUN YOR213 — Ìlò-Èdè Yorùbá, section 5.4.2.3, PDF page 55
Yoruba Library — Oníkòyí family, Oríkì section
Yoruba Library — Okin Olofa family, Oríkì section

body:
Objectives: recognise lineage praise, connect an excerpt to its stated source, and interpret praise language without treating it as a literal description of every descendant.
Teaching: Oríkì orílẹ̀ associates praise with a lineage. Names, images and references can express identity, admiration or gratitude. The following are deliberately short excerpts for close reading; each source contains further context. Their spelling is retained except that broken PDF spacing is regularised in excerpt B. Praise language is not evidence that every member of a family has the same character.
A — Ẹlẹ́rìn: “Ẹ̀gbọ́n tí mo ní, Àlàgbé Ojúbánirẹ́,” / “Ojúbánirẹ́ ò dékùn ẹni.” NOUN YOR215 identifies Ojúbánirẹ́ here as part of Ìmọ̀dú Ẹlẹ́rìn praise. The passage is embedded in a bride's expression of gratitude to her supportive brother. It shows lineage praise functioning within another performance.
B — Olókùn-ẹṣin: “Ọmọ Olókùn ẹṣin da aṣọ sányán bora”. NOUN YOR213 quotes this within a discussion of clothing appropriate to an occasion. The cloth image introduces its caution about overshadowing the host. PDF spacing is regularised; this is not a newly composed traditional line.
C — Oníkòyí: “Iran onikoyi kan kii feyin gb’ofa” / “Iwaju ni won mu l’oju ogun”. Yoruba Library supplies these lines. Their forward-facing battle image praises courage. Treat that as literary representation rather than an instruction to fight.
D — Ọlọ́fà: “Iyeru Okin Omo Olofa Mojo Olalomi”. Yoruba Library supplies this opening line. In a short excerpt, recognising a lineage address is a defensible task; inventing a full ancestral story from it is not.
The school scheme prints 'elerin, olokun, esin, onikoyi, olofa'. This replacement selects the documented Olókùn-ẹṣin example alongside Ẹlẹ́rìn, Oníkòyí and Ọlọ́fà. It does not prove whether the original author intended 'olokun, esin' as one name or two, and it does not substitute deity praise or praise of horses for lineage material.
Original practice: make a four-row chart with lineage, exact excerpt, source and what the context supports. Then answer: 1. Which example is embedded in a bride's performance? 2. Which uses cloth imagery? 3. Which uses a battle image, and what quality is praised? 4. Which short opening explicitly names Olofa? 5. Why is one praise line insufficient proof of every descendant's conduct? 6. Explain the difference between interpreting a supplied line and inventing missing ancestral history. 7. Write four Yoruba sentences comparing two examples, referring to their actual words.
Answers: 1 A; 2 B; 3 C/courage; 4 D; 5 poetic praise represents values and does not establish individual facts; 6 interpretation uses text and context, whereas an unsupported historical claim adds evidence not supplied. Award 2 marks per question 1–6. For question 7 award 4 marks for accurate reference and comparison, and 4 for intelligible Yoruba and suitable tone marking. Accept more than one reading when supported by the excerpt and context.
Assessment extension: a learner may read an excerpt aloud under teacher guidance. Record pronunciation/performance separately from written comprehension; no learner is required to claim the lineage or perform a ritual.

title: Religion-linked oral poetry: ìjálá, iwì egúngún, Ọya pípè, Ṣàngó pípè and iyẹ̀rẹ̀ Ifá
body:
Objectives: identify five religion-linked oral genres named in the scheme (ìjálá, iwì egúngún, Ọya pípè, Ṣàngó pípè, iyẹ̀rẹ̀ Ifá); say who performs each and on what occasion; analyse how any performance of them is delivered; and report only the words a learner has actually heard or been given.
Links to the school's own text: the Second-Term Yoruba lesson on òrìṣà (informal-letter row) already says that iyẹ̀rẹ̀ Ifá is the spoken literature used when Ifá is consulted or the Ifá festival is kept, that ìjálá is the poetry chanted at the Ògún festival and at hunters' gatherings, that Ṣàngó was a powerful king whose devotees (elégùn) are known by their plaited hair, and that Ọya was his wife and became the river called Odò Ọya. That text names Ìjálá and iyẹ̀rẹ̀ Ifá but gives no Ṣàngó pípè, Ọya pípè or iwì egúngún material. This lesson adds those, and adds the analysis that the scheme's phrase 'ewì alohùn' (oral poetry) asks for.
Teaching summary (NOUN YOR215, paraphrased): these genres belong to ìṣàré ajẹmẹ́sìn, religion-linked chanted poetry. The course names ìjálá (Ògún), ẹ̀ṣà or iwì egúngún, and iyẹ̀rẹ̀ Ifá, and the òrìṣà pípè group with Èṣù pípè, Ọya pípè, Ṣàngó pípè and Ọbàtálá pípè. Ìṣàré is chanted speech, not a song with drum accompaniment, and it is performed in front of an audience at the occasion it belongs to.
Genre profile table (what the sources support):
1. Ìjálá — hunters' and Ògún devotees' chant; Ògún festival, hunters' gatherings.
2. Iwì / ẹ̀ṣà egúngún — chant associated with Egúngún performance; Egúngún festivals.
3. Ọya pípè — invocation and praise of Ọya; devotees of Ọya and her occasions.
4. Ṣàngó pípè — invocation and praise of Ṣàngó; his devotees (elégùn) and festival.
5. Iyẹ̀rẹ̀ Ifá — chant for Ifá; when Ifá is consulted or the Ifá festival is kept.
How to analyse a performance (use for any of the five): performer; occasion; audience; voice (speed, loudness, pauses, tone-marked words); opening address or praise name; repetition and parallel lines; images (animals, rivers, fire, iron, cloth); what the chant says the òrìṣà or ancestor is, and what it asks or thanks for. Praise language is poetry, not a literal biography.
Rules for evidence: this lesson supplies no verses. Traditional chants belong to their performers and communities and must not be invented or 'completed' from memory. Work from a recording, a published text with its source, or a chanter who gives permission. Quote only a short line, with who performed it, where and when, exactly as heard, and mark any word you could not hear. Writing about a genre does not require anyone to take part in a ritual.
Practice (questions):
1. Match each genre to its performer or setting: ìjálá, iwì egúngún, Ọya pípè, Ṣàngó pípè, iyẹ̀rẹ̀ Ifá.
2. From the school's òrìṣà lesson, state one fact about Ifá, Ògún, Ṣàngó and Ọya that helps explain who a chant is addressed to.
3. Why is 'ìṣàré' not the same as a drummed song?
4. Give two reasons a learner must not write a missing line of a chant from guesswork.
5. Observation task (needs a teacher-approved recording or invited chanter): fill an analysis sheet with performer, occasion, audience, delivery, one short exactly heard line, two images, and the purpose of the chant.
6. Write six Yoruba sentences comparing two genres, using only your analysis sheet.
Answers and marking guide: 1 ìjálá — hunters and Ògún devotees, Ògún festival; iwì egúngún — Egúngún performance; Ọya pípè — devotees of Ọya, praise of Ọya; Ṣàngó pípè — Ṣàngó devotees, praise of Ṣàngó; iyẹ̀rẹ̀ Ifá — Ifá consultation or festival. Award 1 mark each, 5 total. 2 accept any correct fact from the lesson text, 4 marks across Ifá, Ògún, Ṣàngó, Ọya (1 each). 3 ìṣàré is chanted speech without drum accompaniment; award 2. 4 a chant belongs to its performers and community; invented lines misrepresent a tradition and mislead readers; award 1 each. 5 award 8 marks: 1 each for performer, occasion, audience, delivery, exact line with source, two images (2), purpose; deduct for lines that are not attributed or that complete missing words. 6 award 6: 3 for accurate reference to the analysis sheet, 3 for intelligible Yoruba with tone marks. Where no recording or chanter is available, mark questions 1–4 and 6 only (out of 23) and record that the observation task was not done.
Assessment and feedback: performance, attendance at an event and written analysis are recorded separately. This lesson teaches genre knowledge and analysis, not performance skill. It does not supply authentic chant text; where the scheme intends texts, the teacher must add a source-verified text with permission.

title: Pricing in agriculture: factors that determine the price of farm produce
body:
Objectives: define pricing in agriculture; state and explain the factors that determine the price of farm produce; work a simple cost-and-price example; and explain why prices of farm produce change during the year.
Teaching: Pricing is deciding the amount of money at which a farm product is offered for sale. A farmer, trader or buyer cannot choose a price freely, because several things push it up or down.
Factors that determine the price of agricultural produce:
1. Cost of production. Seed, labour, fertiliser, feed, transport and storage must be recovered. A price below total cost is a loss.
2. Quality. Clean, fresh, well-graded produce sells at a higher price than damaged or mixed produce.
3. Quantity. Large harvests usually lower the price; a small harvest raises it.
4. Demand and supply. When buyers want more than is available the price rises; when more is available than buyers want it falls.
5. Seasonal produce. Perishable crops are cheap at harvest and dearer out of season. Storage and processing let a farmer wait for a better price.
6. Market price. The price already being paid in the nearby market guides what a seller can ask.
Worked example: a farmer harvests 200 tubers of yam. Total cost of growing, harvesting and carrying them to market is 100,000 naira, so the break-even price is 100,000 ÷ 200 = 500 naira per tuber. At 450 naira the farmer loses 50 naira on each tuber (10,000 naira in all). At 650 naira the profit is 150 naira a tuber, or 30,000 naira. If many farmers harvest at once and buyers will pay only 400 naira, the farmer can sell at a loss or store part of the harvest and sell it later.
Why pricing matters: it lets the farmer know whether the farm is making a profit, helps plan what to grow next season, and guides buyers and traders in the market. Preserving and storing produce helps the farmer avoid selling at the lowest seasonal price.
Source note: the list of price determinants follows the school-level Agricultural Science lesson on pricing from the Federal Ministry's Inspire Education platform, with the role of storage drawn from a Nigerian JSS3 lesson note. The wording, example and figures here are new.
Practice (questions):
1. Define pricing in agriculture.
2. List five factors that determine the price of farm produce.
3. A farmer spends 60,000 naira to produce 120 bags of maize. Calculate the break-even price per bag. State the profit or loss if she sells each bag at 450 naira.
4. Why is tomato cheaper at harvest time than months later?
5. Give two ways a farmer can avoid selling at a low seasonal price.
6. Collect the price of two foodstuffs in a local market in two different months, if you can, and explain any difference using the factors above.
Answers and marking guide: 1 the amount of money at which a product is offered for sale (2 marks). 2 any five of cost of production, quality, quantity, demand and supply, seasonal supply, market price, storage (5 marks). 3 60,000 ÷ 120 = 500 naira per bag; at 450 naira the loss is 50 naira a bag, or 6,000 naira in all (4 marks). 4 supply is high at harvest and tomatoes spoil quickly (2 marks). 5 storage, preservation or processing, selling in a different market or season (1 mark each, 2 marks). 6 award up to 5 marks for accurate prices, a stated source and a reason from the factors; accept 'no data collected' with a reasoned prediction for 3 marks.
Assessment and feedback: total 20 marks. Accept answers that explain the same factor in other correct words. Question 6 is a field task and can be marked separately from the written test.

title: Forms of election in Nigeria and the composition of INEC
body:
Objectives: distinguish the main forms of election held in Nigeria; state the composition of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC); and link these to the roles of INEC and State Independent Electoral Commissions (SIECs) already taught.
Teaching on forms of election: an election is the process of voting for those who will hold office. Several kinds are held, and each has a different purpose.
1. Primary election: a political party chooses the candidate it will present. INEC observes the process; it is the party that decides its candidate.
2. General election: voters choose among the candidates of different parties for the offices being contested.
3. By-election (bye-election): held to fill a vacancy that arises between general elections, for example a seat that becomes empty.
4. Run-off election: a second contest between leading candidates when the first does not produce a winner who meets the legal requirement.
5. Re-run and supplementary elections: voting repeated or completed where an election is cancelled in some areas, or where a tribunal or court orders it.
6. Off-cycle election: an election held outside the main election cycle, such as governorship elections in some states.
7. Referendum: INEC may be required to conduct a referendum when the Constitution or an Act of the National Assembly requires one.
Direct and indirect: in a direct election voters choose the office-holder themselves; in an indirect election they choose representatives or delegates who then choose.
Composition of INEC: INEC is set up by section 153 of the 1999 Constitution. Its composition is a Chairman, who is the Chief Electoral Commissioner, and twelve National Electoral Commissioners, making thirteen members. There are also Resident Electoral Commissioners, one for each state and the Federal Capital Territory, 37 in all. The Chairman is the returning officer for the presidential election. The school text already states that a SIEC has its own chairman and seven other persons and lists INEC's functions; this lesson adds INEC's composition and the forms of election.
Source note: composition and numbers follow INEC's published FAQ; the list of election types follows INEC's guidelines for the conduct of elections and a published explainer. The wording is new.
Practice (questions):
1. Match each to its meaning: primary, by-election, run-off, off-cycle.
2. Who chooses the candidate in a primary election?
3. Why would a by-election be needed?
4. State the composition of INEC and how many Resident Electoral Commissioners there are.
5. Give one difference between INEC and a SIEC, using the school text and this lesson.
6. Explain the difference between a direct and an indirect election with one example of each.
Answers and marking guide: 1 primary: a party chooses its candidate; by-election: fills a vacancy; run-off: a second contest when no one meets the requirement; off-cycle: held outside the main cycle (4 marks). 2 the political party (1 mark). 3 to fill a vacancy that arises between general elections (2 marks). 4 a Chairman and twelve National Electoral Commissioners, 13 members; 37 Resident Electoral Commissioners (4 marks). 5 accept INEC organises federal and state elections while a SIEC handles local government elections, or any correct contrast from the school text (2 marks). 6 direct: voters choose the office-holder themselves; indirect: voters or delegates choose representatives who then choose; accept any correct example (4 marks).
Assessment and feedback: total 17 marks. Accept correct answers in other words. Number-specific facts (13 members, 37 Resident Electoral Commissioners) should be checked against INEC's current published figures if the law changes.

title: Introduction to Business Studies
body:
Objectives: explain the meaning of Business Studies; list its components; state its importance; and name career opportunities it leads to.
Teaching: Business Studies is the study of how goods and services are produced, bought, sold and managed, and of the skills used to run an office or a business. A farmer selling yams, a tailor with a shop and a bank all carry out business activities.
Components of Business Studies: 1. Commerce (trade and the services that help trade, such as banking and transport). 2. Office practice (how an office runs). 3. Book-keeping and accounting (recording money). 4. Business management and administration. 5. Entrepreneurship (starting and running a business).
Importance: it helps a person manage personal money, prepares for work in offices, trade and banking, develops entrepreneurial skill, and gives a base for Economics, Accounting and Commerce in senior secondary school.
Career opportunities: accountant, secretary or administrator, banker, trader, marketer, store-keeper, insurance officer, entrepreneur.
Example: Ada buys bread flour, bakes, sells in her street and writes down what she spends and earns. Production, selling and record keeping are all Business Studies in practice.
Source note: the objectives follow the Federal Ministry of Education e-learning topic list for junior secondary Business Studies. The wording, examples and exercises here are new.
Practice (questions):
1. What is Business Studies?
2. List four components of Business Studies.
3. State three reasons for studying Business Studies.
4. Name four careers that Business Studies leads to.
5. Describe one business activity near your home and say which component it belongs to.
Answers and marking guide: 1 the study of how goods and services are produced, sold and managed, with the skills for running an office or business (2 marks). 2 any four from commerce, office practice, book-keeping, business management, entrepreneurship (4). 3 any three of managing money, work preparation, entrepreneurial skill, base for later subjects (3). 4 any four careers listed or equivalent (4). 5 accept any real activity correctly matched to a component (2 marks activity, 2 for matching).
Assessment and feedback: total 15 marks. Accept answers in other correct words.

title: The Office: meaning, types and functions
body:
Objectives: define an office; describe types of office; state the functions of an office.
Teaching: An office is a place where the clerical and administrative work of an organisation is done: information is received, recorded, stored, processed and communicated.
Types of office: 1. Small office: few workers, often one room, common in small shops and clinics. 2. Large office: many workers and departments, as in a bank head office. 3. Open-plan office: one large space with desks shared without walls. 4. Partitioned (private) office: separate rooms or partitions for privacy, used by managers.
Functions of an office: receiving and sending information (letters, calls, emails); keeping records; handling money and accounts; protecting documents and property; helping management make decisions with correct information; dealing with visitors and customers.
Example: in a school office the secretary receives letters, files student records, answers the telephone and prepares notices for the principal.
Source note: the objectives follow the Federal Ministry of Education e-learning topic list for junior secondary Business Studies. The wording, examples and exercises here are new.
Practice (questions):
1. Define an office.
2. Name two types of office and one advantage of each.
3. State five functions of an office.
4. Explain why an office keeps records.
5. Visit or describe your school office and list three things done there.
Answers and marking guide: 1 a place where the clerical and administrative work of an organisation is done (2). 2 for example small: easy to supervise; large: handles many tasks; open-plan: easy communication; partitioned: privacy; 1 mark for type and 1 for advantage (4). 3 any five functions (5). 4 to provide information when needed, prove transactions and support decisions (2). 5 three accurate activities (3).
Assessment and feedback: total 16 marks.

title: Office equipment: meaning, examples and importance
body:
Objectives: define office equipment; list common office equipment; state its importance and how it should be cared for.
Teaching: Office equipment is the machines and tools used to do office work faster, more accurately and neatly.
Examples by use: computing and printing (computer, printer, scanner, photocopier, calculator); communication (telephone, mobile phone, email-enabled computer); filing and storage (filing cabinet, folders, cabinets, shelves); fastening and cutting (stapler, punch, paper guillotine); destroying records (paper shredder); presenting (projector).
Importance: saves time and effort; improves accuracy; produces neat copies; stores information safely; improves communication and efficiency.
Care of equipment: follow instructions; clean regularly; protect from dust, water and power surges; report faults early; allow only trained persons to repair.
Example: a school bursary that uses a computer and printer can issue receipts in minutes and keep a copy for the record.
Source note: examples and importance follow a Nigerian JSS3 lesson note on office equipment and the Federal Ministry topic list; the wording is new.
Practice (questions):
1. Define office equipment.
2. List six examples and say what each is used for.
3. State four importance of office equipment.
4. Give three ways of caring for office equipment.
Answers and marking guide: 1 machines and tools used to do office work faster, more accurately and neatly (2). 2 six correct pairs, 1 mark each (6). 3 any four importance (4). 4 any three care points (3).
Assessment and feedback: total 15 marks.

title: The right attitude to work
body:
Objectives: define attitude to work; list right and wrong attitudes; state the benefits of the right attitude; suggest ways of developing it.
Teaching: Attitude to work is the way a person thinks and behaves toward their job or duties.
Right attitudes: punctuality, honesty, hard work and diligence, responsibility, discipline, cooperation, respect for others and for property, neatness, willingness to learn, politeness to customers.
Wrong attitudes: lateness, laziness, absenteeism, stealing or wasting materials, rudeness, gossip, refusing instructions.
Benefits: promotion, trust from employers, higher productivity, a good reputation, a pleasant workplace, and success of the business.
How to develop it: set goals, plan time, accept correction, learn from good examples, take responsibility for mistakes, and practise honesty in small things.
Scenario: Tunde arrives ten minutes early, finishes his tasks, helps a colleague and reports a damaged printer. Name the right attitudes shown.
Source note: the objectives follow the Federal Ministry of Education e-learning topic list for junior secondary Business Studies. The wording, examples and exercises here are new.
Practice (questions):
1. Define attitude to work.
2. List five right attitudes and three wrong attitudes.
3. State four benefits of the right attitude.
4. Explain two ways a person can improve their attitude to work.
5. In the scenario above name four attitudes Tunde shows.
Answers and marking guide: 1 the way a person thinks and behaves toward their work (2). 2 five right and three wrong (8). 3 any four (4). 4 two ways with explanation (4). 5 punctuality, hard work, cooperation, responsibility, honesty (any four, 4).
Assessment and feedback: total 22 marks.

title: The office staff: categories, duties, qualities and confidentiality
body:
Objectives: name categories of office staff; state their duties; list qualities of a good office worker; explain how office information is kept confidential.
Teaching: Office staff are the people who carry out the work of an office.
Categories and duties: 1. Managerial staff (manager, supervisor): plan, direct and take decisions. 2. Secretarial staff (secretary): take dictation, type, arrange meetings, handle correspondence. 3. Clerical staff (clerks): record, file and process information and data. 4. Junior or auxiliary staff (messenger, cleaner, security): deliver messages, keep premises clean and safe.
Qualities of a good office worker: honesty, punctuality, accuracy, neatness, courtesy, good communication, loyalty, discretion and willingness to learn.
Keeping information confidential: do not discuss company matters with outsiders; lock files and cabinets; use passwords on computers; do not leave documents on desks; shred unwanted papers; share information only with authorised persons.
Example: a clerk who sees salary records must not tell other workers what a colleague earns.
Source note: the objectives follow the Federal Ministry of Education e-learning topic list for junior secondary Business Studies. The wording, examples and exercises here are new.
Practice (questions):
1. Name four categories of office staff.
2. State two duties of a secretary and two of a clerk.
3. List five qualities of a good office worker.
4. State four ways of keeping office information confidential.
5. Why is confidentiality important?
Answers and marking guide: 1 managerial, secretarial, clerical, junior or auxiliary (4). 2 two for each (4). 3 any five (5). 4 any four (4). 5 to protect the business and individuals and keep trust (2).
Assessment and feedback: total 19 marks.

title: Occupation: meaning, types and factors affecting choice
body:
Objectives: define occupation; classify occupations; list factors that affect the choice of occupation.
Teaching: An occupation is any work a person does regularly to earn a living.
Types of occupation: 1. Extractive: taking things from nature, such as farming, fishing, mining and lumbering. 2. Manufacturing: changing raw materials into finished goods, such as making bread, cloth or furniture. 3. Constructive: building roads, houses and bridges. 4. Commercial: buying and selling and the services that help trade, such as retailing, banking and transport. 5. Services: skills used for others, such as teaching, nursing, law and hairdressing.
Factors affecting the choice of occupation: interest and ability; education and training; income; availability of jobs; location; working conditions; health and age; family influence and tradition.
Example: Musa is good with numbers, trained as an accountant and works in a bank in his town. Training, ability and availability influenced his choice.
Source note: the objectives follow the Federal Ministry of Education e-learning topic list for junior secondary Business Studies. The wording, examples and exercises here are new.
Practice (questions):
1. Define occupation.
2. Name the five types of occupation and give one example of each.
3. State five factors that affect the choice of occupation.
4. Which type of occupation is a baker, a fisherman, a builder and a nurse?
Answers and marking guide: 1 work done regularly to earn a living (2). 2 five types with examples (10). 3 any five (5). 4 manufacturing (or services), extractive, constructive, services (4).
Assessment and feedback: total 21 marks.
