title: Introduction to commerce
body:
Objectives: define commerce; state its importance; list the activities that help commerce.
Teaching: Commerce is all the activities involved in the exchange of goods and services from producers to consumers: buying, selling and the services that help them.
Importance: it moves goods from producers to consumers; creates jobs; makes goods available in all places and times; helps producers sell their output; and increases the standard of living.
Activities that help commerce (aids to trade): banking, insurance, transport, warehousing (storage), communication and advertising.
Commerce and trade: trade is the buying and selling itself; commerce includes trade and the aids that help it.
Example: yams grown in a village are carried by a lorry (transport), stored in a warehouse, sold to a retailer in a city and paid for through a bank.
Source note: the objectives follow the Federal Ministry of Education e-learning topic list for junior secondary Business Studies. The wording, examples and exercises here are new.
Practice (questions):
1. Define commerce.
2. State four importance of commerce.
3. List the six aids to trade.
4. Distinguish between trade and commerce.
5. Trace the movement of a bag of rice from a farmer to a family, naming at least three aids to trade.
Answers and marking guide: 1 activities involved in the exchange of goods and services from producers to consumers (2). 2 any four (4). 3 banking, insurance, transport, warehousing, communication, advertising (6). 4 trade is buying and selling; commerce includes trade and the aids that help it (2). 5 accept a correct chain naming at least three aids (4).
Assessment and feedback: total 18 marks.

title: Divisions of commerce: trade and aids to trade
body:
Objectives: classify commerce into trade and aids to trade; distinguish home trade from foreign trade and wholesale from retail trade; explain each aid to trade.
Teaching: Commerce is divided into two parts: trade and aids to trade.
Trade: 1. Home (internal) trade is buying and selling within one country. It is wholesale (selling goods in large quantities to retailers) or retail (selling in small quantities to consumers). 2. Foreign (external) trade is buying and selling between countries: imports (goods bought from other countries), exports (goods sold to other countries) and entrepot trade (importing goods to export again).
Aids to trade: banking (keeps money, gives loans, makes payments); insurance (pays for loss or damage after a premium); transport (moves goods and people); warehousing (stores goods until they are needed); communication (passes information by phone, post and the internet); advertising (informs customers about goods and services).
Example: a trader buys cartons of noodles from a wholesaler and sells single packs in a shop. She is a retailer in home trade.
Source note: the objectives follow the Federal Ministry of Education e-learning topic list for junior secondary Business Studies. The wording, examples and exercises here are new.
Practice (questions):
1. Name the two main divisions of commerce.
2. Distinguish between wholesale and retail trade.
3. Distinguish between imports and exports and give one example of each for Nigeria.
4. Explain three aids to trade.
5. Classify each as home trade or foreign trade: a market woman selling tomatoes; a company shipping cocoa to Europe.
Answers and marking guide: 1 trade and aids to trade (2). 2 wholesale is selling in large quantities to retailers; retail is selling in small quantities to consumers (4). 3 imports are goods bought from other countries, exports goods sold to other countries; accept correct examples (4). 4 three aids explained (6). 5 home trade; foreign trade (2).
Assessment and feedback: total 18 marks.

title: Production: meaning, levels, direct and indirect production, and effects
body:
Objectives: define production; state the levels and kinds of production; explain effects of production on the environment and society.
Teaching: Production is the creation of goods and services that satisfy human wants.
Levels of production: 1. Primary: taking from nature (farming, fishing, mining). 2. Secondary: changing materials into other goods (manufacturing, construction). 3. Tertiary: services (trade, transport, banking, teaching).
Kinds of production: direct production is making goods for your own use, such as growing food for your family; indirect production is making goods to sell and use the money to buy what you need, as in most modern business.
Effects of production: positive effects include jobs, income, goods and services and development; negative effects include pollution of air and water, waste, loss of forests and noise. Producers should reduce harm by treating waste, planting trees and using clean methods.
Example: a cement factory gives jobs and builds houses but produces dust; a filter on the chimney reduces pollution.
Source note: the objectives follow the Federal Ministry of Education e-learning topic list for junior secondary Business Studies. The wording, examples and exercises here are new.
Practice (questions):
1. Define production.
2. Name the three levels of production with one example each.
3. Distinguish between direct and indirect production.
4. State two good and two bad effects of production.
5. Suggest two ways a factory can reduce harm to the environment.
Answers and marking guide: 1 creating goods and services that satisfy wants (2). 2 primary, secondary, tertiary with examples (6). 3 direct is for own use; indirect is for sale (2). 4 two and two (4). 5 any two sensible methods (2).
Assessment and feedback: total 16 marks.

title: Factors of production and their rewards
body:
Objectives: list the factors of production; state the features and importance of each; state the reward for each.
Teaching: Factors of production are the resources needed to produce goods and services.
1. Land: all natural resources (soil, water, minerals, forests). Features: fixed in supply, not made by people, immobile. Reward: rent.
2. Labour: human physical and mental effort. Features: cannot be separated from the worker, can be improved by training, supply depends on population. Reward: wages or salary.
3. Capital: man-made goods used to produce more goods (machines, tools, money for business). Features: made by people, wears out, can be increased by saving. Reward: interest.
4. Entrepreneur: the person who organises the other factors and takes the risk. Features: takes decisions, bears risk. Reward: profit (or loss).
Importance: no production can take place without them, and the quality and mix of the factors decide the cost and quantity of output.
Example: a bakery uses land for the shop, labour of bakers, capital in ovens and flour, and an owner who organises everything and takes the risk.
Source note: the objectives follow the Federal Ministry of Education e-learning topic list for junior secondary Business Studies. The wording, examples and exercises here are new.
Practice (questions):
1. List the four factors of production.
2. State the reward for each.
3. State two features of land and two of labour.
4. Identify the factors in a poultry farm: the pen and soil, the workers, the feeding equipment, the owner.
5. Why is the entrepreneur called the organiser of production?
Answers and marking guide: 1 land, labour, capital, entrepreneur (4). 2 rent, wages, interest, profit (4). 3 land fixed in supply and not man-made; labour cannot be separated from the worker and improves with training (4). 4 land, labour, capital, entrepreneur (4). 5 he or she brings the other factors together, takes decisions and the risk (2).
Assessment and feedback: total 18 marks.

title: Scale drawing
body:
Objectives: explain what a scale means; convert between drawing length and actual length; and make a simple scale drawing.
Teaching: A scale drawing shows a real object or place smaller (or larger) by the same ratio in every direction. A scale of 1 : 100 means 1 cm on the drawing stands for 100 cm (1 m) in real life. A scale can also be written 1 cm : 5 km.
Rules: actual length = drawing length × scale number; drawing length = actual length ÷ scale number. Always change both lengths to the same unit first. Angles do not change in a scale drawing; only lengths do.
Worked examples:
1. A room is 6 m by 4 m. At 1 : 100, 6 m = 600 cm, so the drawing is 600 ÷ 100 = 6 cm by 4 cm.
2. On a map with scale 1 : 50 000, a road measures 7.5 cm. Actual length = 7.5 × 50 000 = 375 000 cm = 3 750 m = 3.75 km.
3. A field is 80 m by 50 m. Use 1 cm : 10 m: draw a rectangle 8 cm by 5 cm. The diagonal measures about 9.4 cm, so the actual diagonal is about 94 m. (Check: the square root of 80² + 50² = 8 900 is about 94.3 m.)
Steps for a scale drawing: choose a scale that fits the paper; calculate each drawing length; draw with ruler and protractor; label with the scale.
Source note: the method follows standard school mathematics treatments (see sources); the wording, numbers and exercises are new.
Practice (questions):
1. State what a scale of 1 : 250 means.
2. On a scale of 1 : 250 a line is 4 cm long. Find the actual length in metres.
3. A wall is 15 m long. Find its length on a drawing with scale 1 : 500.
4. A classroom is 9 m by 6 m. Give its drawing size at 1 : 150.
5. On a map 1 cm represents 2 km. Two towns are 6.5 cm apart. Find the actual distance.
6. Draw a plan of your desk top with a scale of 1 : 10 and label the scale.
Answers and marking guide: 1 1 cm on the drawing represents 250 cm (2.5 m) in real life (2). 2 4 × 250 = 1 000 cm = 10 m (3). 3 1 500 ÷ 500 = 3 cm (3). 4 900 ÷ 150 = 6 cm and 600 ÷ 150 = 4 cm, so 6 cm by 4 cm (3). 5 6.5 × 2 = 13 km (2). 6 award up to 5 marks for correct measured desk size, correct drawing size, neat drawing and a labelled scale (accept any accurate answer).
Assessment and feedback: total 18 marks. Check units before marking.

title: Clinometers: measuring heights and distances
body:
Objectives: describe a clinometer; use the angle of elevation with the tangent ratio to find a height or a distance.
Teaching: A clinometer is an instrument that measures the angle of elevation (or depression) of an object. A simple one can be made from a protractor, a straw for sighting and a string with a small weight. Different home-made clinometers are read differently: some show the angle of elevation directly and some show 90° minus that angle. Before use, test yours on a known angle (for example a 45° sighting on a wall).
Method for height: stand a measured horizontal distance d from the object. Sight the top and read the angle of elevation θ. Height above your eye = d × tan θ. Add your eye height e to get the total height.
Method for distance: if the height of the object above your eye level is h and the angle of elevation is θ, the distance is d = h ÷ tan θ.
Some tangent values: tan 30° = 0.5774, tan 35° = 0.7002, tan 40° = 0.8391, tan 45° = 1, tan 50° = 1.1918, tan 60° = 1.7321.
Worked examples:
1. A student stands 20 m from a tree. The angle of elevation of the top is 35° and her eye is 1.5 m above the ground. Height above eye = 20 × 0.7002 = 14.0 m. Tree height = 14.0 + 1.5 = 15.5 m.
2. The top of a flagpole is 12 m above a student's eye level and is seen at an elevation of 40°. Distance = 12 ÷ 0.8391 = 14.3 m.
Source note: the method follows standard school mathematics treatments (see sources); the wording, numbers and exercises are new.
Practice (questions):
1. What does a clinometer measure?
2. Why must you test a home-made clinometer on a known angle first?
3. A tower is seen at 50° from a point 30 m away. The observer's eye is 1.6 m above ground. Find the tower's height.
4. The top of a tree is 8 m above eye level and is seen at 30°. Find the distance from the tree.
5. At 45° from 15 m with an eye height of 1.5 m, find the height.
6. Field task: measure the height of your school flagpole with a clinometer and a tape, and show your working.
Answers and marking guide: 1 the angle of elevation or depression of an object (2). 2 because the instrument may show the angle or 90° minus the angle (2). 3 30 × 1.1918 = 35.75 m; plus 1.6 gives 37.4 m (4). 4 8 ÷ 0.5774 = 13.9 m (3). 5 15 × 1 = 15 m; plus 1.5 gives 16.5 m (3). 6 up to 6 marks: measured distance, angle, tangent value, calculation, adding eye height, result near the true height (accept measurement error).
Assessment and feedback: total 20 marks. The field task checks method, not exact accuracy.

title: Taking and drawing bearings with a compass and protractor
body:
Objectives: use a compass and a protractor to take and draw bearings; find a back bearing; make a scale drawing from bearings and distances.
Teaching: A bearing is the angle, measured clockwise from North, that a direction makes, and it is written with three figures (east 090°, south 180°, west 270°). The bearing of B from A is measured at A.
Instruments: a magnetic compass has a needle that points to magnetic North; hold it flat, away from metal objects, turn until North on the dial lines up with the needle, then read the bearing of the object you sight. A protractor measures bearings on paper: put its centre on the starting point, its zero on the North line and measure clockwise. For a bearing greater than 180° with a half-circle protractor, measure the angle anticlockwise from North and subtract it from 360°.
Back bearing: the bearing of A from B differs from the bearing of B from A by 180°. If the bearing of B from A is below 180°, add 180°; if it is 180° or more, subtract 180°. Example: B from A is 065°, so A from B is 245°; if B from A is 250°, A from B is 070°.
Worked scale drawing: P to Q is 8 km on a bearing of 110° from P; Q to R is 6 km on a bearing of 200° from Q. Use 1 cm : 2 km. At P draw a North line, measure 110° clockwise and mark Q at 4 cm. At Q draw a new North line, measure 200° clockwise and mark R at 3 cm. Join P to R: it measures about 5 cm, so the distance is about 10 km, and the bearing of R from P measured at P is about 147°. (Calculation check: R is about 5.5 km east and 8.4 km south of P.)
Common mistake: measuring the second bearing from the old North line instead of drawing a new North line at the new starting point.
Source note: the method follows standard school mathematics treatments (see sources); the wording, numbers and exercises are new.
Practice (questions):
1. State the bearing of north-east, south and west.
2. The bearing of Q from P is 070°. Find the bearing of P from Q.
3. The bearing of Y from X is 300°. Find the bearing of X from Y.
4. Explain how to use a protractor to draw a bearing of 250° with a half-circle protractor.
5. A ship sails 6 km on a bearing of 050° using a scale of 1 cm : 1.5 km. State the drawing length and how you would draw it.
6. Why must a new North line be drawn at each starting point?
Answers and marking guide: 1 045°, 180°, 270° (3). 2 070° + 180° = 250° (2). 3 300° − 180° = 120° (2). 4 measure 110° anticlockwise from North (360° − 250°) or draw 250° with a full-circle protractor (3). 5 6 ÷ 1.5 = 4 cm; draw a North line at the start, measure 050° clockwise, mark 4 cm along it (3). 6 each bearing is measured from North at its own starting point (2).
Assessment and feedback: total 15 marks.

title: Ìsúnkì and aranmo in joined words: revising sound change in compound nouns
body:
**Objectives:** (1) say what happens to the sounds when two Yoruba words are joined into one; (2) tell vowel assimilation from contraction in given examples; (3) describe each change by comparing the letters before and after; (4) use the school's own compound-noun examples correctly.

**Scheme wording.** The First-Term scheme (Week 1, language) prints 'Atunyewo fonoloji Ede Yoruba iparoje ati isunki'. The school's Week 1 phonology notes teach vowels, consonants and tone, and the Week 4 notes on compound nouns use the words 'aranmo' (assimilation shows) and 'isunki' (contraction takes place) without explaining them. The term 'iparoje' appears in no executable body and no source consulted defines it. It may name vowel assimilation, but that is not confirmed and no definition is invented here; the owner or a Yoruba teacher should confirm the meaning (recorded as an open question).

**Background (verified).** Linguists describe vowel elision (a vowel dropped where two words meet, for example a vowel-final verb before a vowel-initial noun) and vowel assimilation as common sound changes in Yoruba (Badejo 1986, Studies in African Linguistics 17(1); Èkìtì-dialect study, Lingue e Linguaggi 17). This lesson only reads the school's own compound-noun examples through that idea. It does not state rules for all Yoruba words.

**Teaching — examples from the school's Week 4 notes (unmarked spelling kept, as in the notes).**
Joins where the second word's first vowel becomes the same as the last vowel of the first word (aranmo):
etu + ibon = etuubon; eto + ilu = etoolu; ile + iwe = ileewe.
Joins where one vowel is lost, so the compound is shorter (isunki):
ori + oke = oroke; irun + agbon = irungbon; eran + oko = eranko.
**Compare the letters.** etu + ibon: 3 + 4 letters give etuubon, 7 letters (an 'i' is replaced by 'u'). ori + oke: 3 + 3 letters give oroke, 5 letters (one vowel lost). In these six examples the aranmo joins keep the total number of letters and the isunki joins lose one.
**Care.** Tone marks are not shown in the notes' spelling, so this lesson says nothing about tone in these words. A teacher who marks tone must check each word against a Yoruba dictionary.

**Practice (questions).**
1. Copy and complete: join, result, type (aranmo or isunki), letter replaced or lost. etu + ibon; ori + oke; eto + ilu; irun + agbon; ile + iwe; eran + oko. (12 marks)
2. For ile + iwe and eran + oko, count the letters before and after joining and state what the counts show. (4 marks)
3. Explain in one sentence of your own how aranmo differs from isunki. (2 marks)
4. Say which scheme word, 'iparoje', is not explained in this lesson and why. (2 marks)

**Answers and marking guide (20 marks).** 1. etuubon: aranmo, 'i' of ibon becomes 'u'. oroke: isunki, 'i' at the end of ori is lost. etoolu: aranmo, 'i' of ilu becomes 'o'. irungbon: isunki, initial 'a' of agbon is lost. ileewe: aranmo, 'i' of iwe becomes 'e'. eranko: isunki, initial 'o' of oko is lost. Two marks per row: one for type and one for the letter. 2. ile + iwe: 3 + 3 letters give 6 letters (ileewe), so no letter is lost; eran + oko: 4 + 3 letters give 6 letters (eranko), against 7 before joining, so one is lost. 3. Accept an answer that says aranmo changes a vowel to match the one before it and isunki drops a vowel. 4. 'iparoje' is not found in the school's notes or the sources consulted, so its meaning is unconfirmed. Assessment (teacher feedback): accept spelling variants in learners' unmarked Yoruba; do not penalise missing tone marks in this task.

title: Gbólóhùn ìbéèrè: ṣé, ǹjẹ́, dà, ńkọ́, ta and kí
body:
**Objectives:** (1) tell yes/no questions from questions that ask for information; (2) form a yes/no question with ṣé or ǹjẹ́; (3) form a question with ta, kí, ibo or báwo followed by ni; (4) use the school's dà and ńkọ́ questions correctly.

**Scheme wording.** The First-Term scheme (Week 5, language) prints 'Gbolohun ibeere – awon iwure ti a fi n se ibeere da, nko, nje, taki'. The school's Week 5 notes on sentence types give three question words, da, nko and tani, with three examples, and nothing on nje. 'taki' is read here as the two question words ta and kí; that reading is an inference, not confirmed. 'iwure' is printed in the scheme; it is read as the particles or words used to ask a question, and this is also unconfirmed. A dictionary source gives wúre as 'to pray' or 'to bless' and ìwuré as 'prayer', so a competing reading is 'prayers' or 'good wishes'; that sense does not fit a line about question words, and the school has not said which is meant.

**The school's examples (unmarked spelling kept).** Adegoke da? Badejo nko? Ta ni o wa nibe? The school's notes do not state what dà and ńkọ́ mean. Olaogun (2017, JOLAN 20(1), p. 245) glosses 'Bólú dà?' as 'Where is Bolu?', which supports reading dà as 'where is…?'. The same paper glosses a parallel 'Ṣégun ńkọ́?' as 'Where is Segun?'; the reading 'what about…?' for ńkọ́ was not found in a source read for this check, so both readings of ńkọ́ stay open and a Yoruba teacher should decide.

**Teaching 1 — yes/no questions.** A sentence can be turned into a question that expects 'yes' or 'no' by putting ṣé or ǹjẹ́ at the front. Scholars list ṣé, ǹjẹ́ and bí among the markers of such questions (Ogunbowale 1970, discussed in a Yoruba yes–no question study from the University of Lagos). Examples from the Yorùbá Dictionary (Agoke, University of Wisconsin): Ṣé o fẹ́ràn ìrẹsì? Ṣé o ti rí Títí? Ǹjẹ́ Tolú béèrè ìbéèrè ní kíláàsì Yorùbá? Usual answers are bẹ́ẹ̀ ni (yes) and bẹ́ẹ̀ kọ́ (no).

**Teaching 2 — questions that ask for information.** Question words such as ta (who), kí (what), èwo (which), èló (how much), mélòó (how many), ibo (where) and báwo (how) come at the start and are followed by ni. Examples from the same dictionary: Ta ni olùkọ́ ẹ? Kí ni o fẹ́ràn láti ṣe? Èwo ni o fẹ́? Question words are described as question nouns by Olanrewaju (2023, Lingual).

**Worked examples built on a school sentence.** Statement: Bísí lọ sí ilé ìkàwé. Yes/no question: Ṣé Bísí lọ sí ilé ìkàwé? Question about the place: Ibo ni Bísí lọ?

**Practice (questions).**
1. Sort into 'yes/no' and 'asks for information': (a) Ṣé o ti rí Títí? (b) Ta ni olùkọ́ ẹ? (c) Ǹjẹ́ Tolú béèrè ìbéèrè? (d) Èwo ni o fẹ́? (e) Kí ni o fẹ́ràn láti ṣe? (5 marks)
2. Turn into yes/no questions with ṣé: Adé wá. Bísí mú ìwé náà wá. (4 marks)
3. Ask a question about the underlined part with the word in brackets: Bísí lọ sí **ilé ìkàwé** (ibo). **Adé** ràn án lọ́wọ́ (ta). (4 marks)
4. Answer one of your yes/no questions in two ways, bẹ́ẹ̀ ni and bẹ́ẹ̀ kọ́, with a full sentence each. (3 marks)
5. Explain in one sentence the difference between ṣé and ta ni. (2 marks)
6. State which scheme words the notes cannot confirm. (2 marks)

**Answers and marking guide (20 marks).** 1. Yes/no: a, c. Information: b, d, e (one mark each). 2. Ṣé Adé wá? Ṣé Bísí mú ìwé náà wá? (two marks each). 3. Ibo ni Bísí lọ? Ta ni ó ràn án lọ́wọ́? (two marks each; accept ta ni ó ran Bísí lọ́wọ́). 4. Accept answers such as Bẹ́ẹ̀ ni, Bísí lọ and Bẹ́ẹ̀ kọ́, Bísí kò lọ; the marker and a full sentence earn the marks. 5. ṣé begins a question to be answered yes or no; ta ni asks who. 6. The meaning of 'taki' and 'iwure' is inferred, and the meaning of ńkọ́ needs a teacher's check (dà as 'where is…?' is supported by Olaogun 2017). Assessment (teacher feedback): check tone marks and the use of ni after a question word.

title: Ìbáṣepọ̀ láàrin àwọn àwé gbólóhùn: revising main and dependent clauses
body:
**Objectives:** (1) say how a main clause and a dependent clause relate; (2) separate clauses joined as equals from a clause that depends on another; (3) identify the clause that can stand alone in given sentences; (4) revise using only the school's own examples.

**Scheme wording.** The First-Term scheme (Week 7, language) prints 'Atunyewo lori ibasepo laarin awe gbolohun ede Yoruba' (revision of the relationships between clauses). The school's First-Term Week 5 notes teach sentence types, including gbolohun alakanpo and gbolohun olopo oro-ise, and the Second-Term Week 1 notes teach clause types. This lesson is the First-Term revision that connects them. All Yoruba examples are the school's own, in the notes' unmarked spelling.

**Teaching 1 — clauses joined as equals (alakanpo).** A joining word can combine two simple sentences into one: Ile re tobi, iyara re kere = Ile re tobi sugbon iyara re kere. Two sentences with the same action can be joined with ati: Temidayo lo si ibi ayeye naa + Adeyemi lo si ibi ayeye naa = Temidayo ati Adeyemi lo si ibi ayeye naa. Here neither part depends on the other.

**Teaching 2 — a clause that depends on another (afarahe).** The notes say that a clause that can stand alone as a sentence is the main clause (olori awe gbolohun), for example Aja naa ku, while a dependent clause cannot, for example nigba ti oko ko lu u. The notes name three kinds of dependent clause:
asapejuwe, beginning with ti and following a noun: Apinke ti o sun ti dide (ti o sun describes Apinke).
asodoruko, beginning with pe: Pe oju ka awon ole naa mo dun mo mi.
asaponle, with words such as nigba, ti or nitori ti: Aja naa ku nigba ti oko ko lu u.
**Tip.** Remove the dependent clause. If what is left still makes sense, it is the main clause.

**Practice (questions).**
1. Join with sugbon or ati: Ounje po. Omi kere. / Ayo lo si oja. Ade lo si oja. (4 marks)
2. For each sentence, copy the main clause and the dependent clause: (a) Aja naa ku nigba ti oko ko lu u. (b) Aso Ankara ti mo ra dara. (c) Omoge ti mo n soro re niyi. (6 marks)
3. Say which kind of dependent clause is in (a), (b) and (c) above. (3 marks)
4. Explain why 'nigba ti oko ko lu u' cannot stand alone. (3 marks)
5. Write one sentence of your own with a clause beginning with ti, then underline the main clause. (4 marks)

**Answers and marking guide (20 marks).** 1. Ounje po sugbon omi kere; Ayo ati Ade lo si oja (two marks each). 2. (a) main Aja naa ku, dependent nigba ti oko ko lu u. (b) main Aso Ankara dara, dependent ti mo ra. (c) main Omoge niyi, dependent ti mo n soro re (one mark per part). 3. (a) asaponle, (b) asapejuwe, (c) asapejuwe (one mark each). 4. It has no complete meaning by itself; it depends on the main clause. 5. Accept a sentence where the ti clause describes a noun and the main clause is correctly underlined; judge the sentence, not tone marks. Assessment (teacher feedback): this is revision of the school's own examples; it supplies no new rules.

title: Ọbàtálá: an òrìṣà profile (scheme 'obalale', reading unconfirmed)
body:
**Objectives:** (1) say who Ọbàtálá is in Yoruba belief and what he is credited with; (2) describe the palm-wine episode and what followed from it; (3) name two things associated with him; (4) explain why accounts of the creation story differ.

**Scheme wording and a caution.** The First-Term scheme (Week 7, culture) prints 'Awon orisa ile Yoruba obalale'. 'obalale' is read here as Ọbàtálá, which is a spelling inference: Ọbàtálá is already named in the school's recorded origin story (the Second-Term lesson on oral forms and origin traditions), but Ọbalúayé, another òrìṣà, is also close to the printed word. The reading is unconfirmed and the owner is asked to confirm it; Ọbalúayé is not taught in this lesson. The school's Second-Term notes on the òrìṣà (Ifá, Ògún, Ṣàngó, Èṣù) already list offerings and taboos for those òrìṣà; they contain nothing on Ọbàtálá.

**Teaching (paraphrased from reference works; no verse is quoted).**
1. Standing. In Yoruba belief Olódùmarè, the supreme being, stands above the òrìṣà, and Ọbàtálá, also called Òrìṣànlá, is described as the oldest or greatest of them (SAGE Encyclopedia of African Religion, entry Obatala).
2. Work. He is credited with moulding human beings from clay at Ilé-Ifẹ̀, while Olódùmarè gives them life. For this reason he is called father of humanity, and owner of the heads where human souls dwell (same entry; Wikipedia, Ọbatala).
3. The palm-wine episode. In a well-known account he drank palm wine while at his work and made some people with disabilities. Afterwards he became the protector of people born with disabilities, and drinking palm wine became forbidden to his devotees (SAGE entry). Some versions add that Odùduwà then finished the task.
4. White. White is his colour and white cloth is his symbol; one reference glosses his name as 'king of the white cloth' (Wikipedia).
**Where sources differ.** References disagree about salt and oil in offerings, and this lesson does not list food offerings it could not verify. Ask an elder or a teacher; do not treat the differing points as fact.
**Respect.** This is cultural study. No learner is required to worship or take part in any ritual, and different beliefs are discussed respectfully.

**Practice (questions).**
1. Name Ọbàtálá's work in Yoruba belief and where it is said to have taken place. (3 marks)
2. Tell the palm-wine episode in four sentences and say what followed. (5 marks)
3. Name his colour, his symbol and one taboo for his devotees. (3 marks)
4. Why do versions of the creation story differ, and why should they be discussed respectfully? (4 marks)
5. Copy this table and complete it from the lesson: òrìṣà | work or standing | colour | taboo. Add Ọbàtálá only. (3 marks)
6. Say which printed scheme word is a spelling inference and why. (2 marks)

**Answers and marking guide (20 marks).** 1. Moulding humans from clay at Ilé-Ifẹ̀ (life is given by Olódùmarè). 2. Drank palm wine, made some people with disabilities, became their protector, palm wine forbidden to devotees. 3. White; white cloth; no palm wine. 4. Stories are passed on orally, regions and tellers vary, and people hold different beliefs; accept respectful answers. 5. Ọbàtálá | creator of human bodies, an eldest òrìṣà | white | palm wine. 6. 'obalale' is read as Ọbàtálá, but Ọbalúayé is also close, so the owner is asked to confirm. Assessment (teacher feedback): accept answers in English or Yoruba; do not require worship.

title: Ifáàrà sí lítírésọ̀ alohùn: oral literature with two recorded texts
body:
**Objectives:** (1) explain what oral literature is and why it is performed; (2) name the five parts of a performance and the three kinds of chant; (3) read two recorded texts and describe their language; (4) say what each text shows about the culture it comes from.

**Scheme wording.** The Second-Term scheme prints 'Ifaara lori litireso alohun' (Week 2, literature) and 'Awon asa to suyo lati inu awon ewi alohun' (Week 1, culture). None of the school's executable bodies introduces oral literature; the Week 2 notes on the òrìṣà define only iyere Ifa and ijala in one line each. 'suyo' is kept as printed and is read as 'that come out of'; the reading is unconfirmed. The earlier lessons on oral genres supply profiles but no text; this lesson adds two recorded texts. Text 1 is given in Yoruba with its printed English; Text 2 is an English translation only (of a hunters' chant in the Ijala tradition).

**Teaching.** Oral literature is composed, performed and handed on by mouth rather than by writing. Kolawole (2023) names five parts of an oral performance: the text, the artist, the audience, music and histrionics (gesture and movement). He groups Yoruba chants in three kinds: (a) restricted forms whose words must not change, for example ìyẹ̀rẹ̀ Ifá; (b) forms that began as religious and have taken on entertainment features, for example Ṣàngó pípè, Ọya pípè, ìjálá and èsà egúngún; (c) forms that were secular from the start, for example oríkì orílẹ̀. Chant names are written here in the lesson's tone-marked spelling; the article's own spelling differs in places (it prints Ìyèrèìfa, for example). The NOUN module adds that such poems often belong to the community rather than to a known author and lose much of their life when written and translated.

**Text 1 — the beginning of an Ifá inquiry (Kolawole 2023, p. 86; artist Akano Famoriyo, Odoje Compound, Oyo, Oyo State, 3 December 1987; CC BY-SA 4.0 as stated on the article page). These are lines 1 to 7 of the 12 Yoruba lines the article prints; the other five are not reproduced.**
Yoruba, as printed: Eríwo yà, / Eríwo yà, / Eríwo yà, / Àyà gbó àyà tó / Omo eríwo osinki / Òrúnmìlà Elérìí ìpín / Ikú rí bí àtéwo
English, as printed (the words were checked; the exact line layout, and how 'Eríwo yà' is repeated in the English, could not be confirmed): Eríwo yà (three times) / Aya gbo Aya to / Offspring of Eriwo Osinki / Òrúnmìlà, the sole witness of predestination / Iku is like the palm.
Notes: the article calls the text the beginning of an inquiry process of seeking revelation, and the panegyric of Òrúnmìlà. It keeps 'Eríwo yà' in the English because the words have no English equivalent and because of a tinge of mysticism in them, and it reads the phrase, by inference, as a code that opens the way to Olódùmarè for the diviner. The article says the lines have no variations because the babaláwo (Ifá priest) is forbidden to vary them. After the opening the priest chants the story of an odù, the client is asked whether it fits the purpose of the visit, and in most cases a sacrifice is offered.

**Text 2 — six lines selected from 'Salute to the Elephant', a hunters' praise chant in the Ijala tradition, translated by A. Babalola (NOUN ENG 105 Introduction to Literature II, Module 2, Unit 1, 'Textual Analysis of Poetic Works: African Oral Poetry I'). The poem has 37 printed lines; these are lines 2, 7 to 8, 10, 14 and 17, in printed order, with the lines between them not shown (marked […]). The wording is unchanged and the selection is this app's. First produced by the National Open University of Nigeria; licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/).**
(2) O elephant, huge as a hill, even in a crouching posture
[…]
(7) Mountainous Animal, Huge Beast who tears a man like a garment
(8) And hangs him up on a tree.
[…]
(10) My chant is a salute to the elephant
[…]
(14) O elephant, who single-handily causes a tremor in a dense tropical forest
[…]
(17) The hunter's boast at home is not repeated when he really meets the elephant.
Line numbers count from the poem's first line, as the module's commentary does; 'single-handily' is the module's spelling.
The module notes: hyperbole in the form of descriptive labels or epithets; apostrophe (the repeated 'O elephant', which it says occurs at least fifteen times in the poem); metaphor; simile (it gives 'tears a man like a garment' under that heading); onomatopoeia, with sounds that reinforce the idea that the elephant is extremely big; and ideas stated over and over. It says the poem is best enjoyed in performance, with music, dance and the audience taking part.

**What the texts show about culture.** Text 1: belief that Òrúnmìlà witnesses a person's destiny, the practice of consulting an Ifá priest, and respect for exact words. Text 2: the hunter's world, respect for a dangerous animal, and the saying-in-action that boasting at home is different from meeting the animal.
**Limit.** No Ṣàngó pípè, Ọya pípè or iwì egúngún verse is supplied or invented. A search on 19 October 2026 found none in a source that could be verified and reused, and Kolawole (2023) names these forms but prints no lines for them. No learner is required to take part in worship.

**Practice (questions).**
1. Define oral literature in one sentence and name the five parts of a performance. (5 marks)
2. Name the three kinds of chant with one example of each. (3 marks)
3. Why must the Ifá opening not be changed, and why is 'Eríwo yà' left untranslated? (3 marks)
4. In Text 2 find one simile, one example of repetition and one example of hyperbole. (3 marks)
5. Say what each text shows about the culture it comes from. (4 marks)
6. Why does a printed translation lose something of a performance? (2 marks)

**Answers and marking guide (20 marks).** 1. Literature made and passed on by mouth; text, artist, audience, music, histrionics. 2. Restricted (ìyẹ̀rẹ̀ Ifá), religious turning to entertainment (ìjálá, Ṣàngó pípè, Ọya pípè, èsà egúngún), secular (oríkì orílẹ̀). 3. The article says the babaláwo is forbidden to vary it; 'Eríwo yà' has no English equivalent and carries a tinge of mysticism. 4. Simile: 'tears a man like a garment' (or 'huge as a hill'); repetition: 'O elephant'; hyperbole: 'Mountainous Animal, Huge Beast'. 5. Belief in destiny and consultation of Ifá; hunters' respect for danger and humility. 6. Voice, music, movement and audience are missing, and a translation changes the words. Assessment (teacher feedback): accept answers in English or Yoruba; credit evidence from the texts. Adaptation note: the excerpts are CC BY-SA 4.0 material (Kolawole 2023, © Tydskrif vir Letterkunde; NOUN ENG 105) and may be reused only on those terms. The Kolawole PDF's own front matter says 'Creative Commons Attribution License' while the article page says Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0; the stricter share-alike reading is followed here.

title: Vowel contrast: /ɜː/ and /ɔː/ (scheme prints /3:/ and /c/)
body:
Objectives: tell the long central vowel /ɜː/ from the long back vowel /ɔː/ and from the short vowel of "not"; sort words by sound rather than spelling; say minimal pairs clearly.
Notation note (read first): the scheme prints "Contrasting /3:/ and /c/" in plain keyboard characters. The original .doc contains no symbol-font characters, so nothing more can be recovered from it. In a published plain-text pronunciation guide, 3: is the text form of /ɜː/ (as in her, nurse, learn) and O: the text form of /ɔː/ (as in port, saw). The printed /3:/ is therefore read as /ɜː/. The printed /c/ has no such published equivalent; it is read here as the open-o vowel /ɔ/ by inference, and the scheme does not say whether the long /ɔː/ or the short vowel of "not" is meant. This lesson therefore contrasts /ɜː/ with both. It is not a recovered author's note.
Teaching: /ɜː/ is a long vowel made with the tongue in the centre of the mouth and the lips relaxed, not rounded. Words: bird, girl, nurse, her, fur, learn, turn, work, word, world. /ɔː/ is a long vowel made with the tongue pulled back and the lips rounded. Words: saw, law, caught, thought, door, four, short, torn. The short vowel in not, box and cot is a different, shorter sound; the school's earlier notes on the vowel sounds write it /ɔ/, while British dictionaries write it /ɒ/. Spelling does not decide the sound: "or" is /ɜː/ in word and work but /ɔː/ in short and torn. Use a dictionary with sound recordings to check each word.
Minimal pairs (British reference pronunciation; check each in a dictionary): /ɜː/ against /ɔː/ — bird/board, shirt/short, turn/torn, curt/court, fur/four, learn/lawn. /ɜː/ against the short vowel — hurt/hot, word/wad. Say the pair slowly, round your lips only for the second word of the /ɔː/ pairs, and keep the vowel long. Many speakers in Nigeria merge some of these pairs; assess the learner against the selected reference contrast, not the learner's accent or social background.
Practice A (sorting, say each word aloud first): girl, door, nurse, thought, work, saw, her, caught, learn, four, world, law. Write each word under /ɜː/ or /ɔː/.
Practice B (questions): (1) Which word in each pair has /ɜː/: shirt/short, turn/torn, fur/four? (2) Explain why the letters "or" cannot tell you the sound, using word and short. (3) Describe the lips for /ɜː/ and for /ɔː/. (4) The scheme prints /3:/ and /c/. State one thing this lesson can say about the notation with a source and one thing it cannot.
Practice C (speaking): say "The shirt is too short" and "Turn the torn page", then each minimal pair in a sentence of your own.
Answers and marking guide: A (12 marks, 1 each) /ɜː/: girl, nurse, work, her, learn, world; /ɔː/: door, thought, saw, caught, four, law. B (2 marks each, 8 in all): (1) shirt, turn, fur; (2) word and work have "or" with /ɜː/, short and torn have "or" with /ɔː/, so spelling does not decide; (3) relaxed and unrounded for /ɜː/, rounded for /ɔː/; (4) it can say that a published text guide writes /ɜː/ as 3:, it cannot say what the printed /c/ was meant to be, or whether long or short. Total 20 for the written part. C is assessed by listening, not by writing: award separate observations for vowel length, lip rounding and a clear difference within each pair, and do not infer pronunciation accuracy from a correct written sort.

title: Modal verbs will, would and shall: functions and use
body:
Objectives: use will, would and shall followed by the bare verb; match each to its function (future, promise or decision, request, offer or suggestion, past habit, rule); correct common errors.
Link: the school's First-Term modal-verb lesson lists will, would and shall but gives functions and examples only for must, can, could, may, might, need not and should. This lesson supplies the three missing modals. It is new teaching, not a recovered school note.
Teaching: Like every modal verb, will, would and shall never change their form (no -s, -ed or -ing) and are followed by the bare infinitive, the verb without "to". Questions are made by moving the modal before the subject; negatives add not.
WILL — (1) future prediction or fact: "It will rain tomorrow." (2) a decision made as you speak, or a promise: "I will carry your bag." (3) a request: "Will you open the window?" Negative: will not, shortened won't.
WOULD — (1) polite request or offer: "Would you pass the salt?" "Would you like some tea?" (2) a repeated action in the past: "When we lived in Ibadan, we would visit the market every Saturday." (3) the future seen from the past, as in reported speech: "She said she would arrive by noon." (4) an imagined result: "If I had the money, I would buy a bicycle." Negative: would not, wouldn't.
SHALL — (1) an offer or suggestion with I or we, in questions: "Shall I open the door?" "Shall we begin?" (2) a formal rule or legal duty: "Students shall not enter the laboratory alone." (3) a formal future with I or we: "I shall see you tomorrow"; in everyday speech people usually say will instead. Negative: shall not, rare shortened form shan't.
Practice A: name the function of the modal in each sentence. (1) Shall we begin? (2) I will call you tonight. (3) Would you close the door, please? (4) When we were children, we would play outside until dark. (5) Candidates shall not leave the hall before the bell. (6) He said he would come early.
Practice B: correct each sentence. (1) She wills come tomorrow. (2) He would goes to school early. (3) Will you to help me?
Practice C: write one sentence for each of these: will as a promise; would as a polite request; shall as an offer.
Answers and marking guide: A (1 mark each, 6) (1) suggestion; (2) promise or decision about the future; (3) polite request; (4) repeated action in the past; (5) formal rule; (6) future seen from the past in reported speech. B (1 mark each, 3) (1) She will come tomorrow. (2) He would go to school early. (3) Will you help me? C (2 marks each, 6): 1 mark for the correct modal and bare verb, 1 mark for a sentence that clearly shows the stated function; for example "I will help you tomorrow", "Would you lend me your pen?", "Shall I carry that for you?" Total 15. Accept any correct sentence. Do not reduce marks for the older rule that shall goes with I and we in plain statements, but teach that will is now usual.

title: Revision of JSS 2 work: number, algebra, geometry and data skills
body:
Objectives: revise the number, algebra, geometry and data skills on which the JSS 3 First-Term topics depend (binary numbers need division and powers; algebraic processes, word problems, change of subject and equations need fractions, brackets and equation solving; statistics needs the mean).
Teaching:
1. Fractions: use a common denominator. Worked example: 3/4 + 5/6. The lowest common multiple of 4 and 6 is 12, so 9/12 + 10/12 = 19/12 = 1 7/12.
2. Decimals and percentages: to multiply decimals, multiply as whole numbers and then place the decimal point. 2.5 x 0.04: 25 x 4 = 100, and there are three decimal places altogether, so the answer is 0.1. To increase 8 000 by 15%, multiply by 1.15: 8 000 x 1.15 = 9200.
3. Ratio: to share 560 in the ratio 3 : 5, add the parts (3 + 5 = 8), find one part (560 / 8 = 70), then 3 x 70 = 210 and 5 x 70 = 350.
4. Indices: a^m x a^n = a^(m + n) and a^m / a^n = a^(m - n). Worked example: 2^3 x 2^4 = 2^7 = 128. Powers of 2 are used again when you convert to binary.
5. Algebra: remove brackets by multiplying every term, then collect like terms. 3(2x - 5) - 2(x - 4) = 6x - 15 - 2x + 8 = 4x - 7. To factorise, take out the highest common factor: 12a + 18 = 6(2a + 3). To solve an equation, do the same to both sides: 5x - 7 = 3x + 9, so 2x = 16 and x = 8. Check: 5(8) - 7 = 33 and 3(8) + 9 = 33.
6. Geometry: angles on a straight line add up to 180 degrees. Area of a triangle = 1/2 x base x height.
7. Data: mean = sum of the values / number of values. The mean of 4, 7, 9, 12 and 13 is (4 + 7 + 9 + 12 + 13) / 5 = 9.
Source note: the JSS 3 First-Term scheme lists only 'Revision of JSS 2 work' with no topics. This selection of prerequisite skills is a replacement chosen for the JSS 3 topics that follow; it is not the school's own JSS 2 list.
Practice (questions):
1. Work out 2/3 + 3/4.
2. Work out 3.2 x 0.05.
3. Decrease 12 500 by 12%.
4. Share 840 kg in the ratio 2 : 5.
5. Evaluate (3^2 x 3^3) / 3^4.
6. Expand and simplify 4(x + 3) - 3(2x - 1).
7. Factorise 15m - 25.
8. Solve 7x + 4 = 3x + 28.
9. Two angles on a straight line are (2x + 10) degrees and (3x + 20) degrees. Find x and both angles.
10. A triangle has base 14 cm and height 9 cm. Find its area.
11. Find the mean of 6, 9, 11, 14 and 15.
Answers and marking guide: 1 17/12 = 1 5/12 (2 marks: 1 for the common denominator 12, 1 for the answer). 2 0.16 (2: 1 for 32 x 5 = 160 or equivalent working, 1 for placing three decimal places and simplifying 0.160). 3 12 500 x 0.88 = 11000 (2). 4 240 kg and 600 kg (3: 1 for 7 parts, 1 for one part = 120, 1 for both shares). 5 3^(2 + 3 - 4) = 3^1 = 3 (2). 6 4x + 12 - 6x + 3 = -2x + 15 (3: 1 for each correct expansion, 1 for the collected answer). 7 5(3m - 5) (2). 8 4x = 24, x = 6 (3: 1 for each correct step, 1 for the check). 9 5x + 30 = 180, so x = 30; the angles are 70 degrees and 110 degrees, which add up to 180 (4: 1 for the equation, 1 for x, 1 for each angle). 10 1/2 x 14 x 9 = 63 square centimetres (2). 11 (6 + 9 + 11 + 14 + 15) / 5 = 55 / 5 = 11 (2). Total 27 marks.
Assessment and feedback: 20 or more shows secure prerequisites. Group errors by skill (fractions, percentages, ratio, indices, brackets, equations, geometry, data). Re-teach the weakest skill using short examples before the related JSS 3 topic begins. Check units and the final check step in question 8.

title: Variation: worked examples and exercises for direct, inverse, joint and partial variation
body:
Objectives: write and use equations for direct, inverse, joint and partial variation; find the constant from given values; solve word problems on each type; recognise which type a situation shows.
Teaching: The earlier variation notes define the four types and work two examples (direct and inverse). Joint and partial variation have definitions but no worked example or exercise in the notes. This lesson supplies them.
Forms: direct, y = kx; inverse, y = k/x (so xy = k); joint, z = kxy (z varies as the product of x and y); partial, y = a + bx, where one part is fixed and one part varies. Method: (1) write the relation with its constant; (2) put in the given values and find the constant; (3) write the full equation; (4) substitute the new value.
Worked example 1 (direct): y varies directly as x and y = 12 when x = 4. k = 12 / 4 = 3, so y = 3x. When x = 7, y = 21.
Worked example 2 (inverse): y varies inversely as x and y = 6 when x = 4. k = xy = 4 x 6 = 24, so y = 24/x. When y = 8, x = 24 / 8 = 3.
Worked example 3 (joint): z varies jointly as x and y and z = 60 when x = 3 and y = 4. k = 60 / (3 x 4) = 5, so z = 5xy. When x = 6 and y = 5, z = 5 x 6 x 5 = 150.
Worked example 4 (partial): a cost c = a + bt, where t is the time in hours. c = 1 000 when t = 2 and c = 1 900 when t = 5. Subtract: 3b = 900, so b = 300. Then a = 1 000 - 2 x 300 = 400. So c = 400 + 300t. When t = 8, c = 400 + 300 x 8 = 2800.
Source note: the methods are standard school treatments of variation (see sources); the numbers, contexts and exercises are new, and every answer was computed for this lesson.
Practice (questions):
1. p varies directly as q and p = 15 when q = 6. Find p when q = 10.
2. The cost of rice varies directly with its mass. 5 kg cost 9 000 naira. Find the cost of 8 kg.
3. y varies inversely as x and y = 5 when x = 12. Find y when x = 15.
4. The number of days a job takes varies inversely with the number of workers. 6 workers finish it in 10 days. How many days will 15 workers take?
5. The mass M of a metal sheet varies jointly with its area A and thickness t. M = 18 g when A = 30 square centimetres and t = 0.2 cm. Find M when A = 50 square centimetres and t = 0.4 cm.
6. z varies jointly as x and y, and z = 40 when x = 5 and y = 2. Find x when z = 60 and y = 3.
7. A taxi fare is partly fixed and partly varies with the distance d in km: c = a + bd. The fare is 1 300 naira for 4 km and 2 200 naira for 7 km. Find a and b, then the fare for 10 km.
8. y = k1 p + k2 v (partial variation). y = 17 when p = 2 and v = 3, and y = 18 when p = 3 and v = 2. Find k1 and k2, then y when p = 5 and v = 4.
9. Name the type of variation (direct, inverse, joint or partial): (a) the distance travelled at a steady speed and the time taken; (b) the time to fill a tank and the number of identical pipes used; (c) the area of a rectangle and its length and width; (d) the cost of hiring a hall: a fixed fee plus a charge for each hour.
Answers and marking guide: 1 k = 15/6 = 2.5, so p = 2.5 x 10 = 25 (2: 1 for k, 1 for p). 2 k = 9 000 / 5 = 1800 naira per kg, so 8 kg cost 14400 naira (3: 1 for the relation, 1 for k, 1 for the cost). 3 k = 12 x 5 = 60; y = 60 / 15 = 4 (2). 4 k = 6 x 10 = 60 worker-days; days = 60 / 15 = 4 (3: 1 for recognising inverse, 1 for k, 1 for the answer). 5 k = 18 / (30 x 0.2) = 3; M = 3 x 50 x 0.4 = 60 g (3: 1 for the joint form, 1 for k, 1 for M). 6 k = 40 / (5 x 2) = 4; 60 = 4 x x x 3, so x = 5 (3). 7 Subtract: 3b = 900, b = 300; a = 1 300 - 4 x 300 = 100; fare for 10 km = 100 + 300 x 10 = 3100 naira (4: 1 for b, 1 for a, 1 for the fare formula, 1 for the fare). 8 2k1 + 3k2 = 17 and 3k1 + 2k2 = 18; eliminating gives k1 = 4, k2 = 3; y = 4 x 5 + 3 x 4 = 32 (4: 1 for each equation, 1 for both constants, 1 for y). 9 (a) direct (b) inverse (c) joint (d) partial; 1 mark each (4). Total 28 marks.
Assessment and feedback: 22 or more shows secure understanding. Check that the constant was found before the final substitution, that the type was named from the situation, and that partial variation was solved with two equations. Learners who confuse joint with partial variation should compare z = kxy (a product) with y = a + bx (a sum of a fixed and a varying part).

title: Preparation for motherhood, signs of labour and childbirth
origin: New teaching material prepared under the owner's 16 October 2026 authorisation to provide lessons where no executable body teaches a scheme objective; not recovered school-source text. The Third-Term scheme lines 'Preparation for motherhood' (SL-541) and 'Pregnancy and child birth' (SL-542) are only partly taught by the redistributed row 'PREGNACY AND CHILDBIRTH', which teaches signs of pregnancy, ante-natal and post-natal care and the baby layette but not preparation for motherhood as a topic, the signs of labour or the stages of childbirth. This lesson adds them. The original row is unchanged. It is school teaching, not medical advice.

sources.title: Signs that labour has begun — NHS

body:
Objectives: describe how a woman, her partner and family prepare for motherhood; recognise the signs of labour and the danger signs that need urgent help; outline the three stages of childbirth; state the care needed straight after birth.

Teaching:
1. Preparing for motherhood. Health: attend an ante-natal clinic regularly, eat a balanced diet, rest, take only prescribed drugs and avoid alcohol and smoking (see the ante-natal care list in the Pregnancy lesson). Practical: collect the baby layette, save a little money, decide where the baby will be born with a skilled attendant (a doctor, nurse or midwife) and how to get there quickly, even at night. Emotional: talk with the partner and family, accept help, and learn about breastfeeding and baby care.
2. Signs that labour is beginning: contractions (tightening of the womb) that become longer, stronger and more frequent; a 'show' (a sticky mucus plug passes); backache; the waters breaking. When labour is suspected, contact the health facility or skilled birth attendant.
3. Danger signs needing urgent help at any time in late pregnancy or labour: vaginal bleeding, severe headache or blurred vision, fits, fever, the baby moving much less, waters breaking early or smelling bad or coloured, and labour starting before the expected time. Go to a health facility at once.
4. Stages of childbirth: first stage, the opening of the womb entrance (cervix) as contractions strengthen; second stage, the birth of the baby; third stage, the delivery of the afterbirth (placenta). A skilled attendant checks mother and baby throughout.
5. Straight after birth: keep the baby warm and dry, put the baby to the breast early so that the first milk (colostrum) is received, and let the mother rest. Post-natal checks for mother and baby follow in the first six weeks.

Worked example: Ada is 36 weeks pregnant. She has packed her layette and a bag, told her sister where the clinic is and arranged transport. At night she feels regular, strengthening contractions and her waters break. Because her waters have broken, she goes to the clinic at once instead of waiting.

Practice (questions):
1. State three things a woman can do to prepare for motherhood.
2. List three signs that labour may be starting.
3. Name three danger signs that need urgent help.
4. Name the three stages of childbirth and say what happens in each.
5. Why is a skilled attendant important at birth?
6. Why should a baby be put to the breast early?
7. Explain why a school lesson on childbirth does not replace advice from a health worker.

Answers and marking guide:
1. Any three (3): regular ante-natal visits, balanced diet and rest, avoiding alcohol and unprescribed drugs, preparing the layette, planning where and how to reach the birth place, saving money, learning about baby care.
2. Any three (3): contractions that strengthen, a 'show', backache, waters breaking.
3. Any three (3): bleeding, severe headache or blurred vision, fits, fever, much reduced baby movement, early or abnormal waters.
4. Opening of the cervix (1); birth of the baby (1); delivery of the placenta (1).
5. To check mother and baby, notice danger signs early and give help quickly (2).
6. The first milk (colostrum) protects the baby and breast-feeding comforts and bonds mother and baby (2).
7. Each pregnancy is different and only a health worker can examine and advise the person concerned (1).

Assessment and feedback: total 17 marks. Teach this lesson factually and respectfully; invite a nurse or midwife to answer learners' questions where possible. This content is general school education, not medical advice.

title: Food hygiene and safety, responsible food management, packaging and marketing of food
origin: New teaching material prepared under the owner's 16 October 2026 authorisation to provide lessons where no executable body teaches a scheme objective; not recovered school-source text. The Third-Term scheme line 'Revision of last terms work: food hygiene and safety, responsible food management, preparation, packaging and marketing of food items' names topics that no Second-Term executable row teaches: the Second-Term rows cover the scientific study of food, budgeting, feeding the family, nutritional needs, buying and storage, and food preparation, but contain no food hygiene and safety, packaging or marketing. sources.title: Five keys to safer food — PAHO/WHO

body:
Objectives: state the rules of personal and kitchen hygiene; apply the five keys to safer food; manage food responsibly; package and label a home-made food item; work out a selling price.

Teaching:
1. Personal hygiene: wash hands with soap and clean water before handling food, after the toilet and after touching raw meat or fish; keep nails short and clean; tie or cover the hair; cover cuts; do not cough or sneeze over food.
2. Kitchen hygiene: clean surfaces, knives, boards and utensils before and after use; keep dustbins covered and kitchens free from flies, rats and cockroaches; use clean, safe water.
3. The five keys to safer food (PAHO/WHO): keep clean; separate raw and cooked food; cook thoroughly; keep food at safe temperatures (do not leave cooked food at room temperature for more than two hours; keep cooked food piping hot above 60 degrees Celsius or cold, preferably below 5 degrees); use safe water and safe raw materials. Where there is no refrigerator, cook what will be eaten soon and reheat any leftovers thoroughly.
4. Responsible food management: plan meals and buy to a budget; use older stock first; store dry foods in covered containers; use leftovers safely; avoid waste (peels, bones and spoiled food are waste to be reduced, not ignored).
5. Packaging: packaging protects food from dirt, keeps it fresh, makes it easy to carry and carries information. Use clean, food-safe, well-sealed containers or wrappers of the right size. A label should show the name of the food, the main ingredients, the date made or the use-by date, and the seller's name and contact. Selling food beyond the home may need official registration; the teacher should explain the current rules.
6. Marketing home-prepared food: know the customers, keep quality and hygiene consistent, set a fair price, choose where and when to sell, and record sales. Selling price = total cost + profit.

Worked example: A girl bakes 20 meat pies. Ingredients and fuel cost 6,000 naira and packaging costs 400 naira, so total cost is 6,400 naira. She wants a 25 per cent profit: profit = 6,400 x 25/100 = 1,600 naira. Total selling amount = 6,400 + 1,600 = 8,000 naira. Price of one pie = 8,000 / 20 = 400 naira.

Practice (questions):
1. State four rules of personal hygiene for a food handler.
2. Name the five keys to safer food.
3. Why should raw meat and cooked food be kept apart?
4. How long may cooked food be left at room temperature, at most?
5. Give two ways of managing food responsibly at home.
6. List four items for the label of a packed snack.
7. A learner makes 30 buns. Ingredients and fuel cost 4,500 naira and packaging 300 naira. She wants a profit of 20 per cent. Find the selling price of one bun.

Answers and marking guide:
1. Any four (4): wash hands with soap; short clean nails; cover hair; cover cuts; do not cough over food; wash after the toilet.
2. Keep clean; separate raw and cooked; cook thoroughly; keep food at safe temperatures; use safe water and raw materials (5).
3. Raw meat can carry germs that would spread to food that will not be cooked again (2).
4. Two hours (1).
5. Any two (2): plan and budget; first in, first out; covered storage; safe use of leftovers; avoid waste.
6. Any four (4): name of food; main ingredients; date made or use-by date; seller's name; contact.
7. Total cost 4,500 + 300 = 4,800 naira (1); profit 4,800 x 20/100 = 960 naira (1); total 5,760 naira (1); one bun 5,760 / 30 = 192 naira (1).

Assessment and feedback: total 22 marks. Practical follow-up: learners prepare and label one simple item following the hygiene rules; assess hands-on hygiene by observation, not by the written test alone.

title: Bathing and dressing a baby, and cleaning and sterilising baby's feeding equipment

sources.title: Sterilising baby bottles — NHS

body:
Objectives: bathe and dress a baby in a safe order; choose suitable baby clothes; clean and sterilise baby feeding equipment correctly.

Teaching:
1. Bathing steps. Get everything ready first (the items in the Child Care lesson, clean clothes, a nappy). Wash your hands. Choose a warm room without a draught. Make the water comfortably warm and test it with your elbow. Never leave the baby alone, even for a moment. Wash the face with a clean damp cloth, then the body from top to bottom, including the folds of the neck, arms and groin. Rinse, lift the baby into a towel, pat dry (do not rub) and dress at once.
2. Clothing. Choose soft, loose clothes that open easily and are made of materials that absorb sweat. Dress the baby in layers suited to the weather and avoid overheating. Change clothes when they are wet or soiled. Put a cap on the baby in cool weather.
3. Cleaning feeding equipment. Equipment is cleaned and sterilised because germs left in bottles and teats can cause diarrhoea and vomiting. Wash your hands. Wash bottles, teats and other equipment in hot soapy water as soon as possible after a feed, using a bottle brush kept only for this job and a small brush for the inside of teats. Do not use salt to clean teats. Rinse in clean running water. Check that teats and bottles are not torn or cracked.
4. Sterilising. After washing, sterilise equipment that is safe to boil by boiling it in a clean covered pan of water for at least ten minutes, or use a steriliser following the maker's instructions. Keep sterilised items covered until needed and put teats and lids on at once. Sterilising does not replace washing. The NHS advises sterilising feeding equipment until the baby is at least 12 months old. A cup and spoon are easier to clean than a bottle.

Worked example: Bisi puts the baby's soft towel, clean clothes and nappy within reach, washes her hands and tests the water with her elbow. After the bath she dries the baby and dresses her at once. She later washes the bottle with a brush, rinses it, boils it in a covered pan and leaves it covered until the next feed.

Practice (questions):
1. Why should everything be ready before the bath begins?
2. How do you test the temperature of the bath water?
3. Why must a baby never be left alone in the bath?
4. State two qualities of good baby clothes.
5. Put these in order: wash with hot soapy water; rinse; sterilise; leave covered until needed.
6. Why is salt not used to clean teats?
7. Why is washing still needed before sterilising?

Answers and marking guide:
1. You cannot leave the baby to fetch something (1).
2. With the elbow, so that it feels comfortably warm (1).
3. A baby can slip under water and drown or be hurt in seconds (1).
4. Any two (2): soft, loose, easy to open, absorbent, suitable for the weather.
5. Wash; rinse; sterilise; leave covered (4: one mark each).
6. It can be dangerous for the baby (1).
7. Sterilising does not remove milk and dirt, and germs hide in them (2).

Assessment and feedback: total 12 marks. A demonstration with a doll and a bottle can be assessed by observation: hands washed, items ready, order of steps correct, no unsafe shortcut.

body:
Objectives: choose, plan, carry out, report and present a small Home Economics project; revise the year's topics for the examination.

Teaching: A project answers one question by doing something practical and recording it. Steps: (1) choose a topic from the year's work, for example a baby layette, a one-week family menu and budget, a fabric-care sample book, or hygiene rules for a school snack stall; (2) write the aim in one sentence; (3) list materials and their cost; (4) make a timetable; (5) do the work, keeping notes, sketches or photographs; (6) write the report: title, aim, materials and cost, procedure, what you observed, conclusion, what you would improve; (7) present it to the class.

Revision plan across the year: textiles (fibres, fabric care, design elements, dress for occasions, sewing machine and its faults); food and nutrition (scientific study of food, budgeting, meal planning, nutritional needs, buying and storage, food preparation, hygiene); family living (relationships, courtship and marriage, pregnancy and childbirth, child care, child development). For each unit write three questions and answer them without notes, then check against the notes.

Worked example: Topic: a one-week menu for a family of five. Aim: to plan balanced meals within a budget of 15,000 naira. Materials and cost: a price list from the local market. Procedure: plan seven dinners, list foods from the body-building, energy-giving and protective groups, add the prices and total them. Observation: the cost came to 14,200 naira, leaving 800 naira. Conclusion: the plan fits the budget. Improvement: use more local vegetables when they are in season.

Practice (questions):
1. List the seven parts of a project report.
2. Write an aim for a project on fabric care.
3. Why must the cost of materials be recorded?
4. Choose one unit from the revision plan and write three questions on it.
5. State one safety or hygiene rule you will follow in your project.

Answers and marking guide:
1. Title, aim, materials and cost, procedure, observation, conclusion, improvement (7 marks, one each).
2. An aim stating what will be found out or made, for example 'To compare how cotton and polyester cloth wash and dry' (2).
3. To show whether the project fits the budget and to plan a repeat (1).
4. Three clear questions on one unit (3).
5. Any relevant rule, for example washing hands before handling food or testing an iron on a scrap of cloth (1).
Project marking scheme, out of 20: topic and aim 3; planning and cost 4; practical work and neatness 5; report 5; presentation 3.

Assessment and feedback: written practice 14 marks; project 20 marks. Return each project with one strength and one improvement. Where the school's or examination body's own project requirements exist, follow them and use this frame only to organise the work.

title: Identifying cadences: authentic, plagal, half and deceptive
body:
Objectives: define a cadence; spell the four chords used in cadences in C major and G major; name and recognise authentic, plagal, half and deceptive cadences; and say how each one sounds.
Link to your Week 5 notes: the notes say a cadence ends a phrase, that cadences are divided into four types (authentic, plagal, half, deceptive), and explain the authentic cadence V to I. This lesson supplies the other three types and a method for identifying all four. When four voices sing in parts (soprano, alto, tenor, bass), the bass line normally sings the root of each chord, so you can hear the cadence in the bass.
Teaching - the chords: a chord is built on a scale note. Number the notes of the key. In C major: I = C-E-G, IV = F-A-C, V = G-B-D, vi = A-C-E. In G major: I = G-B-D, IV = C-E-G, V = D-F#-A, vi = E-G-B. A cadence is described by the last two chords of a phrase.
1. Authentic cadence: V to I. In C major, G-B-D then C-E-G. It sounds finished, like a full stop. (A perfect authentic cadence has both chords in root position with the tonic note on top of the last chord; your notes give this definition.)
2. Plagal cadence: IV to I. In C major, F-A-C then C-E-G. It also sounds finished but softer. It is often heard on the word 'Amen' at the end of a hymn.
3. Half cadence: the phrase ends on V, whatever chord came before it. In C major the last chord is G-B-D. It sounds unfinished, like a comma or a question, and makes you expect more music.
4. Deceptive cadence: V is followed by a chord other than I, most often vi. In C major, G-B-D then A-C-E. You expect C-E-G and hear something else, so the ending 'deceives' the ear.
In a minor key the pattern is the same with the minor tonic: in A minor, V (E-G#-B) to i (A-C-E) is authentic.
How to identify a cadence: (1) find the key; (2) look at the last two chords of the phrase; (3) turn them into numbers (I, IV, V, vi); (4) match: V-I authentic, IV-I plagal, anything-V half, V-vi deceptive. Then use your ear to check: finished (authentic, plagal) or unfinished (half, deceptive).
Worked example: a phrase in G major ends with C-E-G then G-B-D. C-E-G is IV and G-B-D is I, so this is a plagal cadence.
Source note: the definitions follow standard music-theory references (see sources). The chord spellings, examples and questions are new. Hearing a cadence needs a teacher or classmate to play or sing it; this written lesson cannot certify listening or singing.
Practice (questions):
1. Write the notes of I, IV, V and vi in C major.
2. Name the cadence: (a) V to I in C major; (b) IV to I in C major; (c) a phrase that ends on the chord G-B-D in C major; (d) G-B-D then A-C-E in C major; (e) in G major, D-F#-A then G-B-D; (f) in G major, C-E-G then G-B-D; (g) in G major, any chord then D-F#-A.
3. Which two types sound finished, and which two sound unfinished?
4. In G major, write two chords (with note names) for each of the four cadences.
5. Why does a deceptive cadence surprise the listener?
6. Teacher-led listening (not marked here): the teacher plays or sings short phrases; the class names the cadence.
Answers and marking guide:
1 (1 mark each, 4): I = C-E-G; IV = F-A-C; V = G-B-D; vi = A-C-E.
2 (1 mark each, 7): (a) authentic; (b) plagal; (c) half; (d) deceptive; (e) authentic (V to I); (f) plagal (IV to I); (g) half (ends on V).
3 (2 marks): authentic and plagal sound finished; half and deceptive sound unfinished.
4 (2 marks each, 8; both chords must be correct): authentic D-F#-A then G-B-D; plagal C-E-G then G-B-D; half any chord then D-F#-A (for example G-B-D then D-F#-A); deceptive D-F#-A then E-G-B.
5 (2 marks): the listener expects V to go to I (the home chord) but hears another chord, usually vi, so the music does not come to rest. One mark for 'expects I', one for 'hears a different chord'.
Assessment and feedback: total 23 marks. 20-23 secure; 14-19 developing (re-spell the chords in question 1 and redo question 2); below 14 reteach with the teacher playing each cadence slowly. Question 6 is observed by the teacher and is not part of the mark.

title: Singing minor scales with tonic sol-fa
body:
Objectives: find the relative minor of a major key; sing the natural, harmonic and melodic minor scales on tonic sol-fa; name the raised notes; and check your own singing against a short list.
Link to your Week 7 notes: they say a natural minor scale starts on the sixth note of its relative major, that the natural minor pattern is W, H, W, W, H, W, W, that the harmonic minor raises the seventh note by a semitone, and that the melodic minor raises the sixth and seventh notes going up and descends like the natural minor. This lesson shows how to sing those scales. Your Music notes on transcription from staff to sol-fa already write A minor with 'se' for the raised seventh; this lesson follows the same usage.
Teaching - la-based minor: in tonic sol-fa the home note of a minor key is lah (l). Doh is a minor third above lah. The relative minor of C major is A minor (lah = A, doh = C); of G major it is E minor (lah = E, doh = G); of D major it is B minor; of F major it is D minor.
Natural minor in sol-fa: l t d r m f s l'. In A minor: A B C D E F G A. These are the same notes as C major, started on lah. Sing it down: l' s f m r d t l.
Harmonic minor: raise the seventh note of the minor scale (soh) by a semitone, written 'se'. A minor: A B C D E F G# A. Sol-fa up: l t d r m f se l'. There is a step of one and a half tones between f (F) and se (G#); listen for this 'gap'. Down: l' se f m r d t l.
Melodic minor: going up, raise the sixth and seventh notes (fah and soh): l t d r m fe se l'. In A minor: A B C D E F# G# A. Coming down, sing the natural minor: l' s f m r d t l. Names differ between books: the raised fah is written 'fe' in many notes and 'ba' in Curwen's own system; the pitch is the same, so use the name your teacher's book uses.
E minor (one sharp, F#): natural E F# G A B C D E, sol-fa l t d r m f s l'. Harmonic: raise D to D#. Melodic up: raise C to C# and D to D#.
How to practise singing a minor scale: (1) sing the relative major scale first (d r m f s l t d') so the key is in your ear; (2) hold the home note lah; (3) sing the scale slowly in tune, saying the sol-fa names clearly; (4) repeat with a steady pulse and good breath control; (5) sing it with a partner who listens for the raised notes. Your teacher will model how the raised syllables are sung.
Source note: the sol-fa names for minor follow standard tonic sol-fa references (see sources); the exercises are new. A written lesson cannot certify singing; the singing task below is observed by the teacher or a partner.
Practice (questions):
1. Write the sol-fa names of the A natural minor scale ascending and descending.
2. In the harmonic minor, which note is raised? Give its sol-fa name, and its letter name in A minor and in E minor.
3. Write the melodic minor scale in sol-fa going up and coming down.
4. Give the relative minor of D major and of F major.
5. Singing task (observed): sing A natural minor, A harmonic minor and A melodic minor on sol-fa. A partner ticks: (a) starts on lah; (b) every note in tune; (c) raised notes sung correctly.
Answers and marking guide:
1 (2 marks each way, 4): up l t d r m f s l'; down l' s f m r d t l.
2 (4 marks, one each): the seventh note of the minor scale (soh) is raised by a semitone; its name is se; in A minor G becomes G#; in E minor D becomes D#.
3 (4 marks, 2 each way): up l t d r m fe se l' (fe may be written ba); down l' s f m r d t l.
4 (2 marks): B minor and D minor.
5 (6 marks, 2 per tick, scored by the observer): does not replace teacher judgement.
Assessment and feedback: total 20 marks. 17-20 secure; 12-16 developing (sing the relative major first and repeat); below 12 reteach with a drone note on lah.

title: Dater et mesurer le temps: la date, l'heure, depuis, pendant et il y a
body:
Objectifs / Objectives: say and write the date and the time in French; measure time with depuis, pendant and il y a; and avoid the usual mistakes.
Link to your Week 2 notes: your notes list important dates, give the dialogue 'Les problèmes de l'embouteillage' ('je t'attends depuis deux heures', 'j'ai passé quarante-cinq minutes') and explain that depuis measures duration. This lesson gives the rules behind those examples.
1. La date (the date). Ask: Quelle est la date ? or On est le combien ? Answer: C'est le + number + month. Use ordinary numbers (le deux mars, le quatorze février, le vingt-cinq décembre). The only exception is the first of the month: le premier (le 1er). Days and months do not take capital letters. The order is day, month, year: le 14 février 2027. Examples: le premier janvier; le premier mai; le premier octobre; le vingt-cinq décembre. Dates of public holidays can change, so check a current calendar.
2. L'heure (the time). Quelle heure est-il ? Il est + number + heure(s). Il est une heure. Il est deux heures quinze (or deux heures et quart). Il est sept heures et demie. Il est cinq heures moins le quart (4:45). Midi = noon; minuit = midnight. A quelle heure ? À + time: à huit heures vingt (your Week 6 notes use this for the school day).
3. Mesurer le temps (measuring time).
- depuis = for or since; the action is still going on now. Use the present tense. J'attends depuis deux heures (I have been waiting for two hours). Elle habite à Lagos depuis cinq ans. With a point in time: Je suis ici depuis lundi. Question: Depuis quand ? (since when?).
- pendant = for, a completed period with a beginning and an end. Nous avons joué pendant une heure. J'ai dormi pendant huit heures.
- il y a + period = ago, with a past verb. Il est arrivé il y a trois jours (he arrived three days ago). Elle est partie il y a une semaine.
Compare: Je suis à Abuja depuis trois jours (still there). Je suis arrivé à Abuja il y a trois jours (arrival was three days ago). Je suis resté à Abuja pendant trois jours (stay is over).
Common mistakes: (a) using the passé composé with depuis for something still going on - use the present; (b) confusing il y a (ago) with il y a meaning 'there is' (il y a trop d'embouteillage); (c) writing capital letters for months and days.
Note for the teacher: in the Week 6 dialogue the line 'maman est partie au village depuis trois jours' would normally be 'maman est partie au village il y a trois jours' or 'maman est au village depuis trois jours'. The original text is kept unchanged in the lesson row.
Source note: the rules follow standard French grammar references (see sources); the sentences and exercises are new.
Practice (questions):
1. Write in words, in French: 3/5; 1/1; 14/2; 25/12; 1/10.
2. Write the time in French: 2:15; 7:30; 4:45; 12:00 (noon).
3. Choose depuis, pendant or il y a: (a) Je t'attends ___ deux heures. (b) Il est arrivé ___ trois jours. (c) Nous avons joué au football ___ une heure. (d) Elle habite à Lagos ___ cinq ans. (e) Ma mère est partie au village ___ une semaine. (f) J'ai dormi ___ huit heures.
4. Translate: (a) I have been waiting for two hours. (b) He arrived two days ago. (c) We stayed in Abuja for three days.
5. Write four sentences about your own week, using the date or time in two of them and depuis, pendant or il y a in the others.
Réponses / Answers and marking guide:
1 (1 mark each, 5): le trois mai; le premier janvier; le quatorze février; le vingt-cinq décembre; le premier octobre.
2 (1 mark each, 4): Il est deux heures quinze (or deux heures et quart); Il est sept heures et demie; Il est cinq heures moins le quart (or quatre heures quarante-cinq); Il est midi.
3 (1 mark each, 6): (a) depuis; (b) il y a; (c) pendant; (d) depuis; (e) il y a; (f) pendant.
4 (2 marks each, 6): J'attends depuis deux heures. Il est arrivé il y a deux jours. Nous sommes restés à Abuja pendant trois jours.
5 (8 marks): 2 per sentence: 1 for the correct date, time or time word, 1 for a correct verb form. Accept any true sentences.
Assessment and feedback: total 29 marks. 25-29 secure; 18-24 developing (redo question 3 with the three-line comparison above); below 18 reteach with a calendar and clock. Spoken accuracy is checked by the teacher, not by this written task.
