sources.title: OpenStax Introductory Statistics 2e — frequency tables

body:
Objectives: tally data, construct frequency tables, interpret and draw pictograms and single/dual bar charts, calculate pie-chart angles and percentages.
Teaching: frequency counts occurrences. Check that all frequencies sum to the number of observations. Relative frequency=f/total; percentage=100f/total. A pictogram uses a stated key consistently, including partial symbols. Bar charts use separate equally wide bars, a labelled frequency axis beginning at zero and a consistent scale. A dual bar chart puts two labelled series side by side for each category with a key. Pie-sector angle=360f/total; angles sum to 360°, percentages to 100%.
Worked source-data check: the 30 phone-call observations give calls 4,5,6,7,8,9,10 with frequencies 3,7,4,9,5,0,2. Total 30; mode 7 calls; 8-call percentage=5/30×100=16 2/3%≈16.7%, not exactly 16%. Draw seven equal-width bars of those heights, including the zero-frequency category.
Worked pictogram: black20, white17, red8, yellow5, green10 cars. With one circle=2 cars, use 10 circles, 8½, 4, 2½, 5 respectively; label a half circle=1 car. Total60. For a bar chart use the same categories with heights20,17,8,5,10; do not replace counts by symbol counts.
Worked dual chart: for years1997,1998,1999,2000,2001, boys65,50,80,70,45 and girls46,55,73,92,64. Draw adjacent boy/girl bars for each year on one scale. Girls highest:2000; boys lowest:2001; 1999 difference=80-73=7. Total2000=162 versus1998=105, increase57.
Worked pie chart: expenditure20,25,70,25,10 million naira totals150. Sector angles are48°,60°,168°,60°,24°. Building projects take70/150×100=46 2/3%≈46.7% (a percentage, not46.7°). Mark sectors cumulatively with a protractor and a key; their angles sum360°.
Practice: 1 For data1,2,2,3,3,3,4,4,4,4 make a frequency table and find the percentage of4s. 2 Draw a pictogram for counts6,9,3 with one symbol=3. 3 Draw a pie chart for those same counts. 4 A class has500 pupils; Physics20%, History40%, Geography30%, Further Mathematics10%. Give sector angles, number studying Physics and fraction studying History.
Answers/assessment: 1 frequencies1,2,3,4; total10;40%. 2 symbols2,3,1 with labelled key. 3 total18, angles120°,180°,60°. 4 Physics72°,History144°,Geography108°,Further Mathematics36°;100Physics pupils;History2/5. Mark correct data, totals, formula, scale/key, labels and plotted values separately. Draw on paper; actual drawing performance remains teacher assessed.

title: Woodwork project: design, make and evaluate a small frame
body:
Objectives: interpret a dimensioned design, plan a cutting list, measure and mark accurately, explain a butt joint, and evaluate a supervised woodwork project.

Design brief: Make a small rectangular display frame from suitable thin timber strips, with outside dimensions 200 mm × 150 mm and strip width 20 mm. It is a classroom display model, not a load-bearing structure. Two full-width horizontal strips are 200 mm long; two vertical strips fit between them and are 150-20-20=110 mm long. All four strips have the same selected thickness. Sketch the front view, label outside dimensions and show how the short members meet the long members. The opening is 160 mm × 110 mm. This is a newly designed project, not the roof description under the original project heading.

Planning and method: First make a paper/card layout and check the arithmetic and orientation. Choose sound straight material without dangerous splinters. A competent teacher chooses tools, holds the work securely and demonstrates measuring from a consistent reference edge, marking a square line and keeping the cut on the waste side. Pupils only use tools for which they have been instructed and supervised; power saws are not part of this pupil activity. Teacher-precut pieces can be used where appropriate. Dry-fit the parts before joining. A butt joint places the end of one part against another surface; it is simple but needs appropriate reinforcement or adhesive for its intended use. Use a teacher-approved adhesive, follow its label, and clamp/hold the assembly square while it sets. Do not rely on glue that has not cured. Remove sharp edges using the teacher's approved method and dust controls; do not blow wood dust into the air.

Worked quality check: Both outside widths should be 200 mm and both heights 150 mm. Equal diagonals help check that the assembled rectangle is square; each diagonal should be 250 mm because 200²+150²=250². Measure actual results and record deviations honestly. A correct drawing does not prove the finished object is accurate.

Practice: (1) Produce the dimensioned sketch and cutting list. (2) Explain why the vertical strips are not 150 mm long in this layout. (3) If outside height becomes 180 mm with the same 20-mm strips, find the two short lengths. (4) Identify one advantage and one limitation of a butt joint. (5) Build only under the stated supervision, record measurements and suggest one improvement.

Answers/assessment: (1) Two 200-mm and two 110-mm strips, width 20 mm, common selected thickness. (2) The top and bottom strips occupy 40 mm. (3) 140 mm. (4) Simple alignment, but limited strength without suitable joining/reinforcement. (5) Mark design accuracy 4, safe approved process 4, fit/squareness 4 and evidence-based evaluation 4. Where materials or supervision are unavailable, assess the design only and leave making/performance pending; never claim that a paper plan is completed woodwork.

title: Shorthand compound signs and controlled speed practice
body:
Objectives: distinguish the six compound-sign groups named in the school scheme; retain stroke direction, weight and hooks; improve speed while checking transcription accuracy.

Teaching: Pitman shorthand records sounds rather than simply copying spelling. A compound sign represents a combination. The accompanying original practice chart shows basic isolated signs, not complete word outlines. KW uses a large initial hook on light K; GW uses the same hook on heavy G. MP/MB uses heavy M. LR uses heavy downward L, normally finally; RR uses heavy downward R, finally. WH enlarges the initial hook of W and is used initially or medially. KW, GW and MP/MB represent adjacent consonant sounds without an intervening vowel. LR/RR have restricted uses; do not join every written l+r or r+r mechanically. The chart is a reference for these groups, not the whole shorthand alphabet. Previously learned vowels, position rules and joins remain necessary for full words. CBSE Unit 8 includes additional groups; the selected six follow the school scheme.

Worked analysis: The k and w sounds at the start of quick are adjacent, so the KW group is relevant. The m and p at the end of lamp illustrate MP. In a word with a pronounced vowel between k and w, a KW compound is not automatically appropriate. A heavier stroke carries information; making every line thick destroys contrasts. A rushed illegible sign is not an improvement in speed.

Practice sequence: First copy each chart sign five times slowly, naming it and checking hook, direction and weight. Then cover the labels and identify all six groups. The teacher dictates the following original sign sequence twice, evenly, over 30 seconds: KW, MP, GW, RR, WH, LR, MP, KW, WH, GW, LR, RR. Write signs, then transcribe them back into their labels. Compare with the printed key only after transcribing. Repeat after correcting the two most frequent errors. This is a sign drill, not a claim of words-per-minute certification.

Optional transfer task: if a teacher supplies the prerequisite consonant/vowel chart, use it and CBSE Unit 8 examples to prepare complete outlines for quick and lamp. Explain which part is supplied by the compound sign and which parts still need other signs. This chart does not supply the full alphabet; without that prerequisite, assess the complete isolated-sign drill above only. A teacher checks the entire outline, vowel position and read-back before timed word dictation. Do not invent a missing school-textbook exercise number.

Answers and marking: the dictated answer is the twelve-group sequence above. Score one point per recognisable, correctly weighted compound sign and one per accurate read-back, maximum 24. Record total time and errors separately. If 10 of 12 signs are correct in 30 seconds, raw rate is 24 signs/minute, accuracy is 10/12×100≈83.3%, and correct-sign rate is 20/minute. This must not be reported as 24 words/minute. For word transfer, quick uses the KW sound combination and lamp uses MP; the remaining sounds and vowels still require their normal notation. Assessment: accuracy first, then smoothness and consistent spacing. Stop speed increases when read-back errors rise; practise the specific failed sign before reassessment.

title: Child care (continued): safe care in diarrhoea, constipation and colic, safe infant feeding, and immunisation

sources.title: Clinical management of acute diarrhoea — WHO/UNICEF joint statement
Diarrhoeal disease — WHO fact sheet
Foods and Drinks to Avoid or Limit — CDC
How to Clean, Sanitize, and Store Infant Feeding Items — CDC
Nigeria routine immunisation schedule — NPHCDA Immunization FHIR IG

body:
Objectives: describe diarrhoea, constipation and colic in babies and say what a caregiver should do; explain why old home remedies are unsafe; state what a baby under 12 months must not be given; explain why immunisation matters and why families follow the current clinic schedule.

Why this lesson corrects the earlier notes: the earlier notes on child care (continued) included a homemade salt-and-sugar drink, advice to add glucose, sugar or honey to a child's food for constipation, and a vaccine table that listed smallpox. Those items are unsafe or out of date. Do not use them. This lesson replaces them.

Teaching:
1. Diarrhoea means three or more loose or liquid stools in a day. The danger is dehydration (loss of too much body water), which is most dangerous in babies. Causes include germs in unsafe food or water, unclean feeding equipment and unwashed hands.
2. What to do for diarrhoea: keep feeding and keep breastfeeding; give extra fluids; use oral rehydration salts (ORS) from a clinic, pharmacy or community health worker, mixed exactly as the packet says with clean water. Do not mix a salt-and-sugar drink by guessing amounts: too much salt or sugar can make a baby worse. A health worker may also give zinc for the days the child needs it. Do not give anti-diarrhoea medicines, antibiotics or herbal mixtures unless a health worker prescribes them.
3. Go to a clinic at once if the child is a young baby, is very sleepy or cannot drink, has sunken eyes, passes blood in the stool, has a high fever, vomits everything, or passes very little urine. Diarrhoea that continues needs a health worker.
4. Preventing diarrhoea: wash hands with soap and clean water after the toilet, after changing a nappy and before feeding; use safe drinking water; keep food covered; clean feeding equipment as in the baby-care lesson (wash with soap and a brush kept for the purpose, sanitise, air-dry and store covered); follow the clinic immunisation card.
5. Constipation means hard, painful or infrequent stools. Do not add honey, sugar or glucose to a baby's food or drink to treat it. Honey must never be given to a child under 12 months: it can cause infant botulism, a serious food poisoning. Children under 12 months should not be given fruit or vegetable juice, and children under 24 months should avoid added sugars. Take a baby to a health worker for constipation. For older children, plenty of safe water, vegetables, fruit and whole foods and active play help; if there is severe pain, vomiting, a swollen belly or blood, go to the clinic.
6. Colic means a baby cries hard and long, often in the first months, for no clear reason. Comfort the baby by holding, rocking and a calm room. Take the baby to a health worker if there is fever, vomiting, blood in the stool, poor feeding or the baby seems very unwell. Do not give herbal mixtures or medicines unless a health worker advises.
7. Safe infant feeding rules: breast milk is the best food for a young baby; a health worker advises when other foods begin (complementary foods begin around six months). Under 12 months do not give honey, cow's milk as a main drink or juice. Avoid salty foods and added sugar. Use clean cups, spoons and bottles. Cook foods well and give them fresh.
8. Immunisation protects children and expectant mothers from serious diseases. Smallpox was eradicated worldwide, so smallpox vaccine is not part of the routine schedule and the old table must not be used. Nigeria's routine schedule is set by the National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA) and can change, so families follow the immunisation card given at the primary health centre. Diseases the routine programme protects against include tuberculosis, polio, diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, hepatitis B, pneumonia, measles, yellow fever and meningitis. Keep the card safe, take it to each visit, and ask the health worker which vaccine is due.
9. Laundering baby clothes (from the original notes): wash and rinse thoroughly so that no soap or stain irritates the skin, and dry in clean air.

Worked example: Tola's baby brother has watery stools. Tola washes her hands, tells her mother, and they keep breastfeeding and take him to the health centre. The nurse gives ORS and explains how to mix it exactly as the packet says. Tola does not give honey, a salt-and-sugar drink or herbal medicine, because she knows these are unsafe.

Practice (questions):
1. Define diarrhoea and say why it is dangerous for babies.
2. State three things a caregiver should do when a baby has diarrhoea.
3. Why must a home salt-and-sugar drink not be mixed by guessing?
4. List three danger signs that mean the child must go to the clinic at once.
5. Why must honey never be given to a baby under 12 months?
6. State two safe ways to help a baby with colic and one sign that needs a health worker.
7. Why must the old vaccine table that listed smallpox not be used? Where do families find the current schedule?
8. Name three ways of preventing diarrhoea.

Answers (marking guide): 1. Three or more loose or liquid stools in a day; the baby can lose too much body water (dehydration) quickly (2). 2. Any three (3): keep feeding and breastfeeding, give extra fluids, give ORS mixed as the packet says, wash hands, go to a health worker, give zinc only if the health worker advises. 3. Wrong amounts of salt or sugar can harm the baby (1). 4. Any three (3): very sleepy or cannot drink, sunken eyes, blood in the stool, high fever, vomits everything, very little urine, a young baby. 5. It can cause infant botulism, a serious food poisoning (1). 6. Hold, rock, calm room (2); fever, vomiting, blood in the stool or poor feeding needs a health worker (1). 7. Smallpox has been eradicated and the schedule has changed (1); the immunisation card and the primary health centre, set by NPHCDA (1). 8. Any three (3): hand washing, safe water, clean feeding equipment, covered food, immunisation. Teacher: this lesson gives no dose and no homemade medicine; do not add any.

title: Depletion of the ozone layer and its effects (corrected: ozone depletion is not the greenhouse effect)
origin: New teaching material prepared under the owner's 15 October 2026 authorisation to use internet equivalents; not recovered school-source text. It supersedes, in delivery, the original First-Term row 'DEPLETION OT OZONE LAYER', which says that ozone gives a cooling effect, that depletion lets more ozone collect in the lower air and causes the greenhouse effect, and that carbon dioxide depletes the ozone layer. The original row is preserved unchanged in the audit record.

sources.title: Are the ozone hole and global warming related? — NASA Earth Observatory
Montreal Protocol — UNEP Ozone Secretariat

body:
Objectives: locate the ozone layer; state its importance; name the substances that deplete it and their effects; separate ozone depletion from the greenhouse effect; state control measures.

Teaching:
1. Location. The atmosphere has layers. The ozone layer is mainly in the stratosphere, above the troposphere where we live and where weather happens.
2. Importance. Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation. Because it absorbs UV, it warms the stratosphere; it does not cool the Earth's surface.
3. Cause of depletion. Chemicals made by people, mainly chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and halons, rise to the stratosphere. Sunlight breaks them up and the chlorine or bromine released destroys ozone molecules. Sources were old refrigerators and air conditioners, aerosol sprays, foam and some fire extinguishers. The Montreal Protocol of 1987 phased out these substances and the ozone layer is slowly recovering.
4. Effects of depletion. More UV reaches the ground. It can cause sunburn, skin cancer, eye cataracts and a weaker immune system in people, and can harm crops and sea life.
5. Not the same as global warming. Ozone depletion does not cause global warming. Global warming is the rise in average surface temperature caused mainly by greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane that trap heat in the lower atmosphere. Carbon dioxide does not deplete the ozone layer. The two problems have a link only because CFCs are also greenhouse gases. Deforestation and bush burning raise carbon dioxide and pollute the air; they add to global warming, not directly to ozone destruction.
6. Control. Support the Montreal Protocol and use ozone-friendly products; have old refrigerators and air conditioners collected and handled by trained people so that the refrigerant is not released; do not buy products that contain banned ozone-depleting chemicals. To reduce global warming, reduce fossil-fuel burning and bush burning and plant trees.
7. Protect yourself from UV: use shade, a hat and sun-safe clothing in strong sun.

Worked example: A scrap dealer is about to cut open an old refrigerator. Ada explains that the refrigerant could escape and damage the ozone layer, so a trained technician must remove it first.

Practice (questions):
1. In which layer of the atmosphere is the ozone layer found?
2. State two functions of the ozone layer.
3. Name two substances that deplete the ozone layer and two sources of them.
4. State three effects of ozone depletion.
5. Explain why carbon dioxide and CFCs are not treated as the same problem.
6. State three control measures.

Answers (marking guide): 1. Stratosphere (1). 2. Absorbs harmful UV (1); protects life, skin and eyes (1). 3. CFCs and halons (2); refrigerators, air conditioners, aerosols, foam, fire extinguishers (any two, 2). 4. Any three (3): sunburn, skin cancer, cataracts, weaker immunity, crop and sea-life damage. 5. CO2 traps heat and warms the surface but does not destroy ozone; CFCs destroy ozone and also trap some heat (2). 6. Any three (3): Montreal Protocol, safe disposal of old fridges and air conditioners, ozone-friendly products, not releasing refrigerant.

title: Magnetism: poles, the compass and the care of magnets (corrected pole naming)
origin: New teaching material prepared under the owner's 15 October 2026 authorisation to use internet equivalents; not recovered school-source text. It supersedes, in delivery, the original Second-Term row 'Magnetism-', which says that the end of a magnet pointing to the geographic north pole is the south pole of the magnet. By the standard convention that end is the north (north-seeking) pole. The original row is preserved unchanged in the audit record.

sources.title: Earth as a Magnet — LibreTexts Physical Science

body:
Objectives: state the law of magnetic poles; name the poles of a freely hanging magnet correctly; detect poles with a compass; describe a magnetic field; state how to care for magnets.

Teaching:
1. A magnet attracts iron and steel. Lodestone is a natural magnet. Every magnet has two poles, found near its ends, where the force is strongest.
2. Law of poles: like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
3. Naming the poles. A bar magnet that is free to swing comes to rest pointing roughly north and south. The end that points to the geographic north is called the north-seeking pole, or north pole, of the magnet. The end that points to the geographic south is the south pole. So the north pole of a magnet points towards the Earth's geographic north. The Earth itself acts like a huge magnet: the magnetic pole of the Earth near the geographic north attracts the north pole of a compass needle, so that Earth pole is magnetically a south pole.
4. Detecting poles. Bring a compass near a bar magnet. The end of the magnet that repels the north end of the compass needle is a north pole. You can also hang the magnet on a thread and see which end points north.
5. Magnetic field: the region around a magnet where its force acts. Field lines leave the north pole and enter the south pole. The field is strongest near the poles. Iron filings sprinkled on paper over a magnet show the pattern.
6. Care of magnets: store them in pairs with unlike poles together and a soft-iron keeper across the ends; keep them dry, cool and away from heat, hammering and dropping, which weaken them. Keep magnets away from phones, cards and watches.
7. Uses: compasses, loudspeakers, microphones, electric motors and generators, door catches, and lifting iron objects.

Worked example: A compass needle swings to point at the right-hand end of a bar magnet. The needle's north end is attracted, so the right-hand end of the magnet is its south pole.

Practice (questions):
1. State the law of magnetic poles.
2. Which end of a freely hanging magnet points to the geographic north: its north pole or south pole?
3. Explain why the north end of a compass needle points to the Earth's geographic north.
4. Describe how to find the north pole of an unmarked magnet using a compass.
5. State three ways of caring for magnets.
6. State two uses of magnets.

Answers (marking guide): 1. Like poles repel; unlike poles attract (2). 2. The north pole (the north-seeking pole) (1). 3. The Earth acts like a magnet; the magnetic pole near the geographic north attracts the needle's north end (2). 4. Bring the compass near; the end of the magnet that repels the compass north end is the north pole (2). 5. Any three (3): keepers, store in pairs, dry place, away from heat, avoid hammering or dropping. 6. Any two (2): compass, loudspeaker, motor, generator, door catch.

title: Electrical energy: circuits, meters and electricity bills (corrected formulas and units)
origin: New teaching material prepared under the owner's 15 October 2026 authorisation to use internet equivalents; not recovered school-source text. It supersedes, in delivery, the original Second-Term row 'Electrical Energy.', which describes the voltmeter as an instrument to detect the flow of current, writes the parallel-resistance rule as 1/RI+1/R2 for total resistance R, and prints a meter example whose cost per unit (1291 naira) does not match the total shown. The original row is preserved unchanged in the audit record.

sources.title: Electric circuits chapter summary — Siyavula Physical Sciences
Resistors in circuits — physics.info

body:
Objectives: use series and parallel rules correctly; name what each meter measures and how it is connected; use V = I x R; calculate an electricity bill from units used; state basic electrical safety.

Teaching:
1. Current is the flow of charge, measured in amperes (A) with an ammeter connected in series. Potential difference (voltage) is measured in volts (V) with a voltmeter connected in parallel across the part being measured. A galvanometer detects a very small current. Resistance is measured in ohms.
2. Direction: conventional current is drawn from the positive terminal round the circuit to the negative terminal. Electrons actually move the opposite way.
3. Ohm's law: V = I x R, so I = V / R and R = V / I.
4. Series circuit: one path; the same current in every part; total resistance R = R1 + R2 + R3. If one lamp fails, all go off.
5. Parallel circuit: separate branches; the same voltage across every branch; the currents add. Total resistance follows 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. Adding a branch lowers the total resistance. Houses are wired in parallel so that one lamp failing does not switch the others off.
6. Fuse and circuit breaker: both stop the current when it is too large. A fuse melts; a circuit breaker switches off and can be reset. Fit the correct rating.
7. Electricity bill: energy used is shown in units (kilowatt-hours). Units used = present reading minus previous reading. Cost = units used x cost per unit.
8. Safety: never touch bare wires, never use wet hands on switches or sockets, do not overload sockets, and have repairs done by a qualified electrician.

Worked example: Two resistors of 4 ohm and 4 ohm are joined in parallel: 1/R = 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4, so R = 2 ohm. In series they would total 8 ohm. A meter reads 47896 before and 48167 now: units used = 48167 - 47896 = 271. At 12.91 naira per unit the cost is 271 x 12.91 = 3498.61 naira.

Practice (questions):
1. Which meter measures current and how is it connected? Which measures potential difference and how is it connected?
2. Write the formula for total resistance in series and in parallel.
3. Find the total resistance of 6 ohm and 3 ohm in parallel.
4. A 12 V battery drives a current of 2 A through a resistor. Find the resistance.
5. A meter reads 1500 then 1620. The cost is 15 naira per unit. Find the cost.
6. Why are houses wired in parallel?

Answers (marking guide): 1. Ammeter, in series (2); voltmeter, in parallel (2). 2. Series R = R1 + R2 (1); parallel 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 (1). 3. 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 3/6, so R = 2 ohm (2). 4. R = V / I = 12 / 2 = 6 ohm (2). 5. 1620 - 1500 = 120 units; 120 x 15 = 1800 naira (2). 6. One failed lamp does not switch off the others; each appliance gets the full voltage (2).

sources.title: HIV and AIDS — WHO fact file
HIV — WHO Western Pacific health topic

body:
Objectives: define STIs, HIV and AIDS; state how HIV is and is not spread; state prevention methods; explain testing and treatment; show respect for people living with HIV; correct dated notes on disease classification.

Teaching:
1. Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) spread mainly through sexual contact. Examples are gonorrhoea, syphilis, chlamydia and HIV. Many bacterial STIs can be cured when treated early by a health worker; viral ones such as HIV are managed with treatment. Some STIs show no signs, so a person cannot tell by looking. Do not buy drugs for self-treatment; go to a clinic.
2. HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) attacks the immune system. AIDS (acquired immune deficiency syndrome) is the late stage when the immune system is badly weakened. HIV is spread through unprotected sex, infected blood (unsafe transfusion, shared needles, razors or other skin-piercing tools) and from a mother to her baby during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding.
3. HIV is not spread by handshakes, hugging, sharing plates or cups, toilets, swimming, mosquitoes or sleeping in the same room.
4. Testing: only a test at a health facility shows whether a person has HIV; signs alone cannot tell. Testing comes with counselling.
5. Treatment: antiretroviral therapy (ART) is a lifelong daily treatment. A person taking it properly can stay healthy and live a long life. A person on ART whose test shows the virus at an undetectable level does not pass HIV to a sexual partner. A woman living with HIV who is on ART and under care can have a baby with a very low chance of passing HIV on. So the old advice not to become pregnant is replaced by: seek care early at a clinic.
6. Prevention: not having sex is the surest way to avoid sexual transmission; condoms used correctly every time lower the risk of HIV and many STIs; do not share needles, razors or blades; accept blood only from tested sources; medical male circumcision done by a trained health worker in a clean setting lowers a man's risk, whereas cutting with unsterilised tools raises it; health workers wear gloves and cover wounds.
7. Stigma harms. People living with HIV deserve care, privacy and respect. Support is practical (company, care, going to the clinic), not only prayer.
8. Correcting related notes on family health: smallpox no longer occurs because it was eradicated, so it is not a current communicable disease; snake-bite is an injury, not an infectious disease; many non-communicable diseases such as stroke or heart disease are not passed from person to person.

Worked example: Bola hears a rumour that she can get HIV from sharing a cup with a classmate. She explains that HIV is not spread that way, and tells her friend that anyone worried about HIV should be tested at a clinic and, if positive, can begin ART.

Practice (questions):
1. Give the full meaning of HIV, AIDS and STI.
2. State three ways HIV is spread and three ways it is not spread.
3. Why can a person not tell by looking whether someone has HIV?
4. What is ART and why is it important?
5. State four ways of preventing HIV.
6. Why is it wrong to isolate or insult a person living with HIV?

Answers (marking guide): 1. Human immunodeficiency virus; acquired immune deficiency syndrome; sexually transmitted infection (3). 2. Any three spread: unprotected sex, infected blood or shared sharp tools, mother to baby (3); any three not: handshake, shared plates, toilets, swimming, mosquitoes (3). 3. Many STIs and HIV show no signs for a long time; only a test shows (1). 4. Lifelong daily treatment that lets a person stay healthy and, when the virus is undetectable, prevents sexual spread (2). 5. Any four (4): not having sex, condoms, not sharing sharp tools, tested blood, trained circumcision, early care. 6. Stigma stops people getting tests and care; HIV is not spread by everyday contact (2). Teacher: do not give personal medical advice; refer questions to a health worker.

sources.title: Puberty — NHS Healthier Together
Menarche (first period) and pregnancy myths — HealthLink BC

body:
Objectives: describe the physical and emotional changes of puberty in boys and girls; explain menstruation and hygiene; state the consequences of teenage pregnancy; name safe sources of help.

Teaching:
1. Puberty is the stage when a child's body changes into an adult body. It begins at different ages for different people, and being earlier or later than friends is normal. Hormones cause the changes: in girls mainly oestrogen, in boys mainly testosterone.
2. Changes in both: a growth spurt, hair under the arms and in the pubic area, more sweat and body odour, oily skin and pimples, and strong feelings and mood changes. Wash daily and wear clean clothes.
3. Changes in boys: the voice deepens (it may crack for a while), shoulders broaden, the testes and penis grow, facial hair begins, and erections and wet dreams happen. Wet dreams are normal.
4. Changes in girls: breasts develop, hips widen, and menstruation (monthly periods) begins. Periods may be irregular at first. Use clean pads or other safe sanitary materials, change them regularly and wash. Cramps are common; see a health worker if pain is severe or bleeding is very heavy.
5. Pregnancy can happen once ovulation starts, which can be before or soon after a girl's first period, and it can happen from the first time a person has sex. Not having sex is the surest way to avoid pregnancy and STIs.
6. Consequences of teenage pregnancy: higher health risks for a young mother and baby, so ante-natal care at a clinic is important; interrupted schooling; loss of plans and income; emotional stress; and risk from unsafe abortion, which can cause severe bleeding, infection, damage to the womb and death. Any girl with bleeding, severe pain or fever after a pregnancy loss or an attempted abortion must go to a health facility at once.
7. Where to get help: a parent or trusted adult, the school counsellor or teacher, and the nearest health centre. Asking early is wise and safe.
8. Resist pressure: say no clearly, leave the situation, and tell a trusted adult.

Worked example: Dayo's voice cracks and he feels embarrassed. His teacher explains that this is a normal change of puberty and that it settles with time.

Practice (questions):
1. Name the hormones mainly responsible for puberty in girls and in boys.
2. State three changes that happen in both sexes.
3. State two changes specific to boys and two specific to girls.
4. How should a girl manage her periods hygienically?
5. State three consequences of teenage pregnancy.
6. Name three people or places where a young person can get help.

Answers (marking guide): 1. Oestrogen; testosterone (2). 2. Any three (3): growth spurt, body hair, sweat or odour, pimples, mood changes. 3. Boys: voice deepens, testes and penis grow, facial hair (any two, 2); girls: breasts develop, hips widen, menstruation (any two, 2). 4. Clean sanitary materials, change regularly, wash (2). 5. Any three (3): health risks, interrupted schooling, loss of plans, emotional stress, unsafe abortion. 6. Parent or trusted adult, school counsellor, health centre (3).

sources.title: Menarche (first period) and pregnancy myths — HealthLink BC

body:
Objectives: define teenage pregnancy; state its causes and consequences; separate myths from facts about pregnancy; state the care needed in pregnancy.

Teaching:
1. Teenage pregnancy is pregnancy in a girl aged 10 to 19, married or not.
2. Causes include lack of accurate information, early marriage and social pressure, poverty, use of alcohol or drugs that lead to unwanted sex, and not using protection correctly. No method other than not having sex is completely certain.
3. Consequences: health risks such as high blood pressure and heavy bleeding; anaemia; unsafe abortion; interrupted schooling; loss of plans and income; and emotional stress.
4. Myths and facts. Fact: a missed period may signal pregnancy but can have other causes. Fact: pregnancy lasts about nine months (around 40 weeks), not over a year. Fact: a girl can become pregnant the first time she has sex. Fact: pregnancy can occur during or soon after a period. Fact: washing after sex does not prevent pregnancy. Myth: every pregnant woman vomits. Myth: pregnant women should not bathe or are unclean. Fact: pregnant women should not drink alcohol or smoke and should take only medicines a health worker approves.
5. Care in pregnancy: a clinic confirms pregnancy and gives ante-natal care; eat nourishing food including iron-rich foods as advised; rest; take only prescribed medicine; plan to give birth with a skilled attendant at a health facility.
6. Danger signs needing urgent help at any time: vaginal bleeding, severe headache or blurred vision, fits, fever, severe abdominal pain, or much less baby movement.
7. If a girl suspects pregnancy: tell a trusted adult and go to a health facility early. Do not take herbs or drugs, or go to an unqualified person, to end a pregnancy: unsafe abortion kills. The law on abortion is strict; the teacher or school counsellor explains it. A girl with bleeding, pain or fever after a pregnancy loss must go to a health facility at once.

Worked example: Hauwa misses her period. She talks to her aunt, who goes with her to the clinic. A test shows she is pregnant and the nurse arranges ante-natal care.

Practice (questions):
1. Define teenage pregnancy.
2. State three causes and three consequences of teenage pregnancy.
3. Say whether each is a myth or a fact: (a) pregnancy lasts about nine months; (b) a girl cannot become pregnant the first time she has sex; (c) every pregnant woman vomits.
4. State four things a pregnant woman should do for her health.
5. Name three danger signs in pregnancy.
6. Why must a girl never use herbs or an unqualified person to end a pregnancy?

Answers (marking guide): 1. Pregnancy in a girl aged 10 to 19 (1). 2. Three causes (3) and three consequences (3) from the lists above. 3. (a) Fact (1); (b) Myth, because she can (1); (c) Myth (1). 4. Any four (4): attend ante-natal care, eat nourishing food, rest, avoid alcohol and smoking, take only prescribed medicine. 5. Any three (3): bleeding, severe headache or blurred vision, fits, fever, severe pain, reduced baby movement. 6. Unsafe abortion can cause severe bleeding, infection and death (2).

sources.title: NAFDAC Mobile Authentication Service (MAS) scheme — NAFDAC

body:
Objectives: define drug, medicine, drug use, misuse and abuse; state the main types of drugs; define dependence, tolerance and withdrawal; explain the dangers of self-medication and fake medicines; state safe choices.

Teaching:
1. A drug is any substance that changes how the body or mind works. A medicine is a drug used to prevent, treat or cure illness. Use means taking a medicine as a health worker or the label directs. Misuse means taking a medicine in a wrong way, for example without advice, in the wrong amount, or for a purpose it was not given for. Abuse means using drugs or substances in a harmful way, often for the effect on the mind.
2. Main types: stimulants (speed the body up), depressants (slow the body down), cannabis, inhalants, hallucinogens and prescription medicines. Some medicines, such as certain sleeping or calming tablets (for example diazepam, sold as valium), are prescription medicines. They are legal only when a qualified person prescribes them, and misuse is dangerous. Illegal drugs include cocaine and heroin.
3. Dependence (addiction): the body or mind feels a strong need for the drug. Tolerance: the person needs more of the drug to get the same effect. Withdrawal: unpleasant illness when the drug is stopped. These are signs of dependence and need help from a health worker, not punishment.
4. Self-medication means buying and taking medicines without a health worker's advice. Dangers: the wrong medicine or amount, side effects, hiding a serious illness, antibiotic resistance, and dangerous mixtures. Use antibiotics only when prescribed. Never share prescription medicines.
5. Fake and expired medicines are common. Buy from licensed pharmacies, check the expiry date and the NAFDAC registration number, and where a pack carries a scratch code use NAFDAC's Mobile Authentication Service. Herbal products can also be harmful when contaminated or taken in the wrong amount; ask a health worker.
6. Reasons people abuse drugs: peer pressure, curiosity, stress, easy availability and trouble at home. Safe choices: learn the facts, say no firmly, keep busy, talk to a trusted adult or counsellor, and avoid places where drugs are used.
7. NAFDAC checks the safety and quality of foods and medicines; NDLEA enforces laws on illegal drugs and offers counselling and rehabilitation programmes.

Worked example: Ife has a headache and her friend offers her some tablets from an unmarked packet. Ife refuses, tells her mother and asks the pharmacist for advice.

Practice (questions):
1. Differentiate between drug use, misuse and abuse.
2. Name four types of drugs.
3. Define dependence, tolerance and withdrawal.
4. State three dangers of self-medication.
5. State two ways to check that a medicine is genuine.
6. State two functions of NAFDAC and two of NDLEA.

Answers (marking guide): 1. Use is as directed; misuse is wrong or unprescribed use of a medicine; abuse is harmful use for the effect (3). 2. Any four (4): stimulants, depressants, cannabis, inhalants, hallucinogens, prescription medicines. 3. Strong need for the drug; needing more for the same effect; illness when stopped (3). 4. Any three (3): wrong medicine or dose, side effects, hides illness, antibiotic resistance, dangerous mixtures. 5. Any two (2): licensed pharmacy, expiry date, NAFDAC number, scratch-code check. 6. NAFDAC: checks quality and safety of food and medicines, registers products (2); NDLEA: enforces drug laws, counselling and rehabilitation (2).

title: Describing emotions: verb or adjective plus the right preposition
body:
**Objectives:** use the common preposition that follows an emotion word; choose between *with*, *about*, *at*, *of*, *in* and *on*; write sentences that describe how a person feels and why.

**Teaching:** Many words that name feelings need a particular preposition before the thing that causes the feeling. The preposition is part of the expression and must be learned with the word. The same feeling can take different prepositions for a person and for a thing.

- afraid of, scared of, frightened of, proud of, ashamed of, jealous of, fond of, tired of, full of
- angry **with** a person, angry **about** or **at** a thing
- worried about, excited about, upset about, anxious about
- surprised at or by, shocked at or by, amazed at or by
- disappointed with or in a person, disappointed **at** or **about** a result
- pleased with, satisfied with, happy with, bored with
- interested in, keen on, good at, sorry for a person, sorry about a thing

After a preposition use a noun, a pronoun or the **-ing** form: “She is afraid of the dark”; “He is proud of winning”. Do not use the infinitive after the preposition (“proud to winning” is wrong).

**Worked example:** “Ngozi was disappointed with her result because she was worried about the mathematics paper.” Here *with* links the feeling to the thing she received and *about* links worry to the paper.

**Practice:** Fill each gap with a preposition. (1) The captain was proud ___ his team. (2) Bola is angry ___ her brother for losing the book. (3) I am fond ___ roasted plantain. (4) We were surprised ___ the sudden rain. (5) The class is excited ___ the trip. (6) Tunde is not interested ___ football. (7) She felt ashamed ___ shouting at the guest. (8) Write two sentences of your own describing an emotion and its cause, using a different preposition in each.

**Answers:** (1) of (2) with (3) of (4) at or by (5) about (6) in (7) of. (8) Marking guide: one mark for a correct emotion word, one for the correct following preposition, one for a noun or -ing form after it; award no mark for a sentence that changes the preposition to fit the sentence without checking the expression.

**Assessment:** 7 marks for the gaps and 6 for the sentences. Written grammar does not by itself show spoken fluency; check use in speech separately.

title: Changing a positive statement into a negative statement
body:
**Objectives:** turn a positive sentence into a negative sentence in the present, past, future and perfect forms; use contractions correctly; change *some* words and other positive words to their negative partners.

**Teaching:** Negatives are formed by adding **not** after the first auxiliary verb. If the sentence has only a main verb in the simple present or simple past, add **do not / does not / did not** and use the base form of the verb.

- **be:** “She is late” becomes “She is not (isn't) late.”
- **simple present:** “They play football” becomes “They do not (don't) play football”; “He plays” becomes “He does not (doesn't) play.”
- **simple past:** “We finished” becomes “We did not (didn't) finish.” After *did not* the main verb returns to its base form.
- **will, can, must, should and other modals:** “I can swim” becomes “I cannot (can't) swim”; “She will come” becomes “She will not (won't) come.”
- **perfect and continuous forms:** put *not* after the first auxiliary: “has not eaten”, “was not reading”.

Some positive words change as well: *some* becomes **any**, *something* becomes **anything**, *someone* becomes **anyone**, *always* becomes **never** and *already* becomes **yet**. Standard English does not use two negatives together: say “I did not see anyone” or “I saw no one”, not “I did not see no one”.

**Worked example:** “Ada has already cooked some rice.” Negative: “Ada has not cooked any rice yet.”

**Practice:** Change to the negative. (1) The headmaster is angry. (2) Uche sings in the choir. (3) They arrived early. (4) I will buy something. (5) The children can read the notice. (6) Segun has finished the homework already. (7) She always walks to school.

**Answers:** (1) The headmaster is not angry. (2) Uche does not sing in the choir. (3) They did not arrive early. (4) I will not buy anything. (5) The children cannot read the notice. (6) Segun has not finished the homework yet. (7) She never walks to school. Accept correct contractions. Marking: one mark each; deduct nothing for choosing *cannot* or *can't*.

**Assessment:** 7 marks. Ask learners to say each sentence aloud so the contraction is practised, because a written correction does not establish spoken accuracy.

title: Question tags: checking and confirming
body:
**Objectives:** add a correct question tag to a statement; use the right polarity; handle the common irregular cases; read the tune of a tag as either checking or confirming.

**Teaching:** A question tag is a short question added to the end of a statement. Use the same auxiliary (or *be*, or *do*) as in the statement and the matching pronoun. A **positive** statement usually takes a **negative** tag, and a **negative** statement takes a **positive** tag.

- “You are ready, **aren't you**?” / “You aren't ready, **are you**?”
- “Tola sings well, **doesn't she**?” (simple present uses *do/does*)
- “They left early, **didn't they**?” (simple past uses *did*)
- “She will come, **won't she**?” / “You can swim, **can't you**?”
- “I am late, **aren't I**?” (the standard tag for *I am*)
- “Let's go, **shall we**?” and “Open the door, **will you**?” (suggestions and commands)
- “Nobody called, **did they**?” — words such as *nobody*, *no one*, *never* and *hardly* make the statement negative, so the tag is positive and *they* is used for *nobody/everybody/someone*.

Tune: when the voice falls on the tag the speaker expects agreement; when it rises the speaker is asking a real question. In speech work listen for the fall or rise.

**Worked example:** “Your brother plays the drums, ____?” The verb is *plays* (simple present, positive), so the tag is negative: “doesn't he?”

**Practice:** Add a tag. (1) The lesson started at eight, ____? (2) You haven't seen my pen, ____? (3) Ife is your cousin, ____? (4) Let's sit here, ____? (5) Nobody told the teacher, ____? (6) I am your friend, ____? (7) Say a sentence aloud with the tag falling, then rising, and explain the difference.

**Answers:** (1) didn't it (2) have you (3) isn't she (4) shall we (5) did they (6) aren't I (7) Falling tune: checking something the speaker believes; rising tune: a genuine question. Marking: one mark each for (1)–(6) and two for (7).

**Assessment:** 8 marks. Pronunciation of the tune must be judged by listening; a written answer cannot show it.

title: Conjunctions: joining words, phrases and clauses
body:
**Objectives:** name the three kinds of conjunction; choose a suitable conjunction for the relationship between two ideas; punctuate the joined sentence correctly.

**Teaching:** A conjunction joins words, phrases or clauses.

- **Coordinating** conjunctions join equal parts: *and* (addition), *but* (contrast), *or* (choice), *so* (result), *for* (reason), *nor*, *yet*. Use a comma before them when they join two full clauses: “The bell rang, so we went in.”
- **Subordinating** conjunctions begin a dependent clause: *because* and *since* (reason), *although* and *though* (contrast), *if* and *unless* (condition), *when*, *while*, *after*, *before* and *until* (time), *so that* (purpose). The dependent clause cannot stand alone: “Although it rained, we played.”
- **Correlative** pairs: *either … or*, *neither … nor*, *both … and*, *not only … but also*.

A subordinating clause at the start of a sentence is followed by a comma; at the end, usually no comma. Do not use *although* and *but* together in one sentence.

**Worked example:** Join “The road was flooded” and “we arrived on time.” With *although*: “Although the road was flooded, we arrived on time.” With *but*: “The road was flooded, but we arrived on time.”

**Practice:** Choose the best conjunction in brackets. (1) He stayed at home (because / although) he was ill. (2) You may have tea (or / but) water. (3) (Unless / If) you study, you will pass. (4) She is clever (and / but) lazy. (5) Join with *so that*: “Kunle woke early. He would not miss the bus.” (6) Write one sentence using *neither … nor*.

**Answers:** (1) because (2) or (3) If (4) but (5) Kunle woke early so that he would not miss the bus. (6) Marking guide: both parts must be parallel, for example “She likes neither rice nor beans.” One mark each, two for (6).

**Assessment:** 7 marks.

title: Prefixes, suffixes and synonyms: building and choosing words
body:
**Objectives:** build new words with prefixes and suffixes; explain how a prefix or suffix changes meaning or word class; choose a synonym that fits the context.

**Teaching:** A **prefix** is added before a root and usually changes meaning: *un-* and *dis-* (opposite: *unhappy*, *disagree*), *re-* (again: *rewrite*), *mis-* (wrongly: *misspell*), *pre-* (before: *prepare*), *inter-* (between: *interschool*). A **suffix** is added after a root and often changes the word class: *-ness* (noun: *kindness*), *-ful* (adjective: *careful*), *-ly* (adverb: *slowly*), *-ment* (noun: *enjoyment*), *-able* (adjective: *readable*), *-er/-or* (a person who: *teacher*, *visitor*). A word made this way is a **derivative**. Spelling may change: *happy* becomes *happiness*.

**Synonyms** are words with nearly the same meaning, but they are seldom identical. Choose by context and tone: *big*, *large* and *enormous*; *begin* and *commence* (formal). A synonym must also fit the grammar: “She was glad” can be “She was pleased”, but “glad with” is not the usual pairing.

**Worked example:** *Help* + *less* = *helpless* (adjective: without help); *help* + *ful* = *helpful*. “The teacher was **pleased** with the work” can use the synonym **satisfied**, but not **happy for the work**.

**Practice:** (1) Add a prefix to make the opposite: *possible, honest, agree*. (2) Add a suffix to make a noun from *kind, govern, enjoy*. (3) Give the word class of *carefully* and *carefulness*. (4) Replace the underlined word with a suitable synonym: “The principal was **angry** with the noisy students.” (5) Explain why *thin* and *slim* are not always interchangeable.

**Answers:** (1) impossible, dishonest, disagree. (2) kindness, government, enjoyment. (3) adverb; noun. (4) furious, annoyed or cross. (5) *Slim* is usually complimentary; *thin* can suggest too little weight. Marking: one mark per item; accept any suitable synonym in (4).

**Assessment:** 12 marks. A dictionary with example sentences is the best check for any doubtful synonym.

title: Personal, possessive and demonstrative pronouns
body:
**Objectives:** choose the correct subject or object pronoun; distinguish possessive adjectives from possessive pronouns; use *this, that, these* and *those* for near and far, singular and plural.

**Teaching:**
- **Personal pronouns** — subject: *I, you, he, she, it, we, they*; object: *me, you, him, her, it, us, them*. Use the subject form before the verb and the object form after a verb or preposition: “She gave **him** the book”; “Between you and **me**.”
- **Possessive adjectives** go before a noun: *my, your, his, her, its, our, their*. **Possessive pronouns** stand alone: *mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs*. “This is **my** pen” but “This pen is **mine**.” Never write an apostrophe in *its* (possessive), *yours*, *hers*, *ours* or *theirs*. *It's* means *it is* or *it has*.
- **Demonstrative pronouns:** *this* (singular, near), *these* (plural, near), *that* (singular, far), *those* (plural, far). “**These** are my books; **those** are yours.”

**Worked example:** “Ade and I went to the market. The bag is **ours**, but the oranges are **theirs**.” *I* is a subject; *ours* and *theirs* stand alone.

**Practice:** (1) Choose: (Me and Tola / Tola and I) won the debate. (2) “The red bag is (her / hers).” (3) “(These / This) shoes are too small.” (4) Rewrite using a possessive pronoun: “That book belongs to them.” (5) Correct: “The cat licked it's paw.” (6) Write two sentences about objects near you and far from you using a demonstrative pronoun.

**Answers:** (1) Tola and I (2) hers (3) These (4) That book is theirs. (5) The cat licked its paw. (6) Marking guide: *this/these* for near objects, *that/those* for far objects, with agreement in number. One mark each, two for (6).

**Assessment:** 7 marks.

title: Consonant practice: /ʒ/ and /dʒ/; /d/, /ð/, /θ/ and /z/; /w/ and /j/
body:
**Objectives:** hear and produce /ʒ/ against /dʒ/; separate /d/, /ð/, /θ/ and /z/; separate /w/ from /j/; use minimal pairs for self-correction.

**Note on the scheme:** the original document prints these items in plain ASCII (“/3/ and /d3/”, “/d/, /0/, /z/”). They are read here as /ʒ/ and /dʒ/ (a published text form of the symbols) and, by inference, as /d/, /θ/ and /z/ (the zero as θ). The author's exact intent is not recovered; the related voiced sound /ð/ is added because it is the usual neighbour of /θ/ and /d/.

**Teaching:** (1) /ʒ/ is a continuous, voiced friction sound as in *vision, measure, leisure, television*; /dʒ/ begins with a tongue closure and then releases friction as in *jam, judge, age, bridge*. Minimal pair: **leisure** /ˈleʒə/ and **ledger** /ˈledʒə/. (2) /θ/ is voiceless (*thin, think, three, bath*) and /ð/ is voiced (*this, that, they, breathe*); the tongue tip touches or comes near the upper teeth. Do not replace them with /t/ or /d/ unless you are consciously marking a contrast: **tin/thin**, **day/they**, **breed/breathe**. /z/ is a voiced sound made with the tongue behind the teeth: **breathe/breeze**, **close** (verb) /kləʊz/ and **clothe** /kləʊð/. (3) /w/ rounds the lips (*wet, wear, well*); /j/ raises the tongue toward the hard palate (*yet, year, yell*). Minimal pairs: **wet/yet, wear/year, well/yell**.

**Practice:** listen to a dictionary recording or your teacher, then say each pair twice: leisure/ledger; tin/thin; day/they; breathe/breeze; wet/yet; wear/year. Write the first sound of *measure, jam, think, that, yell, wine* as an IPA symbol.

**Answers:** /ʒ/, /dʒ/, /θ/, /ð/, /j/, /w/. For production, the teacher checks that voiced sounds vibrate lightly at the throat and that /w/ and /j/ are different.

**Assessment:** written identification 6 marks. Pronunciation is assessed separately by listening; accent variation is respected, and the target is the reference contrast, not the learner's background.

title: Consonant contrasts: /t/ and /s/; /s/ and /z/; the nasals /m/, /n/ and /ŋ/
body:
**Objectives:** hear and say /t/ against /s/, /s/ against /z/, and the three nasal consonants; explain how the spelling *ng* relates to /ŋ/.

**Teaching:** (1) **/t/ and /s/.** /t/ is a stop: the tongue blocks the air and releases it. /s/ is continuous friction. Minimal pairs: **tip/sip, tea/sea, tie/sigh**. (2) **/s/ and /z/.** /s/ is voiceless; /z/ is voiced. The spelling letter *s* can stand for either: **sip/zip, peace/peas, price/prize, rice/rise, face/phase**. A final /z/ can shorten the preceding vowel. (3) **Nasals.** /m/ closes the lips, /n/ closes the tongue tip against the ridge, and /ŋ/ closes the back of the tongue against the soft palate. Minimal triples: **sum/sun/sung, ram/ran/rang, sin/sing**. /ŋ/ does not begin English words. In *sing* and *singer* the *ng* is a single sound /ŋ/ with no separate /g/; in *finger* and *longer* the /ŋ/ is followed by /g/.

**Practice:** say each pair twice with a recording: tip/sip; peace/peas; rice/rise; sum/sun/sung; sin/sing. Mark the sound at the end of *ran, rang, ram*. Decide whether *singer* and *finger* rhyme on their first syllable.

**Answers:** /n/, /ŋ/, /m/. *Singer* /ˈsɪŋə/ and *finger* /ˈfɪŋɡə/ do not rhyme exactly because *finger* has /g/.

**Assessment:** written identification 5 marks; production observed separately by a listening teacher. The scheme's printed symbols are not recoverable in the original document, so these are the contrasts named by their words (“/t/ and /s/”, “/s/ and /z/”, “/m/, /n/ and /ŋ/”).

title: Vowel contrasts: /ʌ/ and /ɑː/; /æ/ and /ɜː/; /ɔː/ and /ɒ/; /ʊ/ and /uː/; schwa /ə/
body:
**Objectives:** hear and say five vowel contrasts in the British reference model; locate schwa in unstressed syllables; link a vowel's length and quality to spelling without treating spelling as proof of sound.

**Note on the scheme:** the Second-Term document prints some of these symbols in ASCII or with substituted characters (“/^/ and /a:/”, “/æ/ and /ӡ:/”). They are read here as /ʌ/ and /ɑː/, /æ/ and /ɜː/. This is an inference from the typed forms.

**Teaching:**
- **/ʌ/ and /ɑː/:** short *cup, cut, luck, hut*; long *cart, lark, heart, car*. Minimal pairs: **cut/cart, luck/lark, hut/heart**.
- **/æ/ and /ɜː/:** *cat, bad, ban, hat* against *curt, bird, burn, hurt*.
- **/ɔː/ and /ɒ/:** long *caught, short, port, stalk* against short *cot, shot, pot, stock*.
- **/ʊ/ and /uː/:** short *full, pull, look, could* against long *fool, pool, Luke, cooed*.
- **Schwa /ə/:** the weak vowel of unstressed syllables, as in *about, teacher* /ˈtiːtʃə/, *banana, support, today*. Many small words reduce to schwa when unstressed: *a* /ə/, *to* /tə/, *of* /əv/. Stress controls it: **photograph** /ˈfəʊtəɡrɑːf/ but **photography** /fəˈtɒɡrəfi/.

Do not treat length marks as decoration: the **ː** shows a longer, usually tenser vowel.

**Practice:** say each pair twice with a recording: cut/cart; cat/curt; shot/short; full/fool. Mark every schwa in “The teacher asked about a banana.” Say the words *about, of, today* in isolation and in a sentence and describe the difference.

**Answers:** schwa in *the* (before a consonant), *teacher* (second syllable), *about* (first), *a*, *banana* (first and last). In isolation *of* is /ɒv/ but in a sentence usually /əv/. Marking guide: accept a correct set if the learner names the stressed and unstressed syllables.

**Assessment:** written 6 marks; production and listening checked by a teacher or recording. Accent variation is normal; assess the contrast against the stated reference model.

title: Formal letter: layout, tone and a complete model
body:
**Objectives:** set out a formal letter correctly; use a polite, impersonal tone; contrast formal and informal letters; revise a draft against a checklist.

**Teaching:** A formal letter is written to an official, an employer, a principal or an organisation. Its parts, in order: **sender's address** (top right), **date**, **receiver's title and address** (left), **salutation** (“Dear Sir/Madam” or “Dear Mr Bello”), **subject line** (“Application for the post of …”), **body** in short paragraphs (reason, details, request or action), **closing** and **signature**. Use “Yours faithfully” after “Dear Sir/Madam” and “Yours sincerely” after a named person. Informal letters use a friendly opening, contractions and personal news; formal letters use complete sentences, no slang and no contractions.

**Model (original):**
14 Unity Road,
Ibadan.
18 October 2026.

The Principal,
Hillview Secondary School,
Ibadan.

Dear Sir,

**Request for permission to use the school library on Saturdays**

I am a JSS 3 student writing to request permission to use the school library on Saturday mornings. Many of us have no quiet place to study at home before the examination period.

If permission is granted, I will be responsible for keeping to the opening hours and for returning every book on the same day. I would be grateful for your consideration.

Yours faithfully,
Ayo Adeyemi
(JSS 3 B)

**Practice:** (1) Name the part that tells the reader what the letter is about. (2) Which closing follows “Dear Madam”? (3) Rewrite the informal sentence “Hi! Just wanted to ask if we can have a trip” as a formal sentence. (4) Write a formal letter of about 120 words asking the vice-principal for a debating club meeting room. Use the full layout.

**Answers:** (1) the subject line (2) Yours faithfully (3) “I am writing to ask whether the class may be permitted to organise a trip.” (4) Marking guide (15 marks): layout 5, tone and formality 4, clear request and reason 3, spelling and punctuation 3. Penalise slang and contractions in a formal text.

**Assessment:** a layout checklist and a short drafted letter. Real-world acceptance by a school office is not tested.

title: Essay writing review: narrative, descriptive and argumentative structure
body:
**Objectives:** plan and structure a narrative, a descriptive and an argumentative essay; write an introduction, body paragraphs and conclusion; revise using a short marking guide.

**Teaching:**
- **Narrative essay:** tells what happened in time order. Parts: setting and characters (opening), problem or event (build-up), turning point (climax) and result or lesson (ending). Use past tense, a clear order and a few vivid details.
- **Descriptive essay:** describes a person, place or thing so the reader can picture it. Plan by sense or by position: sight, sound, smell, touch, taste; or near to far. Use specific nouns, adjectives and comparisons. Do not tell a story.
- **Argumentative essay:** argues one side. Parts: **introduction** states the topic and your position; **body** has one reason per paragraph with a supporting example; one paragraph answers an opposing view; **conclusion** restates the position. Use linking words such as *firstly, moreover, however, therefore, in conclusion*.

**Model plan (original) — “Should students use phones in school?” (argumentative):** Introduction: phones help and distract, but strict rules are needed. Reason 1: access to dictionaries and learning apps. Reason 2: safety and contact with parents. Opposing view: distraction in class, answered by locked-away phones during lessons. Conclusion: allow phones only under school rules.

**Practice:** (1) Which type of essay uses mainly the senses? (2) Which type needs a conclusion that restates a position? (3) Write a plan for a descriptive essay “My favourite subject” with three paragraphs. (4) Write a 150-word narrative beginning: “The generator coughed and the lights went out.” (5) Mark your own draft against the guide.

**Answers:** (1) descriptive (2) argumentative (3) Marking guide: introduction naming the subject, body paragraphs on sights/sounds/feelings or on topics and teachers, conclusion giving the reason it is favourite. (4) Marking guide (10 marks): clear time order 3, interesting details 3, tense control 2, spelling and punctuation 2. (5) Check the draft for introduction, body, conclusion and linking words.

**Assessment:** the pupil's own draft marked with the guide. The model plans are original teaching examples, not past examination scripts.

title: Critical reading: purpose, facts and opinions, and word meaning in context
body:
**Objectives:** state a writer's purpose; separate fact from opinion; work out a word's meaning from its context; read critically by asking what evidence supports a claim.

**Teaching:** Before reading, ask: *Why was this written — to inform, to persuade, to entertain or to describe?* While reading, mark **facts** (can be checked: “The school has 600 students”) and **opinions** (judgements: “The school is the best in the town”). Opinion signals: *I think, in my view, best, worst, should, probably*. To find a word's meaning in context, read the clause before and after it, look for synonyms, opposites or examples, and test your guess by putting it in place of the word.

**Passage (original):** “The new market stalls opened on Monday. There are forty of them, and every stall has a roof. I believe this is the best change the council has made in years, because traders no longer sell in the rain. Some people say the rent is too high; that complaint is exaggerated. A shopper walking through the lane saw that the aisles were wide enough for two carts and that vendors were unusually cheerful.”

**Practice:** (1) What is the writer's main purpose? (2) Give one fact and one opinion. (3) What does *exaggerated* probably mean? (4) What does *unusually* tell you about the vendors' mood? (5) What question would you ask to test the writer's claim that this is “the best change”?

**Answers:** (1) to persuade readers that the new stalls are a good change (2) Fact: there are forty stalls (or every stall has a roof). Opinion: “the best change the council has made in years”. (3) made to seem bigger or more serious than it is, from the contrast with “complaint” and the writer's dismissal (4) the vendors were cheerful more than normal (5) Accept: what evidence compares this change with earlier changes, and how do traders and shoppers feel? Marking: one mark each, with an extra mark for giving a reason in (3).

**Assessment:** 6 marks. The passage is original teaching material, not an examination passage.

title: Literature review: fiction and non-fiction, poetry, and key literary terms
body:
**Objectives:** distinguish fiction from non-fiction; recognise poetry's features; use the basic literary terms to describe a short text.

**Teaching:** **Fiction** is invented writing (novels, short stories, many plays). **Non-fiction** deals with real events, facts or real people (biography, news, essay). **Poetry** uses lines, sound and images to compress meaning. Key terms: **plot** (the sequence of events), **setting** (time and place), **character** (a person in the story), **theme** (the central idea), **narrator** (who tells it), **imagery** (language that appeals to the senses), **simile** (comparison with *like* or *as*), **metaphor** (saying one thing is another), **personification** (giving human qualities to a non-human), **rhyme** (matching end sounds) and **stanza** (a group of lines).

**Poem (original) — “Harmattan morning”:**
The dust lies gold on the window sill,
The sun is a coin in a hazy sky;
Cold fingers of wind wander over the hill,
And the market birds call as they hurry by.

**Practice:** (1) Is a biography fiction or non-fiction? (2) Name the simile or metaphor in line 2. (3) Identify an example of personification in line 3. (4) Give the rhyme scheme. (5) State one theme or feeling of the poem. (6) Define *theme* in one sentence.

**Answers:** (1) non-fiction (2) “The sun is a coin” is a metaphor. (3) “Cold fingers of wind” (4) ABAB (*sill/hill* and *sky/by*). Mark ABAB if the learner lists A for lines 1 and 3 and B for 2 and 4. (5) the quiet beauty of harmattan morning, with accepted variations (6) the central idea or message of a text. Marking: one mark each.

**Assessment:** 6 marks. The poem is original teaching material and is not offered as a traditional or examination poem.

title: Studying any recommended prose or drama text: plot, character, setting and theme
body:
**Objectives:** apply a reusable method to any recommended prose text or play; summarise plot, describe characters with evidence, identify setting and state a theme with support.

**Important status:** the school's recommended prose and drama texts are not identified in the supplied materials. The existing *The Gift of the Magi* and *The Proposal* lessons are labelled stand-ins. This lesson is a text-independent method. It does not replace the school's book and does not claim to cover it.

**Teaching (method):**
1. **Plot:** write five sentences — beginning, problem, rising events, turning point, result.
2. **Characters:** pick two characters. For each, write one trait and one proof (an action or a line of speech). *A trait without proof is only an opinion.*
3. **Setting:** state when and where it happens and how it affects events or mood.
4. **Theme:** state the central idea as a sentence, such as “honesty costs something but is worth it”, and give one event that supports it.
5. **Drama only:** list stage directions, dialogue and any change of scene; say how dialogue reveals character.

**Worked example (original):** In a story where a boy returns a lost wallet at personal cost, *plot* = he finds the wallet; he is tempted; he returns it; the owner rewards him by offering friendship. *Character* = Ibrahim is honest (he walks two kilometres to return it). *Theme* = honesty is more valuable than money.

**Practice:** choose your recommended text, or use the Study my text screen to paste a passage. Write the five plot sentences, one character with proof, the setting and one theme with support.

**Answers / marking guide (10 marks):** plot in correct order 3, character with evidence 3, setting 2, theme with support 2. Reject a theme that is only a topic word such as “honesty”.

**Assessment:** teacher marking from the learner's text. This tool does not establish that the intended text was studied.

title: English exam-style practice with answers (original questions for revision)
body:
**Objectives:** practise the question types that appear in school English examinations — comprehension, vocabulary, grammar, speech work and literature — and check answers against a marking guide.

**Status:** these are new practice questions written for revision. They are **not** past examination questions and do not reproduce any examination board's paper. Third-Term BECE scheduling belongs to a later batch; this resource is a tagged practice set for that later use and is placed here only so it can be reached now.

**Comprehension (original passage):** “Ade's bicycle had a flat tyre on the morning of the examination. He did not panic. He pushed it to a repairer and waited, though he knew he might arrive late. When he reached school, the examiner had not yet distributed the papers. He sat down breathless but calm.”
1. Why did Ade not panic? 2. What does *distributed* mean? 3. Pick out the adjective in the last sentence.

**Grammar and vocabulary:** 4. Change to the passive: “The repairer mended the tyre.” 5. Add a question tag: “Ade is punctual, ___?” 6. Choose the synonym of *calm*: (tense / peaceful / loud). 7. Give the opposite of *panic*.

**Speech work:** 8. Which word has the vowel /ɜː/: *cat, bird, hot*?

**Literature:** 9. Define *theme*. 10. Name the rhyme scheme of this couplet: “The rain is soft, the evening long, / We sit together, sing a song.”

**Answers:** 1. He knew the problem could be solved; accept a sensible reason from the text. 2. given out, handed out 3. breathless (or calm) 4. The tyre was mended by the repairer. 5. isn't he 6. peaceful 7. stay calm, relax (accept *calm*) 8. bird 9. the central idea or message 10. AA (a rhyming couplet). Marking: one mark each, 10 in total.

**Assessment:** 10 marks. A set of original questions practises the skills but does not prove knowledge of an examination paper. Authentic past papers still need lawful source provenance.

title: Àṣà ìgbéyàwó: marriage in Yoruba culture and the steps the school lists
body:
**Objectives:** explain what ìgbéyàwó means in Yoruba culture; name the school's listed steps; explain, with evidence, the steps that credible sources describe (ìwádìí, alárinà, ìtọrọ, ìdána, ijohen, iya gbo baba gbo, and ibale with a caution); note that the other steps are named but not explained here.

**Teaching:** Ìgbéyàwó is the union of a man and a woman as husband and wife in line with Yoruba custom. The school note gives six values that support a good marriage: ìfẹ́sọ́nà (courtship), ìfaradà (perseverance), sùúrù (patience), ìpamọ́ra (tolerance), ìgbọ̀ràn-ẹni-yé (understanding) and ìfẹ́ àìsetàn (unconditional love).

The school's list of fifteen steps is printed in plain spelling: *ifojusode, iwaadi, alarina, isihun, ijohen, itoro, baba gbo iya gbo, idana, ipalemo, ifa iyawo, ojo igbeyawo, ese iyawo wiwe, ibale, ikorun, ojo keje*. The school's tone marks and the exact spelling of some entries are not recoverable, and different Yoruba towns and families order and practise the steps differently.

**Steps explained from credible sources:**
- **Ìwádìí** — inquiry: the groom's family finds out about the woman's family, character and background.
- **Alárinà** — the go-between (the word means “one who goes between”): a trusted person who carries messages between the two families.
- **Ìtọrọ** — the formal introduction and request: the groom's family comes to ask for the woman in marriage; it is described as the first part of the traditional marriage.
- **Ìdána** — sources differ. A West African Examinations Council examiners' report describes it as the ceremony in which the groom's side pays the bride-price and presents gifts; two academic articles (Odejobi 2013; Idowu 2022) list it as the engagement stage. Both readings are given; the school's own meaning is not known.
- **Ijohen** — the first instalment of the bride-wealth, given by the groom's family to the bride's family, which seals the agreement once the inquiry has gone well (Odejobi 2013, citing Akinloye 1999). The article prints it without tone marks.
- **Baba gbo iya gbo** — the school's order of words. Sources print 'iya gbo, baba gbo': a small fee or payment meaning 'the mother and the father agree', a sign of the bride's parents' consent (DiscoverYoruba; Odejobi 2013). Amounts vary.
- **Ibale** (caution) — Idowu (2022) prints 'ibaale' as another name for the bride-eve stage, together with 'aisuniyawo'. This is one source and its link to the school's 'ibale' is not confirmed; do not teach it as settled.

The sources print these terms without tone marks, so none is tone-marked here.

**Not explained here:** *ifojusode, isihun, ipalemo, ifa iyawo, ese iyawo wiwe, ikorun* and *ojo keje* (and *ojo igbeyawo*, the wedding day, which needs no source). The supplied school note names them but gives no explanation. Searches of two academic articles and DiscoverYoruba on 19 October 2026 did not find them as marriage stages; a related term in DiscoverYoruba, omo-orun (a cloth knot tied round the couple's hands), is a different word and is not evidence for *ikorun*. A Yoruba teacher or elder must explain them before they are taught. Do not invent a meaning.

**Practice (ìbéèrè):** (1) Define ìgbéyàwó. (2) Name three of the six values of a good marriage. (3) Explain the role of the alárinà. (4) What happens at ìdána? (5) Why should a pupil say “the families I know do it this way” rather than “all Yoruba do it this way”? (6) What does the payment called iya gbo, baba gbo show?

**Answers:** (1) the union of man and woman as husband and wife by Yoruba custom (2) any three of the values above (3) a go-between who carries messages and helps the two families talk (4) accept either reading given in the lesson: bride-price and gifts are presented, or the engagement is held; sources differ (5) because customs differ by town and family (6) that the bride's mother and father agree. Marking: one mark each.

**Assessment:** 6 marks. Written recall does not replace learning from elders or participation in actual ceremonies.

title: Ìrànra-ẹni-lọ́wọ́: practice on cooperative work and thrift
body:
**Objectives:** revise the Yoruba ways of helping one another (ọwẹ́, àáró, àjọ, ẹ̀ṣúsú, owó ẹlé, san-án-díẹ̀-díẹ̀, fífi ọmọ tàbí ǹkan ìní dúró); explain each with one example; use them correctly in sentences; judge how modern life changes them.

**Teaching (revision of the school's list):**
- **Ọwẹ́** — a communal work gathering: a person invites relatives, friends and neighbours to help with a big task, usually farm work. It is repaid by joining others' ọwẹ́ and by hosting.
- **Àáró** — a rotating work arrangement among friends: each person's farm is worked on by the group on one day until every member has had a turn. Food or drink is not required, but the work must go round.
- **Àjọ** and **ẹ̀ṣúsú** — contribution savings: members each contribute a fixed amount at set intervals and each in turn receives the whole collection. Trust and a trusted collector are essential.
- **Owó ẹlé**, **san-án-díẹ̀-díẹ̀** and **fífi ọmọ tàbí ǹkan ìní dúró** — borrowing and repayment practices named in the school's list. The last historically meant giving a child or property as security for a debt; teach it as history and discuss why a child must not be treated as security today.

**Source status (checked 19 October 2026).** The two marriage pages first listed as sources for this lesson do not support it and have been removed. Credible sources found so far support only these points: àáró is a farming cooperative society (Yorubaname entry Alókoláàró); a related entry describes ọ̀wẹ̀ as a society of elders whose members work on one another's farms in rotation (Yorubaname entry Ọlọ́wẹ, spelled with different tone marks from ọwẹ́); and ẹ̀ṣúsú is a Yoruba savings club (eHRAF Yoruba documents). The WAEC Yoruba paper 2 (May/June 2014, Q12) names àáró together with ìsìngbà and gbàmí-o-ràmí as traditional cooperative concepts. The sources do not tell ọwẹ́ and àáró apart as this lesson does (the lesson gives rotation to àáró; the Yorubaname entries tie rotation to ọ̀wẹ̀ and give àáró no detail), and owó ẹlé, san-án-díẹ̀-díẹ̀ and fífi ọmọ tàbí ǹkan ìní dúró are not source-checked. Treat the distinctions above as the lesson's reading, not as settled, until a Yoruba teacher confirms them.

**Open item:** the scheme's word *obese* (First-Term week 5) is not in the school's own explanation and its intended meaning is not established. It is not guessed here. Ask a Yoruba teacher what the school intended; if the intended item is a thrift or work practice, add it to this list.

**Practice (ìbéèrè):** (1) Match: ọwẹ́, àáró, ẹ̀ṣúsú with (a) friends take turns working on each other's farms, (b) neighbours are invited to help with a large task, (c) members each give money and take turns to receive the total. (2) Give one benefit of group work. (3) Give one risk of ẹ̀ṣúsú. (4) Explain why a person's child cannot be used as security today. (5) Name a modern form of cooperative saving.

**Answers:** (1) ọwẹ́–(b), àáró–(a), ẹ̀ṣúsú–(c). (2) work is done faster and bonds are strengthened. (3) a member may fail to pay or the collector may misuse the money. (4) children have rights and are not property; modern law and values forbid it. (5) a cooperative society, a credit union or a savings group. Marking: one mark each, with a reason expected in (4).

**Assessment:** 5 marks. Tone marks on the Yoruba terms need a Yoruba teacher's check, because the school source is printed without them.

sources.title: Alókoláàró — Yorubaname (àáró: cooperative society around farming)
